show-leah-thomas.html: Leah Thomas lines the ceiling with vintage parachutes so that everyone underneath them can picture the world they are building together. She is an environmental author, advocate, and content creator who works at the intersection of climate and culture. She hosts Earth Sessions climate concerts, is finishing a book on ecofeminism called Earth as Mother, and runs a local crafting club where people learn to mend and sew, because joy and sustainable skill-building belong together. In this conversation Leah and Katherine walk the full arc of her work: what it means to live at the intersection of climate and culture, why she believes how we treat the earth mirrors how we treat women, and how radical imagination changed her from someone who could dismantle every broken system to someone who could also ask what world she wanted to build. They talk about the hidden story of Nicodemus, Kansas, a thriving town built by freed African Americans that Leah discovered as a summer park ranger, and the reckoning that unfolded when her hometown of Ferguson became a hashtag. They talk about Earth Sessions, and nature as her church, and Katherine shivering as she hands that back. This episode is for anyone who has felt worn down by the weight of fixing the world. Leah offers something gentle and fierce at the same time: the reminder that rest, play, and radical imagination are its foundation. Picture a room with vintage parachutes strung across the ceiling, soft and billowing, so that everyone underneath them is standing inside something whimsical and green. There is a rap duo in one corner who also happen to tend a community garden. There is a grassroots environmental organiser at a table nearby. Someone is leaving with a free book about environmental justice they did not know they wanted. The scientists who usually speak on world stages, usually tense, usually braced to be ignored, are allowed, for one evening, to soften. Leah Thomas calls these gatherings Earth Sessions. They are concerts, and they are also exercises in a thing she names carefully: radical imagination. The set design is deliberate. The questions she hands people are deliberate too. What does a future rooted in renewable energy look like? What does the solar punk future look like? She wants attendees to walk in braced for a lecture about collapse and walk out having rehearsed, with their whole bodies, the greener world they are working toward. For a long time, that was the part she could not do. Leah is an environmental author, advocate, and content creator in Los Angeles who works, in her own phrase, at the intersections of climate and culture. She is also a self-described introvert who shares her home with two cats named Cosmo and Sunny, and who treats joy, rest, and play as part of the work. Once you have met her, the parachutes make sense. She is building the room she wishes the whole movement could stand inside. A mud swing, a tennis coach, and a mother who paid for the hard books Leah grew up in St. Louis, Missouri, right in the middle of the country. She was the kind of child who caught toads and kept them, dug holes in the backyard with shovels taken from the garage, and once turned the family swing set into a mud swing out of some weird and glorious idea that arrived and would not leave. Her parents said, do whatever you want. She is grateful for that line to this day. Her father is a tennis coach, a creative with a head full of business ideas, some wonderful and some less so, the kind of man who will always pick up the phone and give her a pep talk. Her mother is a therapist who works in a school district. Most of her family are educators. They were also activists, though Leah did not know that was unusual. I didn’t know that it wasn’t normal to have activist parents. Like, they took me to protests when I was like two years old. Once, her mother offered her twenty-five dollars to read a radical book about race in America and write a report on it. Once, her sister passed a petition around elementary school asking for more recess time and got in trouble for it, and their father came to the school to say his daughters had the right to protest. A strong sense of justice settled into Leah early, so woven through everything that she did not recognise it as activism. It simply felt, as she puts it, like something in her body she could not ignore. The town that became a hashtag At nineteen, studying environmental science, Leah watched her own corner of Missouri break open. The police shooting of Michael Brown happened in Ferguson, about ten minutes from her house. People called to ask if she had known him. She had not, but he was so close. I naively at the time thought as a child that we were almost moving towards this post-racial society and most people were on the right side of history. And then to just see that illusion kind of shatter. She went off to begin her degree while her hometown filled with protests and arrests and journalists being detained. And something in her advocacy began to feel incomplete. If she cared about clean air and clean water, she could not care about them only in the abstract. The communities carrying the heaviest environmental burdens, Black and Brown, Indigenous, rural, urban, were the ones her work had to reach, or it was not finished. The shaping went on. A summer as a park ranger took her to Nicodemus, Kansas, one of the least visited parks in the whole system, a town built after slavery by freed African Americans who followed the stars out of the South and raised homes, farms, churches, and schools from the soil. A hidden story, she calls it, and one that gave her empowerment. There is a chapter she has said she will write about fully in her next book, one she carries with care: her sister lost a friend to domestic violence, and Leah has known that weight herself. Part of why she keeps returning to the link between harm to the earth and harm to women is the number of people who have answered her with their own stories, so casually, so many of them carrying the same weight in silence. What she has built, and what she is building Today Leah works across climate and culture in several directions at once. She is writing a book called Earth as Mother, due out next year, an exploration of ecofeminism rooted in a single conviction: a better future has to be one that treats women and the planet well, because the two are bound together. She hosts Earth Sessions, the parachute concerts that put R&B artists, rappers, scientists, and gardeners in the same joyful room. And while she is deep in the heavier research, she keeps herself tethered to something light. She runs a local crafting club where people gather to learn mending and sewing, ordinary sustainable skills, hands busy, lives a little greener. She makes environmental justice something a person can see themselves inside: creative, communal, emotionally alive. How we treat the earth, how we treat each other Leah returns again and again to one mirror. The ways we treat the planet reflect the ways we treat women. She noticed it in the research: domestic violence rises after natural disasters and climate catastrophe, isolating women further in the hardest moments. Stress goes up, fear goes up, and the harm lands where it always lands. Katherine named her own version of the same pattern: the planet degraded, the economy fracturing, people turning on each other, and now AI accelerating the noise until the anxiety is more than human beings were built to carry. The exploitation of each other and the exploitation of the earth come from the same root, the same survival-based, fear-based ground. The two of them could hear it in each other’s language. And then Leah said where she goes to put it down. She is an anxious person, she said, and when she steps into the sun, into nature, it grounds her. It is the closest thing she has to church. Katherine shivered from head to toe as she handed it back: nature is the ultimate healer, the ultimate church, the place where we remember we are nature, one with it. This is the thread the whole conversation hangs from. The mud swing of a St. Louis childhood and the spiritual ground she stands on now are the same ground. The toads she protected as a girl and the women she protects in her work are the same instinct. Nothing in her is separate from nature, because she never was. What her life is asking us to see Leah Thomas will tell you she does not know exactly where the work is going. She just knows it is what she is supposed to be doing right now, and she is trusting that. Her dream is to teach, to become a professor, to live in a little forest and pop out occasionally with a book. For the foreseeable future, as she puts it with a grin, she will keep yapping about women and nature. What she keeps showing us is that joy is not stolen time. After one global conference, she took a room full of climate activists her own age to an underground club in Scotland and got them into a conga line. She wanted them to carry their wholeness into the work, that play and fun belong there too, sustaining it rather than competing with it. Katherine said she wanted to be in that conga line too. There is a particular grace in a person who honours exactly where she is. So many of us do not. We rush past the present toward the version of the life we have decided counts. Leah holds her dream loosely and her today with both hands, writing the book, running the crafting club, stringing up the parachutes so the rest of us can stand under them and picture the softer world long enough to start believing in it. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Leah Sit with this one when you have an afternoon and a window with some light in it. It runs about an hour, and it moves the way a good long walk moves, from toads and mud swings to Earth Sessions and ecofeminism, with two cats wandering through and purring on the microphone. It is warm, and it is honest, and it leaves you gentler than it found you. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I feel the ways in which we treat the earth really mirrors the ways in which we treat women. So that’s also something I’m very passionate about. I want you guys to know that you don’t have to give your youth away to this movement and that you can be a whole human being and part of you can be an activist but you still deserve to have play and fun and all those sorts of things. It feels so grounding and I feel like it’s the closest thing that I have to church right now because I haven’t gone in a very long time. So it’s a very spiritual connection I would say. Leah Thomas is an environmental author, advocate, activist, and content creator based in Los Angeles, working at what she calls the intersections of climate and culture. She is the author of The Intersectional Environmentalist (2022) and founder of the platform of the same name, and her next book, Earth as Mother, an exploration of ecofeminism, is forthcoming. She hosts Earth Sessions, a series of whimsical climate concerts rooted in radical imagination, and runs a local crafting club teaching sustainable skills like mending and sewing. Raised in St. Louis, Missouri, by activist, educator parents, she makes environmental justice creative, communal, and accessible. She helps people see themselves within the work and within the natural world they belong to.
show-john-abbott.html: Ask John Abbott to draw his company and he draws a sun. At the centre is Centered, a heart-centred marketing and sales agency that amplifies speakers and facilitators around the world. Around it turn the planets, each division running on its own, all of them in orbit around warmth rather than command. This conversation travels the whole arc: how John built by striving, lost everything, and found freedom in the release, and why he now believes that generosity, not pressure, is the truest way to serve. John leads Centered, working with speakers and facilitators from Tony Robbins to Michael Beckwith, helping them reach far more of the people their work was born to serve. Through the Giving Model he discovered in 2013, he invites people into a conversation rather than a transaction. He was raised largely alone on a rural South African farm during apartheid, a boy who stepped between bullies and smaller kids, who later published suppressed history on CD-ROM as Nelson Mandela walked free, and who built a multi-company empire before losing it all and finding something unexpected on the other side. In 2016, he shut everything down, committed to meditate daily until there was nothing left in him that needed to drive anything forward, and waited for the cinders to go cold so the phoenix could rise. In this conversation John and Katherine move through the planetary image at the heart of his company, the Giving Model and what it opened, how he sees money and abundance and the practice of getting out of the way, the 2016 reset, and his closing wish: that people get to live through the eyes of a single statement. Ask John Abbott to draw his company and he draws a sun. At the centre is Centered, the core, the part that radiates resource and light outward. Around it turn the planets, the different divisions, each running on its own and all of them working together. As one moves, it moves the others. As the others move, they move it. A community held in orbit by warmth rather than command. The way I see it and the way that I actually describe it is like a planetary system that in the center is centered or the core part of the organization, which is the sun, which provides the resource out to all of the different planetary divisions and each one of those divisions essentially are running on their own but they all are working together. This is a man who has thought a long time about how light travels between people. Centered is a heart-centred marketing and sales agency, and its work is amplification: helping extraordinary speakers and facilitators, from Tony Robbins to Michael Beckwith, reach far more of the people their work was born to serve. In John’s own words, his role is to shine the light on his team and on these human beings. When Katherine asks him to introduce himself, he does it through his values, in his own words: “a sense of adventure,” a curiosity for people, and a love and hope for our humanity and for our evolution. The kid who said: this is not on He was born and raised in South Africa, an English father, a Sicilian family on his mother’s side, and a childhood spent mostly alone on a rural farm during apartheid. He loved connection and he loved aloneness in equal measure, the two moving through him “like breathing in and breathing out.” You go out into the community, you enjoy it, and then you breathe out and relax back into your own space. Even as a small child with a big personality, he could not make sense of the hatred around him. He did not understand why people spoke so badly of the African people, why they were treated the way they were. He rebelled. He became the kid who said no, this is not on, we don’t treat each other that way. I would often put myself between the bully and the little kid who is sometimes bigger than me. And that’s also why I’ve got a broken nose. Multiple. The refusal ran deeper than the schoolyard. In 1992, as Nelson Mandela was released, John’s small tech company won the contract to publish the suppressed Mayibuye archive on CD-ROM. Sitting inside that centre in Cape Town, reading the true history against the version he had been taught in school, he realised he had been programmed his whole life, that the media and the books and the curriculum had all carried a different story than what actually happened. Once he saw it, he could not stop seeing it. The boy who stepped between the bully and the smaller kid had found the thing he would spend his life refusing: people being manipulated. Letting the last cinder go cold For a long stretch, the refusal lived in him as anger. He built and drove and made things happen. Six companies, close to a hundred staff, deep in debt to the banks. When the global financial crisis came, all of it collapsed, and John dropped into a few million dollars of debt. He fought to save it, and the more he fought, the more he lost. A finance mentor slapped him awake down the phone, and he surrendered it all. He remembers standing at the airport with everything gone, one bag, his ticket in his hand, and a wave of freedom flooding his whole body. He had spent his life believing freedom was something he was building toward. It arrived in the release. This moment of knowing that I do not owe anyone any money. Actually, the freedom was when all of that was released. But the deeper reset came later, in 2016, in Bali. He kept finding himself caught in the same loops, needing to hold everything together, needing to be the one who made things happen, still carrying the old upset. He stopped. He closed everything down and committed to meditate every single day until he could feel there was nothing in him that needed to drive anything forward. Someone he was speaking to at the time gave him an image he still carries. Allow the cinders to become cold ash. While there is any heat left, that is your clue that you are not there yet. And the moment the last cinder goes out, your phoenix will rise and you will feel an overwhelming call to purpose. Over six months of doing very little, closing the business, and losing more than the business, that is what happened. In the surrender, he came home to himself. It is why the company is called Centered, and it is why the word matters to him the way it does. “I’m always off-center. Always off-center. Coming back to centered. Coming back.” A return, practised daily. The giving model The clearest expression of everything he had learned arrived in 2013, in flow, in a moment his team did not agree with. He was two weeks out from filling the last places in a programme and out of ideas. He asked a question nobody on his team expected: what if we gave one away? He emailed 450 people and invited them to apply for a giveaway in 200 words: tell me how this programme would change your child’s life. He gave them twelve hours and went to bed. The applications that came back floored him. One mother wrote about her daughter, and the reading of it opened something John still carries. When he called to tell her she had won, he was already in tears before she picked up. Out of that came the Giving Model, now rolled out across hundreds of campaigns. It is a bridge. Many of the people with the truest missions, the ones showing up for humanity, are often the least resourced. The giveaway becomes a portal, a way to reach people with real work to do and connect them with the tools to do it better. This is the sun’s light reaching the farthest orbit, the planet no other campaign would ever have touched. When Katherine asked him what happens to those lives, he talked about people being seen, being told, I hear what you are up for and I wanted to back you. He measures his work in ripples, not returns. His attitude toward money follows from this. It is all abundant anyway, he says, and we have just been programmed toward scarcity. When a knock comes, he deepens into trust rather than control. He asks his partner, aloud, I wonder what the universe is going to do now to sort that out. His job, as he puts it, is to get out of the way of it as fast as possible. Surrender as the beginning The collapse of the companies was a collapse of ego and identity, the death of a self he had believed was who he was. The reset in Bali was the surrender that let a new calling rise. He built by extraction, lost everything, and found freedom in letting go, and now he teaches that generosity is the truest way to serve. Katherine put it to him plainly: the fracturing between us, the gulf between those who have and those who do not, what we are doing to the planet, the disinformation accelerated now by AI, all of it together producing a level of anxiety human beings were never meant to carry. John looked at all of it and said it could not be more perfect that we are experiencing this now, because it means we are ready. With this much pressure, he said, we become the diamonds. He gave Katherine his wish for humanity, a statement he has held since 2010. Everything is perfect. Our job is to see the perfection in the perceived imperfection. Watch him in the conversation and you see the sun he drew. He stands at the centre so that others can do their work in the world. Katherine put three words on him at the close that stay with you: defiantly curious, loving, and a man who finds the perfection because he trusts it is there. A man who fought bullies as a child and now refuses, at scale, to let anyone be manipulated, and who learned that the light travels furthest when you give it away. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with John This is an unhurried conversation, a little under ninety minutes, and it moves at the pace of someone who has learned to surrender rather than strive. John speaks with warmth and honesty about the solar system he built, the collapses that shaped him, and the daily practice of coming back to centre. Settle in with a cup of something and let it unfold. There is no hurry. The library is always here. It is all abundant anyway. We’ve just been programmed to be in this place of scarcity. The more vulnerable I am, the more I give others permission to be vulnerable. Everything is perfect. Our job is to see the perfection in the perceived imperfection. John Abbott is the founder of Centered, a heart-centred marketing and sales agency that amplifies the reach of speakers, teachers, and facilitators whose work is changing the way people see themselves and the world, from Tony Robbins to Michael Beckwith. Born and raised in South Africa and now based in Bali, he discovered the Giving Model in 2013, an approach that invites people into conversation rather than pressuring them into a purchase, so those with real missions can access the tools to do their work better. He works alongside his partner across summits and live gatherings that bring people together to shift how they see themselves and the world. He leads with adventure, curiosity, and a lasting hope for our shared evolution.
show-judy-wicks.html: On a two-acre homestead in Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, Judy Wicks and her daughter Grace are turning a lawn into a meadow. She is nearly eighty. She has not stopped. Judy spent twenty-six years building the White Dog Cafe from a muffin and coffee shop into a two-hundred-seat, farm-to-table pioneer. She went on to found Fair Food, the Business Alliance for Local Living Economies, and All Together Now Pennsylvania, and to write Good Morning Beautiful Business. Through all of it, she says, she was doing one thing: building the beloved community. This conversation walks backward through the life that built her. A tomboy childhood in Ingomar, Pennsylvania, who asked every birthday for tar paper and a can of nails and built a new fort every year from age nine to high school graduation. A near-year among the Yupik in Chefornak, Alaska, that showed her what an economy of sharing actually looks like. A marriage she left when she could no longer find herself inside it, and a stranger who pointed her toward the restaurant business by accident. The moment when she gave her proprietary farm sources to her competitors and went from me to we. And the homestead she and Grace are building together, which her daughter calls her last fort. This episode is for anyone who has felt they don’t fit where they were placed, and needs proof that following that refusal can become a whole life of contribution and joy. On a hill in the Chestnut Hill section of Philadelphia, a green lawn has become a meadow. There are birches and maples and a red bud, peach and pawpaw and cherry, an arbor with wisteria that bloomed so hard this spring that Judy Wicks calls it gorgeous and means it. Her daughter Grace, a professional gardener, cut the paths through the tall growth at their level so that the older friends can walk. One section of the hill has been levelled into a plateau. That is where the bar goes, and the food, and the fire pit, and the stage when there are performers. Judy calls it the party plateau. She is nearly eighty. She has not stopped. Soon there will be a Black-Eyed Susan party, because the Black-Eyed Susans are about to burst. There will be a Liberty and Justice for All Ball, its second year, after 250 people came the first. Everyone brings their own plate, their own cup, their own wine, and hops from table to table meeting people they have never met. Some of the tables are set for guests who can make it down the stairs and no further. This is what she does. She has always done this. “My life has been about building the beloved community,” she told Katherine. “That whatever I’m doing, whether it’s running my restaurant or having parties, what I’m really doing is building the beloved community.” She said it as though she had only just noticed it, and in a way she had. But it is the through line of an entire life. She has built one fort after another, every one of them a world made on purpose to hold the people she loves and the people who are different from her, which for Judy is the same joy. The girl who wanted tar paper and a can of nails She grew up in Ingomar, a small town in western Pennsylvania, an all-American, Norman Rockwell sort of childhood, and from the start she wanted none of what a girl in the fifties was handed. Every year on her birthday she asked for a roll of tar paper and a can of nails, the same request, every year, because what she wanted was nothing a girl in the fifties was supposed to want. At nine she found a pile of felled sassafras trunks her father had cleared, took his saw, cut them to length, lashed them into a square between four standing trees and built her first fort out of logs, with a roof and a trapdoor at the top. When bullies smashed the roof in, she ran through the woods to the clubhouse they were building, saw the new glass windows they had just installed, and broke every one of them. Nobody said a word afterward, because the boys could never admit they had attacked a girl first. She had got them back, and she had got them back for a reason. Her father was a lawyer, the son of a lawyer, a man with justice in him. Her mother was a Girl Scout leader who stepped forward and led the flag ceremony and gave people their chores, and who ran what she proudly called the loudest classroom in the school. They did not think it was appropriate for a girl to build forts. They never took a single photograph of them. And they never once stopped her. “I think it was a matter of trust,” Judy said. They trusted her to have her own set of values that would keep her from harming anyone, and so they let her be exactly who she was. The red light that turned her into a restaurateur At ten, watching the boys play the baseball she was not allowed to play, she chose the best player on the field and decided she would marry him. She lifted the lid of her school desk, crossed her own name off her tablet, and wrote Mrs. Richard Hain over it. She did marry him. They joined VISTA and spent nearly a year among the Yupik in the village of Chefornak, Alaska, hundreds of miles from any road, waiting together for the mail plane. There she saw a culture built entirely on sharing and giving, where if you admired what someone wore they simply took it off and handed it to you. When the volunteers took the side of the Eskimos over a pipeline and over the men sent to Vietnam, they were fired, given forty-eight hours to leave the state. Judy still keeps the newspaper clipping framed in her bathroom, her badge of honour. Back in Philadelphia she and her husband started a store for students. She drove a Volvo station wagon to New York and filled it with cool things she liked. When she asked how much money they were making, her husband patted her on the head and said, “Don’t you worry your pretty little head about that.” A pat on the head in answer to a direct question about her own business. That was the door. She borrowed the car to drive to Florida and make the break, ran a red light half a block from the store, and wrecked it. The man who witnessed the crash worked at a restaurant called La Terrasse, and told her they were hiring a waitress. “When people say, how did you get into the restaurant business,” she said, “I always say, by accident. Because he was the witness.” The store she left behind became Urban Outfitters. She became a waitress, and then something else entirely. What she built when she got to build her own world From a muffin and coffee shop on the first floor of her own house, Judy grew the White Dog Cafe into a two-hundred-seat restaurant she ran for twenty-six years. She bought from local farmers before anyone used the phrase. She served only Pennsylvania beer and California wine. When she learned how pigs were treated in factory farms, she pulled the bacon and the pork chops until she could find a humane source. She calls it the turn that changed the whole shape of her work. She had spent years assembling proprietary lists of the farmers she bought from, her competitive advantage, and she gave them away to her competitors, because one restaurant doing it right was a drop in the bucket and the whole food system was what mattered. “I went from me to we,” she said. Having founded the nonprofit Fair Food and co-founded the Business Alliance for Local Living Economies, she sold the restaurant to give her full attention to local economies, wrote Good Morning Beautiful Business, and later built All Together Now around four pillars: food, textiles, plant medicine and building materials. That textile work continues today as Pennsylvania Fibershed. As she put it, people used to say she used good food to lure innocent customers into social activism, and she says do, because she is still doing it. Never outsourcing your soul There is a thread that runs from the child who broke the bullies’ windows to the woman who gave her competitors her farmers. She has always known when a place has finished with her, and when it has, she builds the next one. When she left her first marriage she could not even find the words for why. This was before there was language for it. All she knew was that she had to go and find the Judy Wicks she had crossed off her tablet at ten years old. “We need to be our true selves,” she said. “And do what we have to do, to be that person that we truly are.” Katherine named the whole shape of it back to her, that she had always trusted the inner refusal and moved, and Judy went quiet. “Your questions are really interesting,” she said, “because they’re making me think about things I’ve never thought about before. About my own life.” You may know that refusal in yourself. The name crossed off the tablet, the desk lid lifted, a new self written in over the old one. Judy is fifty years of evidence that following it is a whole life. What her life is asking us to see Judy Wicks has a banner in front of her house. It says love is the strongest power, and she believes it plainly. She names a moment of pure joy: dancing in the street at a rum and reggae party, and looking around at Black people and Latino people and Asian people, old people, her children, her employees, her neighbours, her customers, all of them dancing together. Her joy comes from diversity, from opening her arms to those who are different from her. The homestead is her last fort, her daughter’s phrase and now her own. A world of nature, of community, of joy and abundance and peace, made on purpose so that everyone has a table. She has been building it her whole life, in different woods, under different roofs, and she is still building it now. She told Katherine, plainly, that you get to create the world you want to live in. She has proven it more than once. The banner still hangs in front of her house, saying love is the strongest power, and every fort she has ever built has been an argument that she is right. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Judy This conversation runs a little over an hour, wandering from meadows to forts to Alaska to a red light and back to joy. Sit with it when you have the time to let it wander. There is no hurry. The library is always here. My life has been about building the beloved community. That whatever I’m doing, whether it’s running my restaurant or having parties, what I’m really doing is building the beloved community. I was in charge of creating the world in which I lived. And I guess I’ve always done that. It’s where our joy is in opening our arms to those who are different from us. Judy Wicks is a retired social-activist entrepreneur living on a two-acre homestead in the Chestnut Hill section of Philadelphia, which she and her daughter Grace have rewilded into meadow, orchard and garden. She founded the White Dog Cafe, a farm-to-table pioneer she ran for twenty-six years, and went on to found Fair Food, co-found the Business Alliance for Local Living Economies, and build All Together Now around local supply chains in food, textiles, plant medicine and building materials. She is the author of Good Morning Beautiful Business. Nearly eighty, she hosts gatherings that are, in her words, either just fun or political in nature, and names her whole life’s work as building the beloved community.
show-micky-hoogendijk.html: Micky Hoogendijk is a self-taught artist working across photography, sculpture, painting, and stone carving, and the author of a memoir on the art of letting go. She creates bronze figures of people holding onto one another, coaxes stillness from her photographic subjects until they stop performing and simply arrive, and lives from what she calls her child energy. A photograph of seven-year-old Miriam lives on her phone. That child, she says, is the one she works for. In this conversation, Micky and Katherine walk backward through a life lived across twenty-four moves, many countries, and as many forms of expression. They talk about The Artist’s Way and the morning pages that opened Micky’s creative door; about Eric Morris, the acting teacher who asked her to say “I’m a little girl, will you please be my friend?” in front of twenty-five working actors, and what she understood in the tears that followed. They talk about the army of bronze figures she began during the first week of COVID, “the ones,” people holding onto each other. And they talk about her memoir and what she discovered writing it: that letting go means creating space to keep moving forward. This conversation is for anyone who was once laughed at for being wholly themselves, and who is finding their way back to that child. She stands six foot one, a girl from the Netherlands who was once nicknamed the gentle giant when she moved to Los Angeles. Put a camera in her hands and something quiets in the room. No smiling. No redirecting. She waits until the person in front of her stops performing and simply arrives. “In my photography, you see stillness,” she says. “There’s no smiling, there’s no redirecting, there’s this being state, as I call it.” That is Micky Hoogendijk, and stillness is the thread that runs through everything she has made. Her first book of photography she called Strength and Vulnerability, the two words set beside each other with no resolution between them, because she does not believe they oppose one another. She believes vulnerability is the strength. She believes it is the most beautiful part of a human being. When she sees it in someone, she says, she falls a little in love. Over one life she has lived many. Actress for twelve years. Photographer. Painter. Sculptor. Author of a memoir on the art of letting go. Now, most recently, she has gone to Italy to learn to carve stone. She is entirely self-taught in nearly all of it. And through every form, she is doing the same thing: coaxing the unperformed human out into the light, then holding it there long enough for the rest of us to recognise ourselves. The girl who arrived as Princess Miriam She was born Miriam Hoogendijk in 1970, conceived by artificial insemination, one of the first in the Netherlands, raised by her mother alone. When she was around five, her mother told her the whole truth of it. The next morning she walked into school and announced, “I am a very special seed. I am so special.” The children laughed. The parents laughed. The teachers thought she was lying. Nobody there had heard of such a thing, and this beautiful naive girl had simply told them who she was. She drew and sang and danced. She needed a great deal of attention, being an only child, and she gave it back to the world in colour. When the family moved from Amsterdam to the rural east of Holland, she arrived at her new school dressed as Princess Miriam, in her mother’s golden nightgown with a little crown on her head, and introduced herself that way. The room decided she was a dork. Katherine knew that room. She told Micky about being six years old in grade one, putting her hand up to say she had found a dead baby bird and buried it and gone back and found it gone, and being laughed at by the whole class, teacher included. Two dismissed children, decades apart, recognising each other across the conversation. The name she built to survive, and the girl she is walking back toward At around fourteen she named herself Mickey. “I think she came from surviving,” she says. Mickey was the strong one, the good organiser, the one who could put her face on and walk through customs at LAX and be waved through. Mickey protected the sensitive, scattered Miriam through the parts of a childhood that were not safe. There was a stepfather she genuinely loved. He was a painter, a hunter, a man who taught her to draw and paint and sing and play guitar. He also abused her when she was eight. She told her mother. She confronted him, her mother beside her. And as a child, she learned something she carried the rest of her life: that she could say no, that she could say she did not want this. What she came to understand only much later, in the writing of her book, was that her body had learned to step outside itself to survive. “Whenever I enter the room, I know what’s going on,” she says. “But it’s a survival mechanism that I have learned because of all of these things. I’m putting it to good use right now.” She reads a room the way most people breathe. It is the source of the work. Our deepest hurts, as Katherine names it, become our deepest gifts. Her mother’s essence in a camera Micky was an actress for twelve years. In Los Angeles, the master teacher Eric Morris stood her in front of twenty-five working actors on her first day and had her say, out loud, “I’m a little girl, and I need to be loved.” She stood there with tears coming down and had no idea what had happened. He told her: vulnerability is much more interesting than being a tough girl. Nobody had ever told her that. Then her mother died. Her last gift to Micky was a beautiful camera. “I really sincerely believe that her essence was in that camera,” she says, “and it allowed for me to create new lives.” She moved to the United States with it, and her photographs travelled the world within no time. The actress became the artist. She would meet a face, a girl walking out of a dressing room in a Forever 21 in Austin, and her whole body would say: I need to photograph you. Then she would dream the image whole, and make it. The turn to sculpture came in the first week of COVID. She looked at her studio in total isolation and decided either the world would end or she would begin. Within weeks she had an army of figures she calls “the ones”: people holding onto one another, the way children draw people, the thing the whole world was forbidden to do that year. People love the work, she says, because they see themselves, they see their own family in it. She did not plan any of it. It came from the subconscious, which is where she says the healing actually lives, because we so often want everything too literal, printed out one, two, three, four, five, and it is never that. The art of letting go is the art of making room Her memoir is called The Art of Letting Go. She resisted releasing it for years. She did not want to stand in a supermarket beside a stranger who knew everything about her. It took four years to finish, and three weeks of real fear before the launch, until she read that an artwork is at its most vulnerable right before release, because it has not yet found its audience. Katherine knew that fear too, and named the book what it is: a being, another child, given birth to and sent where it is meant to go. She reaches for a more precise word, and finds it. “It’s not really about letting go of anything, but it’s about creating space,” she says. Making room. And the way you make room is to keep moving. As long as you move yourself into certain directions and allow yourself to keep moving and to keep living and to keep doing the things you do and creating and being curious, then things just appear and happen and continue. She does it all from her child energy. To create, she says, she has to be in a playful state, so she wears her work clothes because the little girl loves them, and she lets the child steer the boat. Innocence, as Katherine puts it, is the highest form of wisdom. And there is a second guide now: someone told Micky to picture herself at eighty-three, and the woman she imagines is a daredevil who says yes to everything, more playful even than the child. She juggles the two of them. The hurt little girl she comforts, and the free old woman she is walking toward. What her life is asking us to see Micky places strength and vulnerability side by side and refuses to choose between them. That is the whole of it. The child who was laughed at for being wholly herself did not vanish. She was protected by a stronger self, hidden for a while, and is now being walked, gently, back home. What she has made from what happened to her fills rooms and travels internationally. The lost children have rooms in her work, alive and breathing. The survival that taught her to read a room is the very thing that lets her make what she makes. The wound, she says, quoting Rumi, is where the light enters you. She has made space beside her past and kept moving, and the moving is the creating. The stillness she coaxes out of the people in front of her camera is her gift to them, and it is the same stillness she has learned to hold for the child inside herself. In that stillness, the moving becomes possible. This is what she is walking home toward: Miriam, in the truest and freest and most pure state she began in. Her wish for us is that we learn to live. That we teach children to love themselves first, to be kind, to take care of one another, so that a generation grows up in touch with what it is actually about. Every essence, Katherine reflected back to her, is its own radio station, its own frequency. Micky’s journey is the journey back to hers. Please believe in you, she says. Don’t let that little girl drown. That voice is the purest form of you. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Micky This is a warm, unhurried conversation, a little over an hour, between two women who kept recognising themselves in each other. It moves through art and acting, the inner child, the art of letting go, and the quiet work of coming home to who you were before the world laughed. Settle in with it whenever you have the space. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I actually think and believe that vulnerability is the strength and it’s the most beautiful part of a human being. In order to create, I have to be in a very playful state. I have to be in my child energy. The moment you stop doing, the moment you don’t allow yourself to try, then it stagnates. And stagnation is the worst thing you can do, I think. Micky Hoogendijk is a self-taught artist from the Netherlands who works across photography, sculpture, painting and, most recently, stone carving. Born Miriam Hoogendijk in 1970, she spent twelve years as an actress before her mother’s gift of a camera turned her toward visual art, and her photographic work soon travelled internationally. Her sculptures, figures of people holding onto one another that she calls “the ones,” began in the first week of COVID. She is the author of a memoir on the art of letting go, published in Dutch and titled in English The Art of Letting Go. Her photography book is Strength and Vulnerability. She lives and works in the Netherlands.
show-patricia-gagic.html: She takes people tabula rasa: you arrive not knowing anything, and she believes you are already talented, already holding something inside you that has not yet been scratched. Patricia Gagic is an internationally recognised contemporary artist, author, drummer, and humanitarian whose life is devoted to making that surface yield. She won the Gold Medal at the SNBA at the Carrousel du Louvre. Her Black Madonnas entered the Vatican Museum Library. She has built schools, a library, and an Innovation House in Cambodia since 2006. She teaches the Karmic Art Experience and has written across four books. She is voraciously curious, deeply loving, and chooses presence again and again, in the middle of everything. This conversation moves through the whole of that life. It begins with the friendship itself: Katherine sharing how Patricia, after hearing a talk at the Canadian Museum for Human Rights in 2019, nominated a stranger for women’s awards because she saw a supernova and refused to wait another year to say so. From there it walks backward through the formation of an artist who consumed encyclopedias A to Z as a child, became the youngest female bank manager in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, and followed a synchronicity in France in 1999 when she saw the name Dragic on a horse painting and simply knew she had to meet the man who painted it. Twenty-six years of study with master artist Dragan Dragic followed. The conversation honours the practice she has built across those decades: a faith, a meditation, a daily choosing of love. And at the centre of it all is a teaching about gray. Katherine confesses she once had a bias toward colour, that she stood before Patricia’s dark canvases and felt something she could not name. She asked what happens when you take all the colours of the universe and mesh them together. Patricia said: gray. In gray is where all potentiality exists. This is the heart of the episode: darkness holds all potential waiting to be revealed. Stand in front of one of Patricia Gagic’s canvases and you may notice, at first, only the greys, the whites, the blacks. Katherine did. She confessed it on the show: she had a bias toward colour, and she felt something she could not name looking at these still, dark surfaces from a woman who was so plainly full of light. She asked. What happens, she wondered aloud, if you take all the colours of the universe and mesh them together? Gray, Patricia said. Then Katherine looked at the paintings again, and something turned over in her. Gray is not where colour goes to die. Gray is where all of it lives at once. Under every one of Patricia’s finished canvases there is an underpainting soaked in red and green and yellow, the whole spectrum, and as the truth of the work reveals itself the colour shifts and gathers and comes to rest. That is the teaching she carries and the teaching she gives: darkness is the place where all the potential waits. The child who read her way through every faith She was, by her own account, a quirky and voraciously aware child. She has told her mother she remembers lying in her crib, months old, wondering when she would be allowed to walk. When the other children laced up white skates, she wanted blue ones. When her father brought home the Encyclopedia Britannica in grade three, bought on the doorstep at twenty-five cents a month for life, she sat with every volume from A to Z. Raised Roman Catholic, she turned that same appetite loose on the whole of belief: Hinduism, the Baha’i faith, Buddhism, on and on. Some of it came from wonder. Some of it came from a wound. In 1962, in Omaha, she was sent home from school one day because a Black woman was living in the house her family rented. The injustice made no sense to a small girl, and it drove her deeper into wanting to understand the world. Underneath all of it was her father, her role model, and the ethic he lived. She names it plainly. dedicated flawlessly to servitude where I think that was inbred in me by my father, you know, just like in Rotary, you know, service above self that that never left me. She lost him one month after her twenty-fifth birthday. His mother, her grandmother, followed a week later to the day, of a broken heart. They buried her father on her mother’s birthday. Before that she had already lost her first love, gone in a boating accident. She was young, and she was learning early how to make the choice she would go on making all her life. The name on a horse painting in France In 1999, in a home in France, she looked up and saw a horse painting with a name at the bottom: Dragic. She was not, she says, particularly a lover of that kind of art. But she could not let it go. She learned that a master painter named Dragan Dragic lived three hours away, and she knew, without being able to explain it, that she had to meet him. it’s that moment where you’re sitting there and in your brain you don’t know why you’re saying yes. And I don’t like what it just happened. And I went, I need to meet this man. He did not want to meet her. She made her husband phone back in Serbian. Granted an hour, they arrived two hours late, having taken the wrong way up the mountain, and when she walked into his atelier and saw his name on posters beside Picasso and Christo, she thought she had no business being there at all. He asked what she wanted. Fame? Money? Her husband answered for her: she just wants to know how to paint. She did not speak French. She said she would learn, took thirty-two hours of tutored lessons, and carried her grammar book everywhere until she was dreaming in the language. That began twenty-six years of study. He would not tell her the names of the colours, only numbers. She spent a decade learning to mix, to melange, until she could reproduce any colour she could see. A master, he told her, is someone who can walk into any gallery and analyse a piece, then paint it. That is where he took her. What she has built Patricia Gagic is an internationally recognised contemporary artist, an author, a drummer, and a humanitarian. In 2018 her photograph, one entry among some forty thousand submitted to the Salon National des Beaux-Arts, won the gold medal at the Carrousel du Louvre. Her Black Madonnas, drawn in pointillism, entered the Vatican Museum Library. She has been named among the top ten contemporary artists in books held across tens of thousands of museums and galleries. Since 2006 she has given herself to Cambodia. It began with a phone call and a request for five thousand dollars to build a library near Angkor Wat. She cashed out an RSP and did not think twice. She went back, and then she did not leave: a school in Bueng Mealea, an Innovation House, year after year woven into their world. And she teaches. Through her Karmic Art Experience she takes people, as she puts it, tabula rasa, through painting, meditation, story and music. you’re talented, you definitely have something inside of you, you just haven’t been able to scratch the surface of it yet. Choosing love as a practice She has known more loss than most lives hold. A near-death fall from a spooked horse onto the Trans-Canada Highway, from which she remembers coming back to life. Her mother beaten and robbed. And in April 2024, her forty-one-year-old daughter Kira, a musician and mother of three, whose children she now helps to raise while carrying her own grief. She does not pretend the grief away. She wept telling it, and Katherine held the moment gently: grief is important, it is important to feel. What Patricia has found is not the absence of sorrow but a way to live inside it. Gray is the underpainting beneath every canvas, where all the color and all the potential are already waiting. It is not emptiness. It is everything that hasn’t been revealed yet, and I think that is also a practice. You make a choice, again and again, how you are going to meet what is in front of you. Fear, she says again and again, doesn’t move her. What does is the same faith she brings to the canvas, the same knowing that under the surface, in the gray, the whole spectrum is still there. What her life is asking us to see Patricia meets the world the way she paints: she starts with everything, then lets the truth reveal itself. Watch how she moves through a life and you see her frameworks and Katherine’s meeting quietly. This is a woman remembering who she has always been, essence shining as the armour falls away. This is service as the completion of a whole self, the joy that comes from making a difference in someone else’s life, five thousand dollars for a library given without a second thought. She is voraciously curious. She is present. She chooses love and she chooses faith, over and over, not once but as a daily practice. The losses are chapters in her life. They are not the whole of her, and she would be the first to tell you so. What she leaves us with is the gray. The place we are tempted to read as empty is where all the colour is held, waiting. There is a path through darkness to creativity, to service, to joy, and she has walked it long enough to be trusted on the road. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Patricia This is a long, meandering, luminous conversation between two friends, close to an hour and a half of art, faith, loss, and the practice of presence. Settle in with a cup of something warm and let it unfold at its own pace. There is no hurry. The library is always here. In gray is where all potentiality exists. fear is not my currency. So I will not let that dictate. The most greatest gift in this world we can give ourselves is the feeling of love one feels when they make a difference in the life of somebody else. Patricia Gagic is an internationally recognised contemporary artist, author, drummer and humanitarian. A gold medallist at the Salon National des Beaux-Arts at the Carrousel du Louvre, she studied for twenty-six years with master painter Dragan Dragic, and her Black Madonnas are held in the Vatican Museum Library. She is the author of Karmic Alibi, The Karmic Framework, How to Be Human Today, and Karma and Cash, and she teaches through her Karmic Art Experience. Since 2006 she has built schools, libraries and an Innovation House in Cambodia. She lives art as healing and service, and holds together a life of creative, spiritual and humanitarian work.
show-carlos-delgados-and-craig-alexander: Carlos Delgado grew up in the mountains of Colombia where finding paper to draw on was near impossible. Today he mentors nine young artists in his Colombian studio, provides their materials and space, sells their work internationally, and runs Arte Espiral, an organisation that delivered ninety art workshops to indigenous children in mountain communities last year. Craig Alexander is the founder and owner of Sybil Frank Gallery in Wellington, Prince Edward County, named for his two grandmothers, a place he describes as a happy maker, open and free to anyone who walks through the door. This conversation began inside a live painting performance at the gallery, Carlos working with a knife more than a brush while Craig and Katherine spoke. It walks backward through how Craig found Carlos online and sold his first painting within a week; through Carlos’s fifteen years in Canada riding the Toronto subway and reading the tired faces of rush-hour commuters; and through the day a young artist named Eliasar arrived at Carlos’s studio with an oil painting on cheap paper because he could not afford canvas. His style, the simplicity of chaos, where apocalyptic strokes resolve into beauty and love, runs through everything. This episode is for anyone who has wondered whether the thing that once saved them can become the thing they give away. He works with a knife more than a brush. A collector who owns his paintings and had never watched him make one stood in a gallery in Wellington and gasped, because Carlos Delgado turned a portrait facing straight ahead into a profile with one or two moves of the blade. The music played. People pushed him gently to keep going. And when the music stopped, he turned and said, I’m done. That painting sold before he set the knife down. Someone in the room said they couldn’t leave without it. Carlos calls what he makes “the simplicity of chaos.” Apocalyptic strokes, worked and reworked, until the chaos comes out as love. He believes chaos means new, rebirth, birth. On this episode of The Sincerely Show, recorded on location at Sybil Frank Gallery, he sat beside the friend who first saw his work online seven years ago and drove him out to a small gallery two and a half hours from Toronto. That friend is Craig Alexander, who sold his first painting inside a week. Two boys who found themselves early Craig named his gallery Sybil Frank after his two grandmothers. He was close to both of them. He picks paintings the way he imagines each of them separately, then asks himself what happens if he puts them together. That is how he chooses the artists he represents. Carlos found himself much further away. Today nine artists work from his studio in the mountains of Colombia, he sells their work internationally, and with his wife Diana he runs Arte Espiral, carrying art workshops to indigenous children in the mountains. But he began there, as a boy, drawing from the time he was two or three years old. His father still tells the story of watching a toddler draw and being amazed. Paper was hard to find in the mountains. Paint was harder. And in his country, he says, people think being an artist means being poor. He carried six months of childhood guidance into a whole life of making. Everything else he taught himself. The mountains, and the paper that was never enough The art school was out of reach. He tells it plainly. when I had the chance to be in the art school it was complicated, I didn’t have the funds to kill to pay the rent, to stay and and also I decided to study a different thing to be in art because art is con in my country the people think being an artist being poor So the school never had him. The knife and the canvas would come later, taught by his own hand. A young man knocking on the studio door In 2010, Carlos moved to Canada. He worked part-time jobs and rode the Toronto subway, watching the faces of tired commuters at the end of rush hour, the ones looking down, the ones pretending to sleep. He learned that when a person looks away, they give a little of their soul away too. From those faces, the art came. Over roughly fifteen years he came to feel he was worth something, and the proof was the community of galleries and collectors who gathered around him and became his friends. After the pandemic, the cost of the studio and the apartment in Toronto grew heavy, and he felt his art “was like being killed just to keep expensive.” His parents were getting older. He moved home to Colombia to be near them, back to a town of fifty-seven thousand people in the mountains, back, as he put it, to the beginning. Then the young artists began knocking. One of them, Eliasar, drove four hours to ask Carlos for support. Carlos said no at first. But Eliasar showed him a small painting, two portraits of children, made in oil on cheap paper. I didn’t have money to buy canvas. And I was loyal so touched. I told my wife, look this is he’s so talented but he doesn’t have at least a canvas to do a painting. Carlos offered the young man space to work and materials to work with, canvas for a boy who could only afford paper, and later a knife of his own to learn with. A year later he sold one of Eliasar’s paintings in Norway for six thousand dollars, a sum equal to four or five months of a regular salary in Colombia. What the return home opened in him He went home to be near ageing parents and found himself at the beginning again, in the town where paper had once been scarce. What looked from the outside like a retreat became a gathering. The knocking at his door turned into a studio full of people. He had come back to the mountains he thought he had left, and this time he had something to give away. What Carlos and Craig have built Today nine artists work from Carlos’s studio in the Colombian mountains. He buys big rolls of canvas and oils. Until this January he paid the rent himself, and the materials, and everything else, and the artists have only recently begun to help a little. He sells their work internationally through his own collectors. He looks around his studio and sees who has gathered there: a woman, a young man who is part of the LGBTQ community, a seven-year-old boy who can draw you in a minute. Two years ago he and Diana founded Arte Espiral, which brings art workshops to indigenous children in mountain communities. Last year they ran ninety workshops. When they arrive, they bring snacks for the children and good materials, so the teaching carries dignity. Craig, meanwhile, keeps Sybil Frank Gallery open in Prince Edward County as a place anyone can walk into for free. People ask how much it costs to come in. It is free, Craig tells them, just come in and enjoy. He also runs a talent agency. He brings to it the same care he brings to hanging a room. He calls the gallery a happy maker. It’s not a moneymaker. It’s it’s It’s a happy maker. When someone sees you, and you carry it home Carlos found his worth in Canada, in a world of collectors and curators who told him, in effect, that he mattered. Craig was one of them. Craig drove Carlos out of the city, sold his first painting within a week, then his next two within another week, and became family alongside Diana. Both men have known dark and heavy seasons. Craig speaks of the church of the Sagrada Familia on his seventieth birthday, sitting from nine in the morning until five in the evening to watch the sun move through the stained glass, and feeling everything negative leave and beauty take its place. His mother has dementia and lives in a home. She tells him he is always in a good mood. He tells her it is because he woke up, and every second after that is a gift. Katherine put it to his face: You brought community to Canada. And Canada showed you back the love and the community that was already in you. The gift that once saved someone becomes the gift they hand away. He was sitting on the floor painting while Craig gave his interview. He helps young artists so they can live from what they love, and he asks them for discipline alongside their talent. What their lives are asking us to see Two men met because one of them was searching online in a gallery in Wellington and one of them was making paintings out of the faces of tired strangers. When Craig first saw Carlos’s work, he drove two and a half hours out of the city on the strength of it, and sold the first painting within the week. Carlos’s wish for humanity is balance. He has watched crazy poverty and enormous wealth stand side by side in his country, and he dreams of dignity for people who cannot reach the most basic things. He believes art does its part in that. A canvas for a boy who could only afford paper. Last year, he and Diana carried ninety workshops into the mountains with snacks and good materials for the children. Nine artists learning to live from what they love. Craig believes the same thing from a different angle. Beauty is for everybody. You walk into a room, you see something you have never seen, and you feel held. He keeps the flame of the gallery alive so that others can feel his grandmothers’ presence the way he does. Carlos names his work the simplicity of chaos, and he means that the strokes go in like an apocalypse and come out as love, one or two moves of the blade turning the whole thing over. That is also the shape of a life given over to service. The chaos is real. The beauty it can be worked into is just as real. And the two of them, Craig who saw and Carlos who was seen, are proof that we become ourselves in each other’s company, and then we give what we have become away. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour.
