show-melissa-bernstein.html: There is a woman who has designed close to ten thousand toys, built one of the leading preschool toy brands in the United States, and founded Lifelines to put sensory wellbeing tools into as many hands as possible. She coaches despondent strangers for free, one person at a time, because she has learned, from the Talmud and from lived experience both, that to save one life is to save the world entire. That is who Melissa Bernstein is today. The conversation walks backward from there. Melissa describes growing up with a profound crisis of meaning felt from the earliest moments of her life, and shaping herself into what she calls the three P’s: perfectionism, pleasing, and performance. We trace the arc from that formation through the pivot of her early twenties, when she and Doug left conventional careers and founded a toy company with their pooled savings, and she discovered she could turn off the dark faucet and turn on the light one full tilt. That led to her memoir, to the community that became Lifelines, and to the framework she calls the pie of meaning: building a life from many varieties of slice so that no single loss empties you. Katherine and Melissa also find the same arc in each other and name it plainly, two people meeting in the same truth. This conversation is for anyone who has wondered whether the very quality that made them feel wrong might be the source of their best work. There are no promises of arrival, only an open-handed invitation to keep cultivating seeds and trust they will germinate in lives we will never see. Ask Melissa Bernstein who she is and she does not reach for a title. She reaches for an image. “I am truly a creative being in every cell of my body,” she says, “and I live to channel and transform my innate chaos and darkness into radiant light through tangible forms.” She means it plainly. There is a faucet inside her, the way she tells it, and for most of her life it ran one direction only. Then one day, in her early twenties, she found she could turn it. Turn off the dark one. Turn on the light one full tilt. Let the same unsettledness that had always poured out as heaviness come out instead as something a child could hold. The thing she made first was toys. Close to ten thousand of them. Bright, playful, warm objects, made by a woman who did not once, in her own words, think of herself as bright or playful or warm. The faucet is still running. These days what comes through it is a company called Lifelines, and a habit of picking up the phone for the most despondent person who reaches out, and a verse she wrote when she was eight that she has been living out ever since without quite knowing it. The child who wrote verses no one wanted to see She was born, she says, with a crisis of meaning. Her mother remembers her crying through the whole of her first year. They called it colic. Melissa suspects it was a question. At two and three years old she was already wondering why everyone else seemed to be having so much fun when it all felt so hard, and asking aloud what we have to show for ourselves at the end. The family she grew up in did not want the question. Love there felt conditional, arranged around performing and pleasing rather than around being known. She looked to television for the family she longed for, the Waltons, the Partridges, the big raucous households full of yelling and laughter, and she promised herself she would one day build that. Meanwhile she wrote. Thousands of rhyming verses, most of them dark, poured out of a child who had nowhere else to put what she carried. When she tried to share them, she met horror on grown-up faces and a clear message: we do not make things like that, and your job is to go and play. She had no answer they would accept. She was five. She built a self the world would accept. She calls it the three P’s: perfectionism, pleasing, performance. A’s on every test. The good girl who did what was asked. The bright smile answering “great, awesome” over a well of angst pushed down and out of sight. The one who saw through the performance The three P’s held for a long time, and then they did not. In college both of her pillars gave way in the same season, the social one and the academic one, and she reached the lowest point of her life. She has spoken about this openly, on this show and elsewhere, as part of what shaped her. What matters for the story is what came after. She met a man named Doug the summer of her junior year. She was very ill by then, an eating disorder having taken hold of her, and Doug, who is a fixer rather than a talker, looked at her and decided without much discussion that he was going to feed her. He would sit across a table and refuse to leave until her plate was empty. Because she wanted to please him, she ate. The very habit that had bent her whole life out of shape became, in his company, the thing that pulled her back toward it. Katherine, hearing this, offered Melissa something she had not quite let herself see. Doug may be pragmatic, may not speak of feelings, and still, Katherine said, “you just don’t show up in somebody’s life” and feed them without some draw of love and connection underneath. Melissa went quiet. “That makes me appreciate him in a new way.” What she has built At twenty-two and twenty-four, against everything a stable 1980s career path demanded, Melissa and Doug pooled their savings and started a toy company. She had never taken a design class. She did not even like the word creative. Then she stopped channelling darkness into darkness, and the ideas arrived finished, whole, one after another. That company became the leading preschool toy brand in the United States, close to ten thousand toys over three decades. In her mid-forties a second crisis surfaced, and with it a name. Reading Viktor Frankl again, she understood that what she had carried her whole life had a word, existential angst, a non-pathological condition common in deeply creative people. She said so out loud on Jonathan Fields’ Good Life Project podcast, telling her whole story for the first time. When the episode aired months later, the letters came. Twenty in a day, then fifty, then hundreds. People telling her she had given words to the thing they had never been able to name. Out of that came Lifelines: first free workshops, then her own study to become a meaning coach, and now a consumer products company making sensory tools designed to interrupt the stress response and bring people back into the body and into joy. Alongside it she coaches despondent people for free, one at a time, and mentors young founders through the Melissa and Doug accelerator at Duke University, now in its thirteenth year, with a soft spot for women who lack the confidence that so often comes easily to others. The pie of meaning Her medicine, she says, is meaning, made continually, every single day. And meaning, she has learned, cannot rest on a single source. She calls it the pie of meaning. If your whole pie is one flavour, being a mother, say, then when your children grow and no longer need you, the pie empties and you fall into a vacuum. She keeps many slices. Meaning. Creativity through entrepreneurship. Spirituality. Each with its feet on the ground in the present and its eyes lifted toward something greater. There is a line from the Talmud she keeps close: to save one life is to save the world entire. For years her ego wanted the big stages, the millions of hands her products might reach. About ten years ago something turned. “I have to do it one person at a time,” she says. “And that is more than enough.” One call with one person at their lowest, one thing said that lets them think differently, and the ripple carries where she will never see it. She wrote that truth once already, at eight years old, in a verse she only recently understood. Keep on cultivating seeds, give them water, pull the weeds, then repeat it all again, for we can’t be certain when they will germinate and grow, touching lives we’ll never know. If you have ever felt too sensitive, too much, quietly wrong, her life reads that same quality differently. The thing you were told to hide may be exactly the thing you were sent to give. What her life is asking us to see Melissa lives from three pillars she named herself, and every one of them, when you follow it down, arrives at the same floor: contribution. The meaning she makes, she makes for the despondent stranger. The products she creates need to be in someone’s hands; that is where they become real to her. The mentoring she loves most is the courage she hands a young founder to try. All of it is service, chosen through love. This is what she means when she says she has turned off the dark faucet. She feels the chaos every morning. She has simply learned where to point it. That is the choice she found in her early twenties and has been living into ever since: we solve our problems from darkness or from light, and we are always, always allowed to choose. There is a Greek word Katherine offered her, Enteleki, for the unending desire to express our most fundamental self fully in this lifetime. Melissa has a plainer word for it. A song. “They have a song inside them that wants to be heard by others,” she says of the people she serves. “And I just try to give them one by one the courage to find that song, because some don’t even know if they have one.” She does not cling any more to how it turns out. Some seeds germinate, some do not, and the joy of making is the same either way. She scatters her grains of sand onto the hill from love, not knowing which one begins the landslide, trusting that it is not hers to know. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Melissa This conversation runs close to an hour and a half. Melissa traces her arc from the child writing verses in a dark room to the woman building tools that hand calm to strangers, and at one point she and Katherine sit quietly together in the recognition that they have been asking the same question their whole lives. Come when you have space for it. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I basically saw that I have a choice. I can choose to either create more darkness out of darkness… But now I actually metaphorically and figuratively turned off the dark faucet. I believe in having a bunch of different slices of different varieties of pie in your pie. And I think for me, I live that every day. When you save one life, you save the world entire… I have to do it one person at a time. And that that is more than enough. Melissa Bernstein is a creative entrepreneur, author, and the founder of Lifelines, a company making sensory tools designed to interrupt the stress response and bring people back into joy and into their bodies. With her husband Doug she co-founded one of the leading preschool toy brands in the United States, designing close to ten thousand toys across three decades. She is the author of several books, including Lifelines and The Heart of Entrepreneurship, mentors young founders through the Melissa and Doug accelerator at Duke University, and coaches despondent people one at a time, without charge, from her conviction that to save one life is to save the world entire.
show-eric-farewell.html: A friend asked Eric Farewell two years ago if he could coach him. In what, Eric said. And the friend answered: you own four companies and you don’t work. You have more time than anyone else I know. Eric replied without reaching for it. He calls himself a billionaire in time: a man who, having never had a childhood, is living one now, driving his kids four minutes to school, playing volleyball on the weekends, calling someone he loves every single time he gets in the car. He is a coach and mentor to founders, the builder of a community called Royals for men and women stepping into their highest selves, and a husband of seventeen years who will tell you plainly that presence is the only currency that has ever mattered to him. This conversation walks backward through the life that produced him. The seven-year-old who discovered that hard work made people call him remarkable, and who spent the next twenty-five years chasing that feeling through businesses, broken bones, and a marriage that very nearly ended. The convergence that came at thirty-two, when his body finally stopped him. And the years of somatic work, therapy, community, and radical honesty that brought him to the man sitting here now: loving, present, and genuinely grateful for all of it. In this conversation Eric talks about why grief must be witnessed in community, not carried alone. He talks about the one emotion men are given permission to feel, and the slow, beautiful work of learning to feel the rest. He shares what he looks for in a king or a queen, which has everything to do with where their boundaries are. And he talks about fear as a highway sign: the direction you are most afraid of is very likely the direction you are meant to go. A friend put the question to Eric on a podcast a couple of years ago. Could you coach me? Coach you in what, Eric asked. And the friend said: Eric, you own four companies and you don’t work. I know you. Our daughters are friends. You have more time than anyone else I know. He answered without reaching for it. “I’m a billionaire in time. I built my life. Like I didn’t have a childhood. So I am living my childhood now.” He plays volleyball with his friends on the weekends. He plays video games in the afternoon. He drives his three kids the whole four minutes to school, because he moved next door to it on purpose, and then he gets back in the car and calls someone he loves. Some weeks it runs to three calls. Some weeks five. A brother in the middle of a move and a divorce picks up every time. The businesses he built still run. He put the people and the systems in place so they could. They make less money that way, and he has done the arithmetic on that exactly. “If it cost me five million dollars a year to never have to be told I’m remarkable for working really hard again, I’m good with it.” This is Eric Farewell, forty years old, in Austin, Texas, coach and mentor to founders, husband of seventeen years, father of three. He woke one morning in February with the plain sense that if he passed that day, he had lived well. He had loved enough. He had been loved enough. The seven-year-old who learned that hard work made people call him remarkable He was three when his family began travelling half the year in a motorhome, five children packed in, driving three or four days a week to sell books to homeschoolers. He was seven when he found the thing that changed everything: work. His great-grandmother had a country inn, built in 1931, and Eric would guide tours of retirees around the property. They thought his eyelashes were beautiful. They thought he was kind, and interesting, and that he knew so much. For the first time, someone patted him on the back and told him he was good. He grew up in a hyper-conservative homeschool Christian faith he now names plainly as a cult, in a home where the only affirmation on offer was for what he produced. He produced. By eight he worked a cash register as fast as any adult, an apron of cash tied around him. By thirteen, in 1999, he had built his first business with employees, selling airplanes on the new thing called the internet. Nobody else was doing it. People kept telling him he was remarkable. From the age of seven on, I became obsessed. I became absolutely obsessed with receiving the love I wasn’t receiving at home from other people telling me I was doing a good job. That was the loop. Work, remarkable, more work. It followed him into an internet marketing and speaking career through his teens, and it followed him into the flight school he built with his wife Nelle after she looked at him at twenty-three and said, Eric, you hate this, I don’t care about the money, why don’t we just do what you love. Aviator Paramotor grew to nearly thirty employees and around thirty million dollars in revenue, told through nothing but their own story on YouTube. And still Eric worked one hundred and ten hours a week. Three months straight, then sick, then three days of sleep, then again. His children got up as he left. They slept before he came home. When the pain went to a ten and stayed there Eight years ago, several things arrived at once. His younger brother James died at twenty-two, ejected from a car a mile from home, gone on the operating table an hour later. Eric arranged the funeral. He managed the food. Four hundred people came for a boy who had made that kind of mark. And Eric believed he had grieved, because he had cried, and everybody cries at a funeral. Six months later he could not walk. My pain had gone from a six or seven to a ten at all times. I couldn’t take a full breath. My nervous system was fried. He went looking. Surgeons, chiropractors, Reiki masters, an emotion code therapist who asked him, quietly, whether his pain might be emotional. Eric laughed, and then he began the work: therapy, EMDR, somatic practice. Slowly the pain eased, and slowly he understood he had never truly learned how to feel. On Good Friday of 2020 he told Nelle every secret he had carried since he was eleven, and he lived out of the shame for the first time in his life. What the stillness gave back What he found, when he finally stopped, was a way to be present with whatever came. Not to cope with it, or mask it, or work himself past it, but to sit in it. He learned this in community. He keeps a running count of the hours: forty or fifty a month in circles with good men and women, leading or receiving, sharing his heart or hearing theirs. His way of holding grief came out of it, plainly said. Grief is a contraction of our spirit. And in order for us to fully expand into love, faith, joy, peace, we have to stretch the muscle. When his father-in-law died last year, and when Nelle faced a health challenge, Eric told her: honey, we’ve been training for this. And they had. What he has built, and who it is for Today Eric coaches and mentors founders, and he leads a community he calls Royals, for men and women who want to step into their higher self, the king or queen version of themselves. The work is systems and hiring and numbers, and it is also this: how do we honour our trauma, how do we honour our fear, how do we look at the hard things from our childhood. He counts a client’s restored relationship with her children as worth exactly what revenue is worth. He has a test for who a king or a queen actually is. “It’s not about what they have. It’s about what their boundaries are.” His own boundary is the one he lives by now: he will no longer perform to receive love. He knows what he was raised to feel, and what he was not. “The only emotion I was not told to button up was anger,” he said, “and the last thing we need is more angry men.” So much of his work is teaching men to feel the rest. There was a client, a founder who had done remarkable things, and Eric asked her when she was last in her feminine. She turned to him with tears in her eyes. “I think I was eight.” Eric wept telling it. Katherine named what she saw in him: the ability to see through the layers to the soul, what A Course in Miracles calls true empathy. The client, he said, is back in her feminine now, running a life of flow rather than force. What his life is asking us to see Eric was told he was remarkable when he worked, and never simply because he was. So he chased remarkable across four decades and several reinventions, until his body refused to carry it any further and his marriage nearly ended and his brother was gone. What he built afterward is a life arranged around presence, love and time instead. There is a three-self model Katherine returns to: the lived experience self, the physical and inherited self, and the essence, the soul underneath. Eric saw that essence the day his eldest was born. He looked into the baby’s eyes and found perfection, and his inherited beliefs began to crumble, because he saw the glory of God there rather than anything to be corrected. He has spent the years since trying to see himself the way he saw his child, and to help others do the same. His wish for the world is unadorned. Beneath the skin we all look the same. If we could meet each other with love in our eyes, the love a person makes because they have felt the grief of its absence, we might learn to let one another in. That, he says, begins with doing the work to love yourself. His purpose is to help people overcome the fear that keeps them from being present with who they truly are, because fear is only the antithesis of love, and love is all he wants to be remembered for. He no longer runs from what frightens him. Fear, now, is a signpost. When he feels it, he reads it as the direction he is meant to go. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Eric This is a warm, unhurried conversation of a little over an hour, interrupted at one point by a Texas thunderstorm that Katherine received as the divine putting an exclamation mark on the talk. Eric speaks openly about work and freedom, about grief and community, about masculine and feminine energy, and about building a life around love. Settle in with a coffee and stay a while. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I’m a billionaire in time. I built my life. Like I didn’t have a childhood. So I am living my childhood now. My purpose on this planet is to help myself and others overcome fears to become present with who we truly are. All that fear is, is the antithesis of love. All I wanna be remembered for is loving. So if I can instill that into others, to teach them to love themselves in such a way that they have an abundance of love to give to the world. That’s where the best missions come from. Eric Farewell is a coach and mentor to founders and the builder of Royals, a community for men and women stepping into their higher selves. He built his first business at thirteen, selling airplanes on the early internet, and went on to found Aviator Paramotor, a flight school that grew to nearly thirty employees and around thirty million dollars in revenue. Today he owns four companies while keeping his own hours, describing himself as a billionaire in time. He lives in Austin, Texas, with his wife Nelle and their three children, and recently wrote a book about his life. His work centres on helping people overcome fear and become present with who they truly are.
show-jennifer-hill.html: Jennifer Hill has spent her life learning to see the spark of light in every person she meets, and handing it back to them when they have forgotten it. She is the founder of the Gen Hill Tribe, a global community of entrepreneurs, thought leaders, and creators, and the founder of OptiMatch, an intelligent-matching platform built to connect people around the world according to their motivational makeup, values, and numerological alignment. She shares 180 self-developed tools for self-regulation and inner peace, freely, with anyone who wants them. This conversation walks backward through the chapters that shaped her: a childhood spent contorting herself to earn love, a fierce awakening at a personal development class outside LAX, and a long decade of inner work that slowly rewired the way she lived. It walks through the autism diagnosis that gave her context to understand her own brain, the building of schools in Nepal and Senegal, the founding of OptiMatch, and the vision two Decembers ago of a magical mirror in which she saw not her own reflection but every human being she had ever met reflected back to her. From that mirror came her purpose: to look for and listen for the spark of light in every human and reflect it back when they have forgotten. This episode is for anyone who has tried to earn love by becoming someone else, and is ready to find, and reflect back, the spark of light that was always theirs. It was 10:30 on a Thursday morning, two Decembers ago, and Jennifer Hill was dead sober. A friend in Lisbon, Keith Hodges, had offered her a session as a thank you for the connections she is forever giving away. She had carried the same weight since she was five: a recurring dream that she had to save humanity, and kept failing. He began to intone and chant, and space and time fell away. The first thing she heard was giggling, the gentlest laughter she had ever heard, and it was the universe, and the universe was telling her there was nothing and no one to save. Then it gave her a mirror. In it, she did not see her own reflection. She saw every human she had ever met or would ever meet, reflected back as herself. then your only purpose is to look for and listen for the spark of light in every human you meet and reflect it back to them when they’ve forgotten This is the work Jennifer Hill does now. People call her the fairy godmother of human connections, and she gives away thousands of connections a year the way other people give directions. She founded the Jen Hill Tribe, a global community of several hundred entrepreneurs, thought leaders and creators, and OptiMatch, a matching platform built to help people find one another across the world. She keeps 180 tools she developed for herself, and she has made every one of them public. Watch her for an hour and you understand what she means: her intuition lights up like a net of small fires, and she feels the invisible thread of connection that runs through every human life. The blank book, and the girl who tried to earn her way in Jennifer describes childhood as being handed a book on how to be a human and opening it to find every page blank inside, while everyone around her seemed to have one that was filled in. She tried to earn her way to love by formula: get straight A’s, do the right thing at the right time, and love would arrive. Both her parents were working two jobs and drinking, and she was largely raising her younger sister. She speaks of them with love now. She and her mother talk every day, and her mother has stopped drinking for the most part, which Jennifer calls the happiest she has ever seen her. Her father passed away a few years ago. The good-girl formula did not earn her the belonging she was after, so she went, in her phrase, to the dark side. There was a long, dark stretch through her late teens and early twenties that she has spoken about openly and writes about in her book. She came close to not surviving it. Around 2018, an autism diagnosis arrived and finally explained to her how differently her own brain had always worked. The woman who called her Godzilla She was about twenty-three, dragged to a three-day personal development class by her boyfriend, wearing a t-shirt that said Von Bitch to make it perfectly clear who she was and why she was there. She spent the weekend, by her own account, sitting in self-righteousness, a “judgy bunny” toward everybody getting their breakthroughs. At the close, one of the facilitators asked if she could be really straight with her. What she held up was a mirror Jennifer had spent years avoiding. You are one of the most powerful women I’ve ever met in my life, except you know what? You’re like Godzilla with a huge tail swishing behind you, knocking down buildings wherever you go. Except guess what? Those aren’t buildings. Those are people whose lives you’re destroying. The next morning she went into her office team meeting and asked whether she had ever been mean or condescending to any of them. The room went silent, and then somebody laughed and told her she was the most condescending person they had ever met and they had no idea how she was so successful. She marks that as the moment her life changed, from before she realised she was an asshole to after, and she has been in the twenty-year transformation ever since. Her forthcoming book is called The Recovering Asshole. Its real subject is gentler than its title: that we are hardest of all on ourselves first. until we can first repair that relationship with self, we’re never going to be able to have deep intimacy with others What she found when she finally stopped About fourteen years ago, three influences arrived close together and began to genuinely change how she lived: transcendental meditation, Kabbalah, and a coach who taught her to regulate her nervous system. She had had the dream life before that, three homes, matching cars, two golf memberships, and felt her soul shrivelling inside it. Now she spends two hours a day in prayer, meditation and reflection, and she means it literally. Every night she does what she calls spiritual accounting, asking how she could have lived the day better, what caused pain, what she is proud of, what she is grateful for. It is a nightly mirror she holds up to herself with tenderness rather than blame. She and her husband ask each other three questions before sleep. Whether they did enough spiritual change that day. Whether they would be happy if today were their last. And, gently, whether one caused the other pain. What she has built, and who it is for The Jen Hill Tribe began as a birthday gift. A friend built her a WhatsApp group and dropped in thirty-six people she loved, to thank her for referrals. It has grown to several hundred members across Canada, Australia, Bali, the UK, Europe and Brazil, with twice-monthly socials and member-led trainings on everything from meta ads to building an app in fifteen minutes. OptiMatch grew from her intuition made into an algorithm, work she built for five years with her teacher and business partner Julian Adler, who died the very night their acquisition offer arrived. She carries his memory into the platform still. Inside the matching she uses a fruit typology, lychee, apple, mango, pear, for how people are motivated, and a “plus two” method for reading your own energy after a conversation. Underneath the tools is one finding from twenty years of connecting people: when two people are motivated adversely, they speak the same language and still cannot hear each other. What her life is asking us to see Katherine noticed something and named it. She had watched Jennifer’s mind and its extraordinary reach, and she said she did not sense a stitch of fear, and asked whether Jennifer knew fear at all. Jennifer thanked her, and said no one had ever asked her that before. What followed was the account of a woman who has sat with the fear of death so many mornings that it has loosened its grip, and who now, when a plane shudders, notices she is at peace. Jennifer went right to the crux of her own transformation in the first minutes of the conversation. Katherine heard the arc she listens for in every life the moment Jennifer named the shift from before she realised she was an asshole to after: a collapse, and then the long, unfinished work of waking up, again and again, never in a straight line. Both women, it turned out, had been meant to be in the Middle East as the conflict broke out, and both were turned back, one by a friend, one by an inner knowing. Jennifer read the wish she had written the day before her birthday. If peace is to ever exist in the world, she wrote, it first must exist within us. Katherine met it with her own words for the same truth: inner harmony is the pathway to outer harmony. That is the whole of it. The magical mirror was never only Jennifer’s vision. It is the offer she makes to everyone she meets: that you carry a spark of light you may have forgotten, and that the peace you long for out in the world begins in the only place you have any authority, your own heart. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Jennifer Settle in for a little over an hour with Jennifer and Katherine. Jennifer’s mind moves quickly, and it will surprise you into laughing, then it slows near the end when she reads aloud the wish she wrote the day before her birthday, that if peace is ever to exist in the world it first must exist within us. You may want to hear that part twice. There is no hurry. The library is always here. your only purpose is to look for and listen for the spark of light in every human you meet and reflect it back to them when they’ve forgotten instead of seeing my own reflection, I saw the reflection of every human I had ever met or would ever meet reflected as myself If peace is to ever exist in the world, it first must exist within us. Jennifer Hill, known to many as J-Hill, is the founder of the Jen Hill Tribe, a global community of hundreds of entrepreneurs, thought leaders and creators, and of OptiMatch, a platform that connects people around the world by reading how they are motivated and pairing them accordingly. Over a career that began in recruiting, she has connected an enormous number of people, and she runs twice-monthly socials and member-led trainings across her community. She keeps 180 self-developed tools for self-regulation and inner peace, and shares them publicly. She has helped build schools in Nepal and Senegal, and her book, The Recovering Asshole, is forthcoming. She lives in Lisbon.
show-chip-conley.html: Chip Conley is the founder and executive chair of the Modern Elder Academy, the world’s first midlife wisdom school, with two campuses and 9,000 alumni. He teaches people to find their footing in transitions, cultivate purpose, awaken wisdom, and reframe their relationship with aging and longevity. He has written eight books, and he now measures his life by a single phrase he says plainly and often: the ripple of impact. In this conversation, Chip and Katherine walk the full arc of his life, from his formation as the firstborn of two firstborn Stanford parents, programmed to achieve and perform, through his coming out at 22 on Independence Day in Greenwich Village, through the building of 52 boutique hotels over 24 years, and through the collapse in his late 40s that became the doorway to his life’s next work. They talk about the Enneagram, the shadow side of the performer, and what it means to move from performative identity to essence. They talk about the midlife atrium, and about the Modern Elder, someone as curious as they are wise. This episode is for anyone standing at the threshold of their second adulthood, wondering whether their best work is behind them or ahead of them. There is a beach in Baja, just south of the Tropic of Cancer, where Chip Conley used to run in the mornings. He had a home there, and a life behind him that most people would call finished and complete: twenty-four years of building boutique hotels, fifty-two of them, each with its own name. He had sold the company. He had spent seven and a half years as the “modern elder” to a set of young tech founders, learning what his wisdom was worth to people half his age. And one morning, running on that beach, a question arrived. Why aren’t there any midlife wisdom schools? Why is there no place for people in the middle of their lives to come apart, and reconsider, and decide who they want to be next? He calls the person he became in that season the modern elder. His own definition, borrowed from the day the Airbnb founders came to find him: “someone who is as curious as he is wise.” Older in an earned way. He answered his own beach question by building the thing that did not exist. Two campuses now, one in Baja and one on a high-desert ranch outside Santa Fe. Nine thousand people who have walked through it. He is a father, a grandfather, and a great grandfather. He has written eight books. And he has come to measure his life by a phrase he says plainly and often: the ripple of impact. The firstborn of two firstborns He was the only boy, the eldest of three, the child of two firstborn Stanford parents who prized achievement the way other families prize air. As a small boy he was shy, introverted, socially awkward, with imaginary friends and a creativity he had already learned to be scared of. Around ten or twelve his parents warned him he would be sent to therapy if he did not socialise more. Therapy sounded like prison. He did the other thing. He studied people. He learned to read them, to build a bridge to whoever was in front of him. “Very much a chameleon,” he told Katherine, “and all the while doing everything I could to achieve because I got love and sense of worth by being a great athlete.” Student body president. All-American water polo player on a national champion team. A father who said, when Chip was still a boy, “I want you to just be a better version of me.” He was the best little boy in the world, to borrow the title he borrows for himself. He was, in his own word for it, programmed. At twenty-two, in the summer of 1983, he walked from the Upper West Side down to Greenwich Village, knowing he would step into a gay bar for the first time. He walked into Uncle Charlie’s on Independence Day, full of fear, and something in him turned from fear to liberation. He described the shift the way Dorothy’s world turns from black and white to colour. He found community. He came out into a family that could not yet hold it, and into three years in which he could not tell his mother the truth. The dark night of the ego By 2007 the hole he had dug for himself was deep. He was still, in his words, an accomplishment addict, an admiration addict, running a company of thirty-five hundred people with no easy way out of it. Then the Great Recession came, and much of what he had built stood at the edge of collapse, and a stretch of grief arrived that no one should have to carry at once. And in St. Louis, an allergic reaction to an antibiotic sent him to what he calls the other side, nine times over ninety minutes. He came back with a phrase he had earned. People say the dark night of the soul. He calls it the dark night of the ego. Katherine took that phrase and held it up to the light for him. That’s profound. Cause it isn’t that it isn’t the dark night of the soul. It’s, it’s actually where you find truth. It’s where you find your essence, which is all love and light. It’s the enlightenment of soul, not the dark night of soul. “No, no, exactly,” he said. “Exactly.” What was being crushed was the performative identity, the image built to survive, the thing that no longer fit the soul underneath it. In the collapse of the ego, a person finally gets to ask the real question: who am I, really? What he found when he stopped After the company sold, he took two and a half years of nothing much. show-florence-shaffer.html: Florence Shaffer is the founder and CEO of Becoming, which she describes as the first strategic advisory for human flourishing: a diagnostic across the mental, emotional, physical, spiritual, and social dimensions of a person, matching leaders with world-class experts for an immersion so that success no longer erodes the life it was meant to serve. She has spent more than twenty years leading technology and transformation across BMW, Lucasfilm, Burberry, and Estée Lauder, and founded Becoming four years ago to hand others a way to reroute from a performative way of being onto a coherent and regenerative one. In this conversation, Florence and Katherine walk the full arc of a life built in pursuit of human potential. Florence traces the thread from a third-culture childhood shaped by a South Korean mother who built ferocious love into every sacrifice, and a South Dakotan physicist father who earned a PhD out of pure curiosity, through Harvey Mudd’s creative sandbox, and into the twenty-year career that gave her everything the game promised. They talk about the “slip,” Florence’s name for the moment when success and joy begin to diverge, and about fragmented optimization. They build a new language for boundaries together, moving from the image of a wall to protecting the sources of energy that feed you. And they sit with what it means to make decisions from coherence rather than from the accumulated noise of performing a self. This episode is for anyone who is winning by every external measure and losing the creativity, energy, and joy that made the winning worth it. Florence offers the recognition that the invitation to reroute arrives before the wheels come off, and that the body has been speaking long before we choose to listen. Florence Shaffer will tell you she does not have to catch every wave anymore. There was a version of her that treated the ocean as a thing to be beaten: more waves coming, so swim faster, hold your breath longer, get better tools. That version won a great deal. She describes something else now. You actually get out of the water and you start to surf, and you start to realize: wait a second, I don’t have to surf every wave. I’m with the environment because I am grounded. I’m anchored. She is six foot tall, a self-described car girl, a poet who reads about longevity and the future of society. She has led transformation across BMW, Lucasfilm, Burberry, and Estée Lauder. She founded a company. And when Katherine offered her a line early in their conversation, that she is a human being, not a human doing, Florence caught it and turned it straight toward the eight-year-old she once was. That child already knew the work. Florence says she has known since she was eight that she was here to support and inspire other people to live in the full expression of who they are. Everything after that, the companies, the countries, the titles, was the long way round to the thing she started with. The third-culture child of a physicist and an entrepreneur Florence is what she calls a third-culture kid. Her mother is South Korean, disciplined and entrepreneurial, a woman who at eighty-four was still watching skincare tutorials and building a terrarium in the kitchen to make snail cream from scratch. Her father is a humble, endlessly curious physicist from South Dakota, the first in his family to go to college, who once accidentally got a PhD by simply not stopping the courses, and who keeps a stack of linear algebra on the table because he thought it would be fun to derive it from nothing. They met when they were nearly forty. They raised Florence in Silicon Valley, inside a belief that whatever you want to build, you can make happen. Her mother’s own mother had been killed in the Korean War when her mother was six, and out of that loss came a single determination that shaped a whole family: to be the mother she had not had. Florence names what she inherited from it plainly. I confuse this idea of love and sacrifice. I thought love is sacrifice. She thought the fastest way to honour her parents’ sacrifice was to win the game they had worked so hard to give her a place in. She did. Harvey Mudd College first, which she wandered into almost by accident and found a creative sandbox, a place where the whole point was to protect what you were building rather than fence it in. A professor there mirrored back the thing she could not see in herself: that she was the only one who began every design with the human who would use it. Then twenty years of transformation work, Hong Kong, Nepal, the Americas, thirty brands. The night in the Hong Kong office She was alone in the Burberry office, ten-thirty at night, and she was weeping, which was not something she did. Being Korean, she says, we don’t have those moments. Her boss found her, this woman she still admires, and asked what was wrong. And then said it. We sell trench coats. Florence heard it. She had known since she was eight what she wanted to give the world, and she had let the titles and the making-her-parents-proud carry her somewhere else. Katherine has a word for that night. She offered it gently: call it a collapse, collapse number one, and told Florence about her own three or four collapses across nine years before she finally surrendered. Florence calls it the slip. The successful leader inflection point. She is an engineer, so she draws it as a graph: success and enjoyment rising together for a long while, and then the two lines part. You keep performing. The performance holds. But somewhere the joy that made it worth it has thinned out, and you tell yourself maybe you need a new wardrobe, new friends, a therapist. The world keeps moving, so you keep moving with it. The graph she had been ignoring Two and a half years ago, out of nowhere, Florence was told she had stage four cancer. She had already started building her company. Her team said, well, it is time for you to go through the programme you built. She moved through it fast, she says: shock, then tears, then, in about forty seconds, an image that came to her whole and has stayed as the picture of her entire life before that moment. I was driving the car of life and the warning lights went off and I was like, no problem, I can drive. The trench coats were the first light. She had kept driving. The windshield cracked; she was resilient, she kept driving. Steam came off the engine; still driving. The wheels, she says, blew off. She was supposed to have stopped. Her body had been telling her to pause and reorient her whole life, and she had normalised every ache and headache the way high performers do, folding the exhaustion into her identity until being tired was simply what leadership meant. Later in the conversation Katherine returned to the thing Florence had said, that she was supposed to stop. She would not let it sit as a failure. You did the best you knew how, she told her. And Florence received it: well, and I wouldn’t be here, would I. I wouldn’t be doing this. She was learning, slowly, to stop fighting the water and to be with it. What she has actually built Florence founded Becoming four years ago, and she frames it as the first strategic advisory for human flourishing. She built it by speaking with more than 250 experts, asking one question: how would you recalibrate a person from making decisions out of an extractive, performative system to being driven by their own coherence? The answer she built is a diagnostic across the whole of a person, mental, emotional, physical, spiritual, social, that finds where someone is working against themselves. It matches them with world-class experts, individual contributors kept out in the world so the programme stays alive and evolving. Then a five-day immersion, a modern rite of passage, designed to make one or two shifts at a deep enough level that everything downstream gets simpler. The point she guards most carefully is that it happens without blowing up your life. You stay in your life. The adjustments reintegrate into it. The byproducts, she says, are great health, real relationships, joy, and genuine performance. They come from being anchored. Selling us back what was always free Florence laughs that we have built whole industries because we forgot how to be. Rest, health, movement, eating well: things that were always ours, packaged and sold back to us until we feel we must perform them too. She once heard of a company in New York selling memberships to sit in an empty room. Brilliant, she thought, and then: how far have we come that we pay to sit quietly. When she and Katherine reached the word boundaries, they found a better one together in real time: Katherine offered it, Florence affirmed it. Protecting the sources of energy that feeds me. It means about knowing myself well enough so I know what brings me joy, what brings me rest, what brings me peace. This is what Florence hopes to make reachable earlier, before the slip, before the warning lights go unheeded. She is winning by every measure and she is also holding stage four cancer with a self-observation so steady it disarms you, calling it, of all things, a gift, saying her relationship to it will be love, because her body decided to tell her where she had stopped listening. You may be somewhere on that same graph right now, success still climbing, joy quietly slipping. She would tell you the invitation is already here. What her life is asking us to see Florence Shaffer is curious, playful, radiant, and she watches herself with a gentleness most of us reserve for other people. She grew up believing love was sacrifice, and she has spent her adult life learning that love is coherence: the state of being so at home in yourself that you are not doing anything, and somehow everyone around you feels freer to be who they are. She said it plainly: she is part of the ocean, and she flows with it. She put it plainly: intelligence is becoming a commodity, and the real question is what our role is now. Her answer is to come back to the whole self, the morality, the humanity, and the wide-open wonder a child still carries before anyone tells them to stop, and to build from there. A regenerative life instead of an extractive one. A soft reroute off the conveyor belt before it reaches the cliff. She is doing all of this while not knowing what next week’s scan will say. And she is enjoying her life anyway, being exactly who she wanted to be, which she says is the only thing that ever mattered. She got out of the water and started to surf, and she is still out there, with the environment rather than against it, grounded because she is anchored. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Florence Settle in for a conversation of a little over eighty minutes. Bring your own graph if you have one. There is no hurry. The library is always here. When you start to realize that you feel so coherent in who you are and how you show up that you’re not really doing anything and somehow you’re giving other people permission to just show up as who they want to be. We’ve created industries because we’ve forgotten how to be, right? So we’re really selling you back rest, your own health, and eating well, and moving. You don’t need to command the ocean. You don’t need to control it. You’re just part of it, and to really just flow with it. show-tom-lenoble.html: There is a question Tom LeNoble asks the people who come to him. He asks it after he tells them about the storm. Every storm, he says, leaves fertile ground to plant. The storms in our lives do the same. What are you going to plant? Tom is a confidential advisor to founders, executives, and nonprofit leaders, CEO of the Academy for Coaching Excellence, an award-winning bestselling author of My Life in Business Suits, Hospital Gowns, and High Heels, a professional speaker, and host of the podcast Opening Pathways. He names himself, above all, a philanthropist, and what he means is not a name on a building or a seat at a gala. He means a smile. A hello. Sitting with someone in need, without expectation of anything in return. This conversation walks backward through the chapters that made him: a one-bedroom Florida shack, a curious child his grandfather nicknamed Varmint, a corporate career from MCI to Facebook, a healing wheel of his own design, and three diagnoses that each gave him six months to live. He is 71, and retired from being retired to be inspired. There is a photograph Tom LeNoble keeps in his memory of Maui after the storm. All that rain, and then the sun on the wet ground. He has a way of holding that picture and turning it into a question he asks the people who come to him. What the storm does, he says, is make fertile ground. The storms in our lives do the same thing. What are you going to plant? He calls the hardest things that happen to us “terrible gifts.” A relationship that ends. A pet that dies. A disaster we are sure we will never get over. Terrible, he says, we would not wish them on anyone. And then, in a month or a year or five years, a gift comes from it. He speaks from a life he has lived all the way down and back up again, more than once. Tom is a confidential advisor to founders, executives, and nonprofit leaders. He is the CEO of the Academy for Coaching Excellence, twenty-four years old now, training coaches around the world. He wrote an award-winning bestseller called My Life in Business Suits, Hospital Gowns, and High Heels. He hosts his own podcast, Opening Pathways. And above all of it, he names himself a philanthropist, though not in the way most people mean that word. “I retired being retired to be inspired,” he told Katherine, near the beginning. It is the kind of line he offers with a smile, and then it turns out he means every syllable of it. The varmint in the shack He grew up in a one-bedroom house in Florida that his grandfather built, and the family called it “the shack” with real fondness. His brother and he shared the bedroom. Their parents slept in the living room, though nobody called it that. There was no hot water; his father boiled vats of it on a kerosene stove, and there was a pecking order to the baths. Being the baby, Tom was last, except on his birthday, when he got to be first. There was no refrigerator, just a block of ice carried home each day. And there was a lot of love in that house. He was five when he came home from his first weeks of school and understood two things at once: that his life was going to be different from the one he was living, and that he himself was different. Curious past the point of caution. His grandfather took one look at the small boy exploring every corner of the old house and shouted that there was a varmint loose, and the name stuck for life. Katherine met him there. She told him about crawling out of her own crib as a child, hunting for the man she was sure lived inside the radio. “My nickname was Varmint,” Tom said, and for a moment the two of them were the same curious child in two different humble houses. The curiosity got him into trouble and it also carried him. A bullied boy who was called a sissy, he puzzled his way through, once trading his daily brownie for the protection of the tallest girl in fifth grade. He found his people in the drama club, an international thespian back on a stage. And he was drawn, early, toward the care of others. He tended his dying grandmother as a teenager because there was no one else to do it. He volunteered where he was spat on, and kept volunteering. The virus in the rearview mirror There was a decade-plus corporate career, real and remarkable: MCI, walmart.com, Palm, and then a phone call from an unknown little company called Facebook, an interview with a nineteen-year-old Mark Zuckerberg in an office above a Chinese restaurant, and the setting-up of that company’s first customer operations. He did all of it while gravely ill. In San Francisco, after his brother had died of AIDS in Ward 86 in 1985, Tom went to an anonymous clinic and waited seven long days for a result he already suspected. When the woman began her careful script, he asked her only for the answer. A smile given without expectation, a moment of real presence offered freely, Tom calls that a philanthropic gesture. Generosity, he says, doesn’t require a checkbook. It just requires you to show up. Then he started the car and drove back to work. He has been told he had six months to live three times. He is in his thirty-seventh year with HIV, and he has lived fourteen years with metastatic cancer. Each time the sentence came, he says a small voice crawled up and whispered in his ear: watch this. The hub of the wheel During AIDS, and again with cancer, Tom built something he calls the healing wheel. Picture a wheel with spokes running out to Western medicine, Eastern medicine, acupuncture, massage, and on and on. He was the hub. He learned enough to have the difficult conversations, and then he made the decisions himself. His current oncologist calls him a clinical trial of one. Out of that came the work he does now. He advises leaders on resilience, which he refuses to treat as a pose of toughness. Resilience, he says, is a muscle, like a bicep, that you use to get stronger. His keynote Living Fully While Dying moves through three phases: living fully without regard to dying, living fully while being told he was dying, and living fully knowing he was dying all along. And there is the philanthropic mindset. People kept telling him they would be philanthropists one day, when they had the money. It made him ask what the word really meant. your smile, a hello, sitting with someone that’s in need or in pain is a philanthropic gesture. You don’t have to have your name on a building, write a check or go to a gala. The only condition is that you give it without expectation of anything in return. Tie the knot, and never tie it for someone else In 1985, standing in Ward 86 where his brother was dying, Tom saw a framed poster on the wall: a rope with a knot at the end of it. If you feel that you’re at the end of your rope, tie a knot and hold on. It was the first time he had seen the line, and it never left him. He carries it now as a discipline about other people. When someone is at the bottom of a hard passage, the answer is often obvious to the one watching. It is not obvious to the one inside it. Tom will hold their hand, encourage them, lift them up until they can reach the knot themselves. He will not tie it for them. He calls this the Haystack method. He believes people have their own answers, like a needle somewhere in the hay. His job is to hold the space so a person can clear the hay away and find the needle that was always theirs. Katherine gathered his qualities and read them back to him: fiercely curious, inventive, expressive, sensitive, courageous. Like an artist, she said. Tom stopped. Everything she had just named, he told her, was exactly what he had used to make his whole life happen. No one had ever handed it to him that way. What his life is asking us to see Katherine has her own word for what Tom calls a terrible gift. She calls it a collapse: a moment that breaks a life open, where you have a choice to cope and mask it, or to surrender and sit with it. In that surrender, she says, we find our next calling. Two people describing the same weather from two windows. The philanthropist and the artist turn out to be the same man. The essential self Katherine speaks of, the innate energy each of us is born with, was there in the five-year-old who knew he was different, in the varmint exploring every corner. It was there in the young man who reclaimed himself and set out to find what he was for. Service was always at the centre, and the storms only cleared more ground for him to plant it in. Fear, he says, is an opportunity for growth. He asks us to be here now, because we got up this morning and some people didn’t. And when we meet someone who has not yet found the strength to tie their knot, he asks that we hold their hand rather than reach for the rope ourselves. His wish for the world is that we remember horrible things have happened before, and that we survived them. That we thank the housekeeper with her dust mop as readily as the general manager. We are all far more the same than we will ever be different, and none of us is meant to plant the fertile ground alone. Thirty-seventh year in, still here, still planting, Tom keeps asking the one question the storm leaves behind: what are you going to plant? This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. Tom tells his story with humour and a startling openness, and Katherine receives all of it. Pour something warm and settle in. There is no hurry. The library is always here. show-master-mingtong-gu.html: Partway through this conversation, Master Mingtong Gu stops talking and reaches for a song. He has not prepared it. He says so, and then he invites Katherine and everyone listening to close their eyes, to place a hand on the heart, to feel the heartbeat underneath the palm. He sings three lines, over and over, each one a truth about the body he has spent a lifetime returning to. Master Mingtong Gu is the founder of Wisdom Healing Qigong and the Southwest Sanctuary near Santa Fe, where he leads people through month-long and longer retreats, teaching them to reconnect mind and body. He has been teaching full-time for twenty-five years and has just released a new book. He introduces himself first as a whole human being: a playful inner child, an artist, a devoted teacher. This conversation moves through the philosophy of the body as home; the missing piece Mingtong adds to Descartes and the Buddha (“I feel, therefore I am”); the three truths he sings into the room; the medicine-less Qigong hospital in China where he lived for close to two years and found what he had been searching for; the ancient grandmother trees of the sanctuary and the glacier Katherine watched calve into the Arctic ocean; and the wish he sends out at the close: that every human being discover the deepest connection of their own mind and body, because that one reconnection can change everything else. Partway through the conversation he stops talking and reaches for a song. He has not prepared it. He says as much, and then he asks Katherine and everyone listening to close their eyes, to put a hand on the heart, to feel the heartbeat underneath the palm. Then he sings. Three lines, over and over, each one a truth about the body he carries. Without this body, I do not exist as a human being. Without this body, I cannot experience life as a human being. Without this body, my soul cannot evolve in this lifetime. He asks Katherine afterward how she feels. She tells him: shivers all the way through, from the moment it started, and tears of love and peace and honour. He receives that plainly, the way he receives everything. This is Master Mingtong Gu. He is a Qigong master teacher, the founder of Wisdom Healing Qigong and of the Southwest Sanctuary near Santa Fe, where he leads people, one month and sometimes longer at a time, back to themselves. He has taught full time for twenty-five years. He has just released a new book. And when Katherine asks him who he is, he begins with a little child playful inside him, an artist who loves what he creates, and a person devoted to a vision he means to give away as widely as he can. The long search for a place to belong He grew up poor in a rural farming village in China. His birth family had seven children and not enough food, so he was given to another family, and then, when his adoptive parents divorced, he moved again, and again, across three different homes before he came back to the family he was born into. A childhood like that does not hand a person a stable sense of belonging. He carried illness too, from very early, including asthma he later traced to a fall at six years old into a septic pit, a fall that cost him consciousness. His breath stayed broken for decades. He tells this gently, in his own words. “I grew up poor and lost, disconnected, and our disease, you know, challenged.” He came to the United States looking for happiness, looking for a sense of belonging he had never been able to find. He studied mathematics. Then he found his heart through art, through photography and video, taking off his clothes to meditate in snow and waterfalls and empty rock, making double-exposed images of his own body dissolving into the wild. He was reaching, but the reaching still pointed away from himself. The hand on his shoulder, and the run up the hill The turn came in his later thirties, inside what he calls the medicine-less Qigong hospital in China, where thousands of people practised together, day and night, a month at a time. He lived and trained there for close to two years. His asthma left him. And near the end of that healing, an old childhood memory surfaced, the fall, the pit, and with it something began to close. His teacher’s wife touched him on the shoulder. she touched me on my shoulder gently. She said, Now you have found your home. Now you can return your home as often, anytime. Something loosened in his chest and moved outward into his whole body, and only afterward did his mind put words to what had already happened. The home he had been looking for across families and cultures and careers and relationships was here, all along, inside the body he had been trying to escape from. “This body is my home. This is my home. That’s what I’ve been missing.” He ran up the hill behind the centre and screamed it to the whole world. And from that moment, he says, he stopped seeking outside himself. Katherine hears the shape of this and names it back to him: first the becoming, the recognition of the full self, then the being, the arrival, witnessed years later when his teacher looked at him at graduation and time simply stopped. Mingtong agrees, and then he refuses to let it stay tidy. The journey is a spiral, he says. You pass the same nine gates again, at another level, and then again. It never finishes. Katherine offers her own image, up then down then up, a descent into our true humanity as much as an ascent, and the two of them recognise each other across it. What he has built near Santa Fe Nine years ago he opened the Southwest Sanctuary. He took on real risk to do it, with no way of knowing whether people in the West would commit to a retreat a month long, whether the numbers would ever work. He built it anyway. The land does part of the teaching: high desert, spring blossom, water and fountains and the Kiva. And three grandmother trees, each one older than five hundred years. The word he uses for the healing that happens there is rebirth. “healing is about recovering yourself to the wholeness. It’s about realizing yourself to the truth of who you are. And that’s everything else come as a side effect.” He is interested in giving a person back to themselves, and letting the rest follow. His diagnosis of our moment is exact, and it comes from a lifetime of watching the mind climb up over the neck and stay there. We have built a civilisation on thinking, he says, and now the digital world has hijacked even that. When Katherine names her three layers of self, the lived experience self, the physical and inherited self, and the essential self you could call the soul, he recognises them all, and then he adds the thing he has been discovering: these three are inseparable, and it is the body that holds them together. Descartes said, I think, therefore I am. The Buddha, in his reading, said, I am aware, therefore I am. Mingtong offers the piece he believes we have been missing. “I feel therefore I am.” What his life is asking us to see During the pandemic he passed through his own dark night. He questioned the meaning of all of it. He asked the grandmother tree whether the earth needs human beings, and the answer came back clear and humbling: no. And then the second truth: human beings need the earth. Katherine met him there with her own glacier calving into the Arctic ocean, and her guide’s words, that the earth does not need saving, that what needs saving is humanity and ourselves. Out of that wilderness came a second song, sung beside the water in San Diego, about everybody looking and looking for themselves, and the welcome home that ends it. Everything we are looking for, he says, is already inside our own body. Living so far up in our heads, we come to feel like nobody. Coming back to the body is how we discover we are somebody at all. Katherine names his essence back to him in the room, the way she does: innocent, devoted, embodied, joyful, present, in service. When she reflects the word innocence, he receives it as the truest thing said all day. Wisdom lives there, she tells him. He is beginning, after thirty years of practice, a new chapter of asking the most innocent question of all. What is this body? His wish for us is a single change he believes changes everything. That each of us discovers the deepest connection of our own mind and body, because until we do, nothing else moves. It costs no resources. It waits on no one. This moment, he says, we can do it. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Mingtong This conversation runs a little over an hour, and it moves the way the best conversations do, without rehearsal, following feeling from one truth to the next. There is a song in the middle you are invited to sing along to, a hand on the heart, a grandmother tree, a glacier. Come and sit with it when you have the space to feel it. There is no hurry. The library is always here. In that moment, I realized the home is here. This body is my home. This is my home. That’s what I’ve been missing. I’m aware, therefore I am. But what I’m adding to, to this conversation about humanity is I feel therefore I am. Everything we’re looking for is already inside of us, inside of our body. Master Mingtong Gu is a Qigong master teacher and the founder of Wisdom Healing Qigong, a global movement now in its third decade. He is also the founder of the Southwest Sanctuary near Santa Fe, New Mexico, where he leads month-long and longer retreats teaching people to reconnect mind and body. He has taught full time for twenty-five years. He trained for close to two years at a medicine-less Qigong hospital in China and received parallel transmissions from teachers in the Tibetan Dzogchen tradition, and his own early life in a poor farming village, shaped by illness and loss, is part of what he now teaches from. His new book, Coming Home to Embodied Awakening, is available in Spring 2026. Free Chapter Here: Reclaim Your Body in an Age of Disconnection
show-jem-fuller.html: Jem Fuller has spent the last decade helping very senior leaders build something most leadership programs never reach: inner alignment first, then coherence in their relationships, then coherence across every system they are responsible for. He coaches one-to-one with leaders running organisations of significant scale, runs conscious leadership retreats in the Himalayan mountains, Bali, and Australia, writes award-winning books, and founded the Centre of Love, a non-profit building an education sanctuary in Northwest India and gathering twelve founders of global movements fuelled by love into an alliance aiming to touch 150 million lives. He recently landed the phrase that holds all of it together: coherence architect. This conversation travels the full arc of how a person becomes that. It begins with the life Jem is living now, on a coastal farm at Bells Beach in Victoria, with his partner Tahlia and their four young adults, three generations under one roof. Then it walks backward: years of purposeful wandering as a fire dancer, tattooist, and barefoot traveller, an adopted Himalayan family he has belonged to for almost thirty years, a corporate career that fed his children and cost him his coherence, and a sweat lodge ceremony and the dream that followed, which showed him the belief he had carried since he was six and began the daily practice that rewired it. If you have ever built an outwardly successful life and felt a quiet gap widening beneath it, this conversation is for you. An open door, and a reminder that the path inward is available. The word arrived recently, and it fits him the way a home fits the person who built it. Coherence architect. He tried it out with his community, then with his clients, and it held. It is the umbrella over everything he does in the world, and underneath the umbrella is a simple sequence: inner alignment first, then coherence in relationships, then coherence across whatever systems a person is responsible for. Most people would call him a leadership coach. He lets them. He works one to one with very senior leaders, the sort who are turning over a hundred and fifty million dollars a year and carrying a hundred and fifty staff, and the first thing he helps them build is a foundation inside themselves. He helps a leader find equanimity, the steadiness that lets you meet a hard day without losing yourself in it, and from there the feeling, the mental and the spiritual begin to line up. From there the work moves outward, to how a leader understands the people around them, and then to the moving parts of the whole organisation. “You are the common denominator that shows up in every aspect of your life,” he told Katherine. The personal and the professional are the same weave. If your inner life is capping your outer one, no amount of competence will free it. This is Jem Fuller. He speaks at the CEO Institute one week and runs conscious leadership retreats in the Himalaya the next. He is an award-winning author. And when Katherine asked him to introduce himself, he began much further in. The boy on the outskirts of Melbourne He was born in Haarlem, near Amsterdam, spent his first year in England, and at one was carried out to the outskirts of Melbourne, where his parents built a house in horse paddocks and orchards. He was the oldest of four. From the outside it looked like a very normal, loving family, and in many ways it was. There was a lot of love in that house. His father was from Leeds, a good man to a great many people, secretary of the church council, secretary of Rotary, an entrepreneur who built his own business. He was also, in Jem’s words, “a somewhat secretly tortured man,” and his drinking grew over the years. When Jem was six, his father lost his temper in a way he never had before. Only decades later, through deep work, could Jem look back and name what that day planted in him: the quiet belief that he was not good enough. He would spend the next thirty years unknowingly gathering evidence for it. At eighteen, five days after his birthday, his closest friend died after a motorbike accident. Jem drank his way through the end of school, then left for London, lived in squats, acted, sang, and became what he calls a peaceful punk. He wanted no part of the system. That refusal turned into something gentler and stranger than rebellion: a hunger to immerse himself in the cultures least like his own. Through his twenties he earned his way as a fire dancer, a tribal tattooist working by hand, a kindergarten teacher in Taiwan. In India, barefoot and asking the big questions, he found a family who adopted him. He has belonged to them for almost thirty years. The sweat lodge and the serpent The turn came around a fire, on Wadawurrung country near his home, in a sweat lodge run by men trained in North American practice. It was pitch black and very hot, and Jem flew. He had an out-of-body experience as a five-year-old, light and playful, his age of innocence returned to him for a night. He crawled out covered in mud, ran down to the lake under a full moon, and named himself, laughing, Naked Wet Boy. He went home to his sleeping boys and that night the real work came in a dream as vivid as waking life. A serpent lived in his core, and he had to pull it out of himself, and every time he freed it, it slithered straight back home into him. His toddler stirred; he half-woke, settled the child, and consciously went back into the dream, because the work was not finished. Faceless brothers appeared around him, and together they got the serpent out and found a way to keep it out. I immediately knew, wow, that serpent was the belief that I’ve been growing inside of me since I was six years old, that I am not enough. And it’s time for that belief to be out. He had read no psychology, no books on being good enough. It all came to him at once. And then the practice: sleeves rolled up, every single day. I am enough. I am enough. For the first six to twelve months he did not believe it. He said it anyway, over and over, until the neurology began to wire together and one morning it was simply true. What the collapse cleared the way for There is a piece of his story that sits underneath all of this, and Jem asked to add it himself. His father died at sixty-five of a brain tumour, with a reconciliation at the end, a man who could no longer speak but could look his son in the eyes and say he loved him. Four months later Jem’s youngest brother Tim, thirty years old, a bright shining star, died instantly in a motorbike accident. His mother lost her partner and her youngest child within a season. That grief was part of what led Jem into his midlife awakening, his own reframe of the crisis everyone else names. Around the same time the outer scaffolding fell too: the job, the marriage, the house. He walked away with a hundred thousand dollars of debt and his two boys, and gave the rest to his then wife rather than fight over things. And what he found on the far side of all of it was the truest, happiest chapter of his life. I’ve brought together 12 founders of global movements fueled by love and it’s called the Center of Love Alliance. And I’m weaving these worlds together so that we can be a tide that lifts all the boats. He does not build alone. His non-profit, the Centre of Love, incorporated only last year, is raising money to build a meditation and education sanctuary on two acres gifted to him by his adopted family in the Himalaya, funding schooling for children in the local villages. He has gathered twelve founders of global movements into the Centre of Love Alliance: one who has put more than seven million children through school in India, another who built a love curriculum for primary schools now downloaded in a hundred and thirty-two countries. His for-profit retreats feed the non-profit, so he never has to go asking. A tide that lifts all the boats, he calls it. His mission underneath the mission is to remind people that their true value in the workplace lives in their human-to-human abilities, in bringing love to work. What his life is asking us to see Somewhere in the conversation, Katherine stopped and named what was happening between them. Sincerely carries the same shape as the Centre of Love: a revenue-generating body funding a foundation devoted to love. Two people who had never met were describing the same architecture from opposite sides of the world. Jem heard it and said it out loud, the spark of two worlds coming together, being shared in public so that others might witness it. Living proof. The belief that you are not enough can be rewired. The identity that collapses is an invitation. And the life you rebuild afterward, from your essence rather than from the world’s instructions, can be truer than the one you lost. Jem does not retire from this. You don’t retire from your life’s purpose, he said, and he means to be doing it until the day he dies. He wakes convinced that goodness and love keep finding each other through what he calls a mycelium network, the one we are all part of, rising to the surface. He holds no attachment to the outcome. He simply knows. Coherence architect. The word fits him the way a home fits the person who built it, room by room, from the inside out, and the door of it is open to anyone still looking for their own foundation. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Jem This is a long, unhurried conversation, close to an hour and a half, and it moves the way a good fireside talk moves: two people recognising each other, following the tangents, laughing, going quiet, going deep. Settle in with it when you have the time to stay a while. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I’ve recently landed with a term to be the overarching title of my outer work, and it’s coherence architect. I’m weaving these worlds together so that we can be a tide that lifts all the boats. It’s not something to retire from. You don’t retire from your life’s purpose.
