Jem Fuller is a leadership coach, award-winning author and retreat facilitator who describes his life’s work as coherence architect: helping senior leaders build inner alignment, then coherence in their relationships, then coherence across the systems they carry. He runs conscious leadership retreats in the Himalaya, Bali and Australia, and founded the non-profit Centre of Love, which supports education in the Himalaya and gathers global founders into a shared mission of bringing love into the workplace. He lives on a coastal farm at Bells Beach in Victoria with his partner Tahlia, their four young adults, and his mother. He describes himself first as a kind, generous, open-minded, loving, action-taking man.
show-debra-poneman.html: On a playground in Skokie, Illinois, a thirteen-year-old girl watched two girls invite an outsider into their club and then cruelly take it back. In that moment, Debra Poneman saw something she has never been able to unsee: one person’s pain radiating out through a universe she could suddenly see as a matrix, boomeranging back into the very people who caused it. She made a silent promise that day. She would never consciously do anything that hurt another person. That promise became the through-line of everything she has since built. Debra is the founder of Yes to Success, the seminar company she launched in 1980 that grew within three years to twelve major U.S. cities and representatives in nine countries on four continents, without the internet, without fax machines, on phones attached to walls with curly cords. She has spent decades teaching meditation through the Art of Living Foundation and her AWAKE Method, reaching hundreds of thousands of people. And when Katherine asks her what matters most in her life right now, she answers without hesitation: being a good friend and a good mother. This conversation moves through the formation of a philosophy, the morning in 1980 when Debra woke up knowing what she would do for the rest of her life, a near-death experience in 2014 in which she watched words pull her back from death and push her toward it, and the quiet conviction she carries now that every act of presence, every refusal to judge, every moment of treating the person in front of you as the most important person in the world, adds light to a world that needs it. There is a picnic bench at East Prairie School, somewhere in the suburbs of Chicago, and on it a group of girls who call themselves the Cleftos. They are not mean girls. They are the cool girls, which is a different thing, and on this particular day one of them walks over with a girl who is decidedly not cool and says, guess what, we brought you here because we want you in the club. The uncool girl’s eyes light up. You could have handed her a million dollars and it would not have meant as much. And then they tell her they were only joking. They would never let her in. The thirteen-year-old sitting at the bench feels her heart break into pieces. But something else happens too, something she has never quite stopped describing in the decades since. She sees the universe open up like a matrix. She watches the rejected girl’s sadness travel outward to the furthest ends of creation. And she watches it boomerang straight back into the two girls who caused it, and fry the hell out of them. That girl at the bench is Debra Poneman. She is now in her seventies, the founder of a seminar company that reached the world before the world had email, and she will tell you that everything she has taught since traces back to that bench. One person’s pain radiates into all of creation. And it returns to its source. A street in Skokie full of kids She wants you to know her childhood was happy. She says it almost as an apology, the way some people apologise for not having suffered enough to be interesting. Two loving parents. A small house in Skokie. A street where every door let out two or three more children, and the games of kick the can ran until someone’s mother stood on a porch and called a name into the dark. She attended East Prairie School with the same children from kindergarten through eighth grade. Some of them are her friends still, sixty-seven years on. When one of her oldest friends lost her husband, Debra flew to Chicago without thinking twice. The Cleftos still gather when she comes to town. Her former husband, Fred, once told her she should write a book called something like, even though I had a happy childhood, I could still become someone who changes how people live. It made her laugh. But it points at something true about her. The playground did not crush her by way of hardship. It opened her by way of clarity. She watched what cruelty does and made a vow on the spot, to the God of her understanding, that she would never knowingly do anything to hurt another person. She was thirteen. She has not kept it perfectly. She will tell you that herself, plainly, more than once. She has kept it well. Years later she put the vision to a teacher. She had begun Transcendental Meditation in 1970, and by 1971 she was training to teach it, turning twenty-one during the course. The Beach Boys were in her small group. They sang her happy birthday. For the whole decade of the 1970s she taught TM full time and served as director of admissions at Maharishi International University in Fairfield, Iowa, where she also took her degree. When she finally met Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, she asked him whether it was true, what she had seen at thirteen. That one person’s pain radiates into all of creation. That it boomerangs back and embeds itself in whoever caused it. He said yes. The morning after the seminar that was not about money By the end of the seventies, she had reached a private conclusion she states with characteristic bluntness. Woman does not live by mantra alone. She needed health insurance. She needed a car to insure. She did what seemed obvious from Fairfield, Iowa: she moved to Los Angeles, where everybody is rich, and she began selling investments because that looked like a fast way to money. She was, by her own accounting, a complete failure. In a full year she sold exactly one investment, and the buyer was her father. A friend at her financial firm, watching her struggle, invited her to a seminar at the Learning Annex billed as a money event. It was not a money event. It was a new-age gathering, and the man on stage was talking about vibration twenty years before Rhonda Byrne’s The Secret made the idea a publishing phenomenon. If you spend your life talking about how poor you are, he said, you vibrate with lack, and success will approach and bounce off you like a note off the wrong tuning fork. And here is the part that lodged in her: one of the surest ways to become prosperous is to help other people prosper. Mentor them. Connect them. Wish them well. She went home. She slept. And the next thing is the whole hinge of her life. I woke up in the morning and I thought, I know what I’m going to do for the rest of my life. I’m going to teach what that guy is teaching, how to change your vibration so that you attract what you want. For six months she read. Napoleon Hill. Wallace Wattles. Florence Scovel Shinn. Catherine Ponder. She built her own seminar out of what she found and called it Yes to Success. The year was 1980. Within three years it had spread to twelve major American cities, with representatives teaching in nine countries across four continents. She wants you to hold that against the calendar. This was a quarter of a century before the internet. The telephones were attached to walls by curly cords. Calling overseas meant shouting can you hear me into static. There was no fax machine. She built it on belief and curly cords, and it went around the world. She has an explanation for how, and it is not about her cleverness. An idea arrives, she says, because you are the one meant to bring it into being. It is whispered into your ear, and if you do not move on it, it goes to someone who will. When the path is unclear, that is the flow Her second husband, Fred, telephoned her one day to say he had finally understood something that had nagged her for years, why the law of attraction never felt completely accurate. Fred called it the attraction of law: natural laws already running through the universe, already in current, and the work is to fall into them. Katherine met that idea with a sentence of her own, from the territory she has been living in since she left a long corporate life. When the path is clear, she said, you are not in flow. When the path is unclear, that is when you are in flow. Debra took it gently, the way she takes most things, and turned it back toward silence. Because the current is not loud. Source does not speak to a person running around like a chicken with its head cut off, or sitting in a corporate meeting spinning twenty plates. It speaks in quiet. This is why meditation, which she has now taught for fifty-three years, sits underneath everything else she does. Try to build a skyscraper of success without it and you are pouring a tower onto no foundation. The tall buildings go down deep first. She is exact about her own practice, and unhurried in describing it. She rises, washes, drinks water with lemon, no coffee, no food before the morning sitting. A short stretch, eight or ten minutes of asanas. Then about fifteen minutes of breathwork, then twenty minutes of meditation, then a further ten of advanced practice she learned through the Art of Living Foundation. She teaches meditation now through that foundation and earns nothing from it. No fee. No toaster, as she puts it, if someone signs up. She does not promise it makes life perfect, because she does not believe in perfection inside a relative world. What she describes instead is a slow loosening. There is a man in a purple shirt, and something about him makes you want to flee, and you do not know that the reason is a uncle who wore a shiny purple shirt and frightened you as a child. The impression is lodged in the nervous system, what the Sanskrit calls a samskara. Meditation, she says, does not require you to relive it or analyse it. The deep rest simply dissolves it. First the man in the purple shirt is unbearable. Then he is merely uncomfortable. Then there is nothing left in you for the purple shirt to strike against, and he is just a man in a shirt. Maharishi gave her an image for it that she still hands on. An inflexible nervous system holds a hurt like a line carved in stone. You replay the moment you embarrassed yourself, and you cringe at it for years. After enough meditation, a fresh hurt lands more like a line drawn in sand, and a day’s wind and rain take it. Eventually it is a line on water. The impression is made and does not stay. A nurse said she would be fine, and she saw the words In 2014 she came home on a Sunday from a country far from home where she had not been careful about what she ate, sitting on ashram floors eating off banana leaves. She thought she was only dehydrated from the flight. By the following Saturday she was lying in bed thinking she could die there and nobody would know, because she lived alone. She called her favourite healer. He looked in on her from a distance and told her she was in serious trouble and would help her only if she did exactly as he said. She agreed to anything. He told her to call 911 immediately. The paramedics had to break into her apartment. Her blood pressure was 52 over 28, a reading she says should have meant she was already gone. There was no time to reach the hospital she asked for, so they took her to a small one around the corner, and in the emergency room she began to die. She knew it because she could see the room from two places at once. With her eyes open she watched the staff rush around her. With her eyes closed she watched the same scene from somewhere else entirely. And from that other vantage point she saw something she has spent the last decade telling people about. A nurse fumbled an IV bag and dropped it on the gurney, and the others shot her a look. But Debra saw that in bending down, that nurse moved her head clear of a monitor, and another nurse gasped and made an adjustment that saved her life. There are no mistakes in the universe. She saw it, she says, not as a slogan but as a fact, every movement of every hand orchestrated by a divine light. Then came the part that became her life’s second vow. A nurse put a hand on the shoulder of her weeping former husband, who had been called to her side, and said, don’t worry, she’s going to be fine. And Debra saw the words leave the nurse’s mouth. They were carried on a sparkling light, and they entered her body and began pulling her back toward life. Moments later the doctor looked at the monitors and said in an urgent voice, get that blood pressure up, we’re losing her. And those words came out too, but they came out as a grey-brown gunk that smelled like a swamp, and they pushed her back toward death. She made a deal with God, which she says she is fond of doing. If you let me live, I promise I will tell everybody I can about the power of their words. Thou shalt decree a thing. She’s going to be fine. I started becoming fine. We’re losing her. I started dying again. She lived. She has since told that story to something like a hundred thousand people. The lesson she draws from it is hard and unsentimental. We are forever blaming our lives on a lousy partner, ungrateful children, a witch of a mother, an insecure boss. But the words we speak over a person, he’s an idiot, he’s a moron, he’s evil, do not merely describe them. They strengthen in that person the very thing we say we cannot stand. She quotes Jack Canfield: take full responsibility for your life and it becomes a blessing. What she has actually built, and what she will not call the most important thing Yes to Success is forty-six years old. It has run in twelve American cities and through representatives in nine countries on four continents. Tens of thousands, probably hundreds of thousands, have gone through her programmes or heard her online; she says she does not count. She came within reach of her own daytime television talk show and walked away from it to be a full-time mother at home, to people’s horror, because she has always told her students to follow their hearts and saw no honest way around following her own. There is a story she tells that holds the whole philosophy in miniature. At one of her earliest seminars in 1980, a college student came bouncing up afterward, declaring she would quit graduate school to be Debra’s assistant. The room was full of people who wanted Debra’s attention. She could have glanced past the eager girl. Instead she gave her her whole attention and listened to her ideas without judging her for being young. That girl was Marci Shimoff, who went on to sell twenty million Chicken Soup for the Soul books and to appear in The Secret. Fifteen years later, when Debra was at home raising her children, it was Marci who handed her the chance to write a bestseller of her own. This is the engine of everything she teaches. The person in front of you, at any given moment, is the most important person in the world at that time. The only reason we scan the room for someone more useful, she says, is that we do not trust we live in a benevolent universe. Give a stranger your full presence and the universe brings you the person who signs your book. And yet, asked what matters to her now, she does not lead with any of it. She thought, before the conversation even began, about what she would say if she were asked. She has the company, yes. But what is important to her in this season is being a good friend and a good mother. Two biological children, two more who lived with her for years, seventeen godchildren, several of them in Minneapolis having a hard time of it, one of them a security guard who calls at night from a ten-hour shift in thirty-below wind and says, Auntie Deb, I can’t do this anymore. She shows up. She pours love in. That is the whole of it. What’s important in my life right now is being a good friend and being a good mom. Watch your talk; the children are watching everything Of all the moments in a long and visible life, the one she names as the greatest happened in a sentence she did not even speak. Her son, an NBA agent who fights for the pay owed to young athletes, was asked once whether he had learned his sense of justice from sitting in on his mother’s Yes to Success seminars. No, he said. He did not really know much about what his mother teaches. He learned it from watching how she and his father actually live. She says she could die happy on that sentence. Then she turns it toward anyone reading who is raising a child or being watched by a younger person: your actions are so loud the words underneath them cannot be heard. The children arriving on the planet now see everything. Do not tell them to be one way and live another. This is the quiet centre of her practice. Guard your words because they have dominion over life and death. Refuse to need to be right, because being right at the cost of another person’s feelings makes them wrong, and a week from now no one will remember who won. Stop being the discouragement committee for other people’s dreams. When a friend tells you what they hope to build, do not list the ways it could fail, because you have just planted those failures, and the mind builds what it is given. There is a softer practice she shares too, born of an evening when she and her friend Mary Pat sat at lunch tearing apart a spiritual teacher who had been dishonest and cruel. They stopped themselves and made a game of it. Three good things. Each of them had to name three good things about the woman. By the third, they were in tears, because hurt people hurt people, and the wound underneath the cruelty had become visible. She does the same now with the people whose politics frighten her. There but for the grace of God. Had she grown up where they grew up, she would believe what they believe. You do not have to like a person’s positions. You can still love the divine spark in them and put your attention on whatever good you can find. What her life is asking us to see Go back to the playground. A girl watches another girl’s heart break and sees, in the same instant, two things most of us spend a lifetime refusing to believe. That what we do to one another does not stop at the edge of the moment, but travels out and comes back. And that the harm we cause lodges first and deepest in ourselves. Everything that followed is a working-out of that single vision. The seminar built on the idea that helping others prosper is how you prosper. The years of silence underneath the success, the insistence that the skyscraper needs its foundation poured first. The vow on the emergency-room table to never again speak over anyone a word she would not wish made true. The son who learned justice not from a lecture but from a kitchen. What she offers is a current you can step into, again and again. We live in a relative world, she says, and perfection is not on offer inside one. She puts her own record at about ninety-five per cent and laughs. It is not a destination but a current you can fall into on an ordinary morning before coffee, in a sentence held back, in the full attention given to a stranger who looks like nobody. For anyone carrying the weight of the world’s darkness more than they can explain, she would say this: you feel it because you are the kind of person who feels it, and that same sensitivity is the reason you want to add something good. The darkness was not made by your noticing it. It was already there. What is being asked of you is only the next small thing: one cruel word held back before it can leave your mouth. Each time, she says, the universe says yes back to you. And she keeps a promise made between life and death, decades ago, in a room that smelled of swamp and sparkled at the same time. She tells people their words have power. She watched it with her own inner eye. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Debra This conversation runs a little over an hour and moves the way the best conversations do, looping back on itself and ending somewhere neither of them expected. There are near-death visions and playground heartbreaks and Beach Boys singing happy birthday, and underneath all of it a single steady invitation to slow down and watch what your words and your attention are doing in the world. Pour a cup of something. Sit with it. There is no hurry. The library is always here. The person standing in front of you at any given moment is always the most important person in the world at that time. Now is the time to cling to your spiritual practices so that when the world shakes, you remain unshakable. Every time we treat somebody as the most important person in the world, every time we don’t need to be right, we bring more light into the world. Debra Poneman is the founder of Yes to Success, the seminar company she created in 1980 after a decade of teaching Transcendental Meditation and serving as director of admissions at Maharishi International University in Fairfield, Iowa. Within three years her programmes had spread to twelve American cities and to representatives in nine countries across four continents, long before the internet existed. A bestselling author and a teacher of meditation for more than fifty years, she now teaches breath and meditation practices through the Art of Living Foundation and her AWAKE Method, having reached hundreds of thousands of people. She divides her time between San Miguel de Allende, Mexico, and the people she loves.
show-robyne-hanley-dafoe.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Dr. Robyne Hanley-Dafoe, award-winning educational behaviourist, globally recognised resilience and hope researcher, bestselling author, and one of the most trusted voices on what it actually takes to keep going when everything says stop. Robyne has delivered more than 2,000 keynotes worldwide and written three books including Calm Within the Storm and Stress Wisely. She is also a woman who was institutionalised at 16, got sober, and then drove her car off a road in a snowstorm into the Otonabee River. The car sank fifteen to twenty feet. She swam out through the window, exhaled in complete darkness, and followed the bubbles from her own breath to the surface. A stranger named Joseph, who had seen her tyre tracks in the snow, crawled across the ice with a chain and pulled her to shore. He was later awarded the Governor General’s Award for bravery. Robyne woke up in hospital with one thought: you’re here, do right by it. This conversation covers resilience, hope as a skill, what it means to borrow someone else’s belief until you can find your own, and why the helpers need to get their hope back. She could not see anything. The car had gone off the road, down the embankment, through the ice, and sunk fifteen to twenty feet into the Otonabee River with her inside it. The seatbelt would not release. The door would not open; the water pressure had already begun to crush the frame. She worked her fingers into the seam where the window met the door, pulled it off its tracks, slid it down, and swam out into darkness so complete she had no way to know which direction was the surface. She exhaled. The bubbles rose. She followed them, swimming toward her own breath, up through the black water, until her face hit ice. She was downstream now, pinned beneath sheets of it, the current pulling at her winter coat, her boots, everything heavy and cold and dragging her back. She clawed toward the middle of the channel where the ice thinned. Every time she tried to pull herself out, the ice cracked and she fell back in. Her palms were bleeding. She held on. A man named Joseph had seen the tyre tracks in the snow and pulled over. He fashioned a piece of wood into the shape of an axe to spread his weight, crawled out across the ice, and slid her a chain. He was later awarded the Governor General’s Award for bravery, the highest honour a Canadian civilian can receive for risking their own life to save a stranger. Robyne Hanley-Dafoe woke up in hospital thinking not about what she had survived, but about what she owed. You’re here. Do right by it. She has been doing right by it for thirty years. The girl who felt the world differently Robyne grew up in Ontario in what she describes simply as the best childhood you could hope for. Two parents who loved hard and showed up. Security, structure, sports. A life that looked, from the outside, complete. From the inside, from as early as kindergarten, she felt the world differently. She ached when her mother dropped her off at school, clung in ways her peers didn’t, felt things with an intensity that nobody around her had the language for. The word ADHD was not applied to girls like her in those years. The word neurodivergent did not exist in that classroom. What existed was the experience of being pulled from her mother by teachers, of feeling separate in a crowd, of emotions that arrived bigger than the room could hold. She carried that intensity into high school and it made her, in her own word, susceptible: to rejection, to the wrong crowd, to the particular shame of struggling in a life that looked like it should be easy. A grade-eight teacher told her, in front of her classmates, that she was not smart enough to finish high school. She says she believed that person. And from grade eight onwards it was, in her words, an absolute free fall. She dropped out. She was dealing with addiction and self-harm and a family who loved her helplessly, who would go to the ends of the earth for their daughter and could not get to where she was. She was institutionalised at sixteen in an adult psychiatric facility, simply because no one knew what else to do to keep her safe. And she was ashamed, deeply ashamed, that she was struggling at all. Her life had every ingredient for happiness. She could not account for the darkness. This is the part of the conversation that Katherine holds very carefully. Because this kind of darkness is not dramatic. There is no visible wound, no obvious cause, no single story to point to. There is simply a pilot light going out. A vast black hole where possibility used to be. Robyne could not imagine herself at eighteen. She could not wish-cast a year ahead. And beneath the darkness, a quiet inner voice told her that her family would be better off without the weight of her. She was sixteen. She was still a child, holding something no child should have to hold alone. What her mother saw Sitting with Robyne in that facility, Robyne’s mother did something that neither minimised nor drowned in the swamp of despair. She did not argue. She did not reassure. She said: let me share with you what I see for you. And then she described it. She told Robyne that she would be an amazing mother. That her capacity for compassion would change the game. She spoke over her daughter the future she could already see, the one Robyne could not see for herself. And Robyne, who respected her mother deeply even when she could not feel anything else, made a decision. She would borrow that belief. She did not feel it. She did not see it. But if her mother believed it, she was willing to fight for it. I borrowed her belief until I could find my own. And it was enough to fight for. There is a distinction Katherine draws in this conversation between empathy and what she calls true empathy, and Robyne’s mother is the proof of it. Empathy sits with someone. True empathy sees the soul when the person cannot see it themselves. What Leslie Hanley-Dafoe did in that facility was not comfort. It was witness. She held an image of her daughter’s future with such clarity and certainty that Robyne could lean against it like a wall. Years later, Robyne’s mother told her something she had kept to herself for a long time. Before Robyne’s dark season, her father, a television producer, had been taping an interview with a woman from the Catholic diocese. Her mother had gone along and found herself drawn to this woman. The woman had pulled Leslie aside. She said: there will be hard times for your daughter. But don’t lose faith. She will make it through. Leslie had held that message quietly through everything that followed, and it had been part of what made it possible for her to show up, day after day, steady and certain, when her daughter was not. Robyne got sober. She re-enrolled. She was getting ready to step back into her life. And then she drove into the river. What the bubbles taught her She says it is not lost on her that her hope book comes out thirty years to the day of the car accident. Some things are too precise to be coincidence. What she discovered in that river, fifteen feet underwater in the dark, was not courage in the inspirational sense. It was something more pragmatic and more profound: she had only what she had, and what she had was enough. Her mother had always told her she could figure things out. Step by step. So she looked at what was available. She could not open the door. She could pull the window off its tracks. She did. She swam out. She could not see the surface. She could exhale. She did. The bubbles rose. She followed them. She did not know which way was up. But she knew that bubbles rise in water. She moved toward the one thing she knew to be true. A Navy SEAL commander named Mark Devine told Robyne something at the start of this year that she says dropped her to her knees. After hearing her story, he said: do you know that you made yourself saveable that night? He meant it technically; most people, he told her, would not have gotten out of the car. But Robyne has been sitting with the phrase differently. Making yourself saveable. Getting yourself to the point where help can reach you. Being willing, when you have almost nothing left, to follow what you know toward the surface, so that the Joseph waiting at the edge of the ice can do the rest. She woke up in hospital with her mother beside her and knew, without equivocation, that she had been spared. She had watched teenagers she’d known die in the same circumstances she had survived. She felt no survivor guilt. She felt a calling. You’re here. Do right by it. She says it was less obligation than vocation. The work was there. She had been given time to do it. Now get to work. The work she has built What followed was years of methodical construction. Correspondence school to finish her high school diploma, because she was too raw to go back in person. College at St. Lawrence in Kingston, the only school that would take her with her mishmash of transcripts. They took a shot on her. She got the reps in: showed up, put in effort, discovered that school, given the right supports, was not nearly as difficult as the social world had been. She did her first undergraduate degree. Then a second. A master’s. Then, much later, her doctorate at Western. Almost two decades as a university professor, teaching and researching human resilience. And then, in 2019, a deliberate step away from the academy to take the work somewhere it had not been: directly into the hands of the people who needed it most. She has delivered more than 2,000 keynotes worldwide. Her first book, Calm Within the Storm: A Pathway to Everyday Resiliency, introduced her framework for what it actually takes to keep showing up when life is hard. Her second, Stress Wisely, addresses what she found as a through-line in her research: that stress, understood and channelled correctly, can be an ally rather than an enemy. Her third book, on hope, arrives thirty years after the river. She describes it as the natural conclusion of everything she has studied, and the most urgent thing she knows how to offer right now. She trained as a behaviourist, which shapes how she sees everything. She looks at habits, routines, rituals. She asks what practices allow people to stay well while doing the work that matters. Her ADHD, which she describes with genuine joy as the biggest gift, lets her take in vast amounts of information and find the simplest through-line. She is a knowledge translator: someone who takes complex science and makes it accessible to the person standing in front of her who is tired and scared and still trying. The three puppies causing a ruckus in her studio during this recording are not a distraction. They are exactly the point. She lives the whole thing at once. Why the helpers need this most Katherine names the four existential crises of our moment in this conversation: Social Fracture, Economic Fragility, Planetary Breakdown, Information Collapse. They are not metaphors. They are the actual conditions inside which the people who show up for others are trying to hold the line. And the fourth, Information Collapse, is what Katherine calls the gasoline on the fire of the other three: a world in which truth is no longer anchored, in which disinformation accelerates faster than wisdom can catch it. Robyne says something in this conversation that will sit in the chest of anyone who has spent years trying to be useful in that world: the helpers are tired. The people who care most, who give most, who have been showing up heroically for others through pandemic, through political fracture, through the particular grief of watching the world become stranger and harder, are running low. And the world does not stop needing them. She names something that I suspect many of us have not admitted out loud: that getting our hopes up right now feels dangerous. That it is actually easier to expect the worst and be pleasantly surprised, and that the body processes its resources completely differently in a state of hope compared to a state of fear or despair. The aperture of how we see the world changes when we are in a place of possibility. Hope, in her research, outperformed mindfulness during times of adversity. Co-creating bright futures in community, sitting with someone and asking what are you hoping for right now, and may I hope with you, produced measurable effects that mindfulness, for all its gifts, did not replicate under extreme conditions. This is not sentimentality. It is science. The practice she offers is intentionally low to the ground. Gather people. Ask what they are hoping for. Hold it with them. You do not need to fix anything. You do not need to know the answer. You need to stay in the room and say: I will hope alongside you until you can hold it yourself. Borrowed belief, expressed in community, scales in a way that individual inner work cannot. Her mother held hope for Robyne when Robyne had none. Joseph held his body on the ice so Robyne could hold on long enough to be pulled out. The image is not complicated. The image is very old. We walk each other home. She says this quoting Ram Dass, and she means every word of it. What she learned after loss Robyne lost her mother in 2012, at thirty-three. She says she had not yet hit her stride of true service. Things were better than they had been, but the fullness of what she was meant to do had not yet arrived. Losing the person who had been her anchor, the only person from whom she could receive, sent her into a grief that was also a recognising. She realised, sitting with the loss, that in the thirty-three years they had together, her mother had been preparing her to live without her. The skills. The empathy. The capacity to see the person underneath the label, the behaviour, the fear. All of it had been given to her by a woman who knew she would not always be there to hold the belief herself. Everything Robyne has built since, the research, the books, the work with military families and healthcare workers and school systems across the world, came from a woman who sat in a psychiatric facility and refused to see her daughter as broken. Who described a future with such specificity and conviction that her sixteen-year-old daughter, who felt nothing, was willing to fight for it. I know what it feels like to have somebody show up for you without the judgment. And at the end of the day, we’re just walking each other home. My mom walked me as far as she could. Now I get to help other people on their walk. What their life is asking us to see There is a particular kind of person this conversation is for, and I suspect you know if you are one of them. You have been the helper. You are the person others come to when they cannot find their own way through. You have sat with people in hard seasons and tried to see clearly enough for both of you. And somewhere in the last few years, quietly and without much announcement, your own pilot light has started to flicker. Robyne’s story does not ask you to compare your suffering to hers. She would be the first to resist that. She has never believed that because she survived something, you must be able to survive yours in the same way. What she offers is quieter and more specific: evidence that borrowed belief is real. That hope does not have to originate inside you to work. That if one person in the room can hold the image of your future with enough certainty, you can lean on that until you find your own. Katherine shares something of herself in this conversation that deserves its own quiet moment. In the autumn of 2018, she had a plan. Her life was, by every external measure, full: marriage, four children, a long corporate career. She had arrived at a place where she genuinely believed her children would be better off without the weight of her. A friend named Leanne said nothing prescriptive and nothing comforting. She asked a single question: would you like me to send you the intergenerational trauma research resulting from suicide? And in that moment, the plan cracked. Because Katie’s hope, in the season that followed, was not yet about herself. It was about her children, about their futures, about refusing to pass the darkness forward. It was borrowed. It was external. It was enough to begin. Hope does not need to be whole to work. It needs to be present somewhere in the room. For anyone reading this who has been carrying something in the dark for a while: you do not need to know which way is up. You just need to exhale. The bubbles will rise. Follow what you know to be true, step by small step, toward the thinner ice in the middle of the channel. And trust that there is a Joseph somewhere, watching the snow, who will see where you went. Robyne spent thirty years building something from the material of her own survival. She did not prettify it. She did not rush past the dark parts to get to the after picture. She made herself saveable, as many times as it took, and then she turned around and held the chain for everyone who came after her. Her third book arrives thirty years to the day she swam out of that river. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on this conversation This episode runs just over an hour and moves, as most Sincerely conversations do, between the deeply personal and the professionally specific. Robyne is warm, funny, precise, and at one point genuinely moved. The three puppies are a recurring presence. The conversation is one of the most complete portraits the show has produced of what it looks like to build a life out of the hardest material, with honesty and without performance. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I borrowed her belief until I could find my own. And it was enough to fight for. Hope is not a feeling. It is a practice. And it can be built, maintained, and borrowed from someone who holds it for you when you cannot hold it yourself. Getting our hopes up right now is a form of being heroic. Because it is scary to get our hopes up. But the body processes its resources very differently when we are in a state of hope versus a state of fear or despair. Dr. Robyne Hanley-Dafoe is an award-winning educational behaviourist, globally recognised resilience and hope researcher, and bestselling author based in Ontario, Canada. She spent nearly two decades at university researching human resiliency before stepping away from academia in 2019 to bring research-informed practices directly to organisations and communities worldwide. She has delivered more than 2,000 keynotes and written three books: Calm Within the Storm, Stress Wisely, and a forthcoming work on hope. She is a mother of three teenagers, a lover of trivia, and the woman who followed her own breath to the surface of a frozen river.
show-eila-park-robertson.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Eila Park Robertson, former ABC News journalist, award-winning filmmaker, crisis communications strategist, and founder of Anecdotia, a production agency focused on racial, social, and climate justice storytelling. Eila led communications for the City of Portland during over 100 consecutive nights of civil unrest, navigating daily racial harassment, hundreds of death threats, and a period of personal crisis she speaks about with complete honesty. What she built from that experience is a mission: to help progressive governments, advocates, and organisations communicate in ways that actually reach the people they most need to reach. Her central argument is simple and urgent. Calling people out has failed. Calling people in is the only thing that works. This conversation covers her Korean immigrant parents, her violent father, the seven-minute video she posted after the Atlanta spa shootings that changed everything, the husband who fell in love with her when she could see nothing worth loving in herself, and what she now knows with certainty: the price of peace is pain, and there is no shortcut through it. She was in her apartment in Vancouver. It was 2021. Her wedding had just been featured in Vogue, a celebration months in the making, and the publication date had landed on the same day as the Atlanta spa shootings, when six Asian women were killed and the continent was still absorbing what that meant. She had her tweet deck open. She was watching the responses arrive in real time. The messages were in the thousands. What they said, I will not repeat here in full. The gist: she was a mail-order bride. She was a servant. She had been collected. The words aimed at her body, her race, her marriage, her presence in public life alongside a prominent white man were the kind of words that, as she told me, even now she will not say aloud on a podcast. She collapsed to the floor of her apartment. She wept for hours. And then something shifted, the way things shift when you have been broken to the point where there is nothing left to protect. She stood up. She took her phone out. She put it on a tripod. She pressed record. And for seven minutes, Eila Park Robertson spoke. The formation She was born in Queens and raised in New Jersey, the daughter and granddaughter of Korean immigrants who had arrived in North America with barely enough language to get by and a vision for a life they could not build in South Korea at the time. Her parents started a business. They built something in a country that did not always make room for them. “One does not do that,” she said, “unless you are really exceptional and extraordinary. You have a vision.” The ethos was baked into her, she told me, over and over through childhood. That ethos was survival married to belief. It was not passive. It was not modest. It was the insistence, inherited rather than learned, that the world contained more than it was currently offering. Her childhood was, in her own words, a life of real polarities. Eastern mindset in a Western world. She was in classrooms that were, as she put it, eighty percent white or higher, trying to explain to classmates why her food smelled the way it did while they held their noses. She navigated all of it. And somewhere in the navigating, she developed what she calls buoyancy: an ability to move through all sorts of spaces with ease that came from having always been between worlds. Her father was brilliant and violent. He would take scissors or staplers and throw them at her mother in the office. She witnessed this as a small child. She watched it and she understood, even then, that her father was in a great deal of pain. That knowing did not make the violence less. It sat alongside the violence, strange and unresolvable, the way children often carry things that adults cannot. What it produced in her, she told me, was a desire. A long, determined desire to become strong. Years of reading about women who were strong. Years of absorbing them. Years of wanting, with the kind of wanting that does not let you go, to be someone who could not be levelled by what she had seen. “I became someone who dreamed of becoming strong,” she said. “And years and years and years of dreaming that ultimately got me to a place where I finally have that strength. Because I desired it.” I keep coming back to that word, desired. She did not say she worked for it, or earned it, or survived her way into it. She desired it. As though strength were something you could call toward yourself across the years of a childhood, quietly and with great seriousness, until it arrived. The journalism years, and the turning She spent more than a decade in broadcast journalism, working as a reporter, anchor, and foreign correspondent for ABC News, KOIN-TV in Portland, and WNCN in North Carolina. She covered the climate crisis on the west coast. She covered geopolitical tensions in East Asia. She won an RTDNA award. She worked across the United States, South Korea, and internationally, doing the work of making the world’s events legible to the people watching at home. She also navigated, throughout those years, what it costs to be an Asian woman in newsrooms and on camera. The sexualisation. The questioning of competence based on appearance. The rooms that looked past her. None of this is abstract for Eila. She was there for it, professionally and personally, through more than a decade of it. When Donald Trump began campaigning heavily in 2015, she was covering those campaigns. She described watching, in real time, the rapid shift the media was undergoing. It had been moving towards entertainment-style journalism for years, she said, but this was different: swift, accelerating, a turning point. She found herself becoming increasingly unable to report on both sides of what she was witnessing. “I started to get to a point,” she said, “where I realised this isn’t a matter of both sides anymore. This is a matter of truth and lies.” She left journalism. In September 2018, she was appointed Director of Communications for the City of Portland, Oregon, in the Office of the Mayor. She walked into one of the most violent periods in the city’s history. Portland had held the record for the most consecutive nightly riots, over a hundred in a row. Federal agents. White supremacists in the streets. Antifa. A mayor’s office in disarray. She described the city as being in a state of complete crisis and chaos when she arrived. Every day for two years, she walked into City Hall and walked out of it. She was followed. She was spat on. She was harassed by bloggers and YouTubers who held cameras four inches from her face and shouted every racial slur they knew, looking for a reaction. As a Korean woman who had also been on broadcast television, there was an extensive inventory of ways to try to dehumanise her, and they used all of them. There were also the daily press conferences, the national reporters descending on the city whenever an event broke, the sparring with colleagues she admired over news coverage she believed was reckless. Every day, she said, was warfare. Two years of that really breaks you down in every imaginable way. The breaking point, when it came, did not arrive in a dramatic form. She got a bicycle. Within an hour it was stolen, and an anarchist tweeted about it, offering to return the bike if she stopped working for a fascist. She worked for a Democratic mayor. The next day, they came to her home, unbolted the secured gate, took the new bicycle, and tweeted again: you are never going to be safe. The death threats had been ongoing. The deepfake pornographic images had been ongoing. This was one bike, one tweet, one small thing in a long inventory of things. It was, somehow, the thing that broke her open. She lay awake at two in the morning in the middle of all of it, the workload, the threats, the social humiliation, and she began to think that not waking up would be a gift. “For the first time in my life,” she told me, “it got me to a point where I was actively thinking about suicide.” What she said next I have been sitting with since. That experience, for the first time thinking of ending my own life, was strangely where I was reborn. What the floor revealed She met her husband, Gregor Robertson, during the Portland years. He is the former Mayor of Vancouver, one of the city’s longest-serving, who had built a global climate leadership profile after leaving office. She was manically depressed, she told me. Actively thinking about suicide. Being followed home by white supremacists and Antifa. And somehow, in the middle of all of that, Gregor saw her. “He could not see anything else,” she said. “He saw the purest light in me.” She was confounded by it. She could not see what he was seeing. She did not know what about her, in that state, could possibly be worth seeing. But he kept seeing it, and it took someone who showed her, for the first time, what unconditional love was, to bring her back. I wish it was a story of where I was able to rise up on my own and find myself and heal from it. But it was really my current husband who saved me. I have heard many versions of this story across the conversations I have had for this show: the moment another person’s seeing of us becomes the mirror we could not hold for ourselves. Katherine’s own coming through required someone who could hold her when she could not hold herself. What Eila is describing is the same human truth. We are not solitary creatures. We do not save ourselves alone. Sometimes the most courageous thing a person can do is allow someone to see them clearly, at the exact moment when they cannot see themselves at all. They married in 2020, in an intimate ceremony at Stanley Park in Vancouver, beneath the largest maple tree in Canada. A marriage commissioner and two close friends as witnesses. The families couldn’t be there; it was the pandemic, and they had chosen to elope. They held the news privately for four months before their Vogue feature published in March 2021. The day it published was the day of the Atlanta spa shootings. She sat on her apartment floor, she wept, and then she stood up. What emerged was seven minutes of radical honesty, recorded on her phone, posted to the world: what it costs to be an Asian woman in public life, how she had been sexualised for standing beside male colleagues, how her professional accomplishments had been erased in favour of the story people wanted to tell about her body and her marriage. She called out everyone who had been holding her accountable to their projections of what an Asian woman should be or do or belong to. She said: this is who I am. How dare you. That was the turning point. It was the moment I found my voice, and it was the moment the world heard my voice. She was asked to appear on national news for a month to discuss the hypersexualisation of Asian women and its history. There was, as she said, a hunger for it: Asian women were being beaten and killed on the streets, and suddenly the world was listening. That was when her voice was injected into that space. And she has not stopped since. What she carries Psychologists have studied what happens to the brain when a person is socially humiliated. The research Eila cites is striking and precise: when you are reading threatening and dehumanising messages, the part of your brain that activates is the same part that activates when you touch something hot. Your nervous system cannot differentiate between physical pain and social attack. The experience is the same. The body registers both as injury. This matters for understanding what two years in Portland actually cost her, and what it cost the hundreds of elected officials and their teams whose mental health and wholeness Eila now cares deeply about. She has a vast love, she told me, for bringing awareness to the humanity of people in government service: the people holding cities, states, provinces, and countries together, who are seen from the outside as political agents or dehumanised figures, who absorb the weight of a community’s needs and fears every single day. “When that becomes so toxic,” she said, “it has a profound impact on your ability to be effective and whole and continue on.” She told me about an early lesson from Portland: she came in with precision, ready to fix the immediate mess, and what she found was that her team needed something else first. They needed to grieve. You cannot fix an absolute mess at the same time as the people around you are still in the middle of the experience of it. The fixing and the healing have to happen together, and neither can happen without the other being acknowledged. I have carried that observation since she said it. It reaches far beyond government communications. It reaches into every organisation that has been through something hard and moved too quickly past the human cost of it into the business of rebuilding. The work Anecdotia is Eila’s production agency, founded in August 2020, focused exclusively on climate, racial, and social justice storytelling. The name reflects her philosophy: anecdotes with weight, with meaning, with the power to shift what people know and feel and do. She works with national and subnational governments, international agencies, and nonprofits at global climate negotiations, using documentary film and strategic communications to amplify voices that have historically been marginalised from the rooms where decisions are made. She serves on the Global Board of Directors for the International Fund for Animal Welfare, appointed in 2024. She is an ambassador for #Elimin8Hate, standing alongside other prominent Asian-Canadian voices in the work of racial equity and systemic change. Her thesis, stated plainly in our conversation, is this: progressive and left-leaning institutions have largely failed to communicate with emotional resonance, while conservative movements have mastered it. “They have created a world of inclusivity,” she said, and she meant it analytically, not approvingly: a movement that said, are you a little racist? Come on in. Are you frustrated and afraid? You belong here. Progressive messaging, by contrast, had defaulted to cancellation, to purity tests, to the message that if you were imperfect you had no place. The result was predictable. People who were apolitical, confused, or simply wounded looked at those two options and chose the one that didn’t threaten to exclude them the moment they made a mistake. Her mission now is bridge-building. “We have to call people in and stop calling people out.” She is direct about the difficulty of this: it requires progressives to do something genuinely hard, which is to hold space for people whose views they find painful, to resist the pull toward public shaming, to believe that shared humanity is still accessible across the divide. But she has seen it work. She has sat with conservative friends and MAGA friends and watched them pause when she told her story. “It is the only thing that works,” she said. “Our shared humanity is what needs to get messaged out.” She calls the communications philosophy she has developed “emotional comms,” and the distinction she draws is precise. Traditional communications: press releases, internal communications, media strategy. Emotional communications: the storytelling arm, the layer that reaches billions because it speaks to what people feel before it speaks to what they think. “If you are able to really tap into that world,” she told me, “you have got an audience of millions waiting at your doorstep. Billions.” The film “Lynda (RYN),” which she directed, screened at the 2021 Vancouver Asian Film Festival. It is one entry in a body of work she is building at the intersection of image, story, and systemic change. The price of peace There is a line Eila said in our conversation that I have returned to many times since. The price of peace is pain. There is no other way. There is no shortcut. She was talking about the process by which people become who they are fully meant to be: the breaking down that has to happen before the rebuilding, the forced softening of the shell, the alchemisation that occurs when you are finally stripped of the unnecessary. “There’s an alchemisation that happens in you when you’re being broken down, who you are, and as you’re rebuilding who you are, that fundamentally changes, and it gets stronger and stronger,” she said. She is not romanticising suffering. She is making an empirical observation about what she has witnessed in herself and in the people she has been closest to: that the quietest, most grounded, most peaceful people she knows are often the ones who have been through the hardest things. That the correlation is direct. The price of peace is paid in pain, and there is no route around it. For anyone reading this who is in the middle of something hard and cannot yet see the shape of what it is making of them, I know Eila would want me to say this: the experience is trying to crack you open to your truest self. And when you have the courage to go there, you will find yourself. You will find them. You will find the person you were always meant to be. And then the real becoming begins. There is something particular about Eila’s story that I want to sit with carefully, because it is easy to read it as a story of individual resilience and miss what it is actually about. Her voice did not arrive because she became stronger in isolation. Her voice arrived because Gregor saw her when she could not see herself, because the weight of being witnessed by someone who loved her clearly gave her the ground to stand on. Her becoming was relational. Her speaking out was made possible by partnership. Her husband, now a Canadian federal minister, stood beside her at rallies and in the aftermath of the Vogue piece. He used his platform to amplify her voice rather than speak over it. That choice, in a world where powerful people often flatten the people beside them, was itself a form of advocacy. What Eila and Gregor have built together models something specific: that equity is a practice between people, not just a political position. That allyship, when it is real, means stepping back. What her life is asking us to see Eila Park Robertson walked into our conversation on a winter morning from Ottawa, a city alive with a kind of patriotism she described as serious, warm, and unburdened by rigidity. Her husband had just been elected to federal parliament and appointed Minister of Housing and Infrastructure. She was building Anecdotia at the frontlines of global climate negotiations. She was doing, every day, the work she believes she is on earth to do. She carries her parents and grandparents with her into all of it. She carries the Korean immigrants who survived what they survived and built what they built, who gave her not a formula but an ethos: you have a vision, and you hold it, and you do not let the world tell you it is wrong. She carries her father’s violence as the strange gift it became: the seed of a desire for strength so persistent and so clear that it finally became her. She carries Portland. She carries the floor of the Vancouver apartment. She carries the tripod and the seven minutes and the decision to say everything she had never been allowed to say. What she is asking all of us to consider is whether the stories we tell are wide enough to hold the full range of what people carry. Whether our institutions, our governments, our movements have learned yet to communicate from the heart rather than from the press release. Whether we are calling people in or pushing them away at the moment when they most need a place to land. These are not gentle questions. Eila asks them without flinching and with great tenderness, which is the particular combination that only comes from someone who has learned, through the body, that peace has a price and the price is worth paying. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Eila This conversation runs close to an hour and a quarter. Eila speaks in the way she has learned to speak: without a script, without performance, with the steady and sometimes surprising clarity of someone who has earned her words. She talks about Portland, about the floor in Vancouver, about her parents and her father’s violence, about the communications philosophy she is building and why she believes storytelling is the only mechanism that has ever genuinely moved people across the divide. There is a moment toward the end, when she talks about what she would say to anyone in the middle of their own darkness, that I hope you will find for yourself. There is no hurry. The library is always here. The price of peace is pain. There is no other way. There is no shortcut. The softest and the most peaceful people are the ones who have been through hell and back. It is the only way, it is truly the only way people’s hearts and minds move. I have witnessed my conservative friends, I have witnessed my MAGA friends pause when I am in front of them telling my story or pleading with them: please see the humanity in this situation. And it works. Eila Park Robertson (full name Eileen Park Robertson; Korean name: 박아린 / Park Arin) is an award-winning documentary filmmaker, former broadcast journalist, and founder of Anecdotia, a production agency working exclusively on climate, racial, and social justice storytelling. She spent more than a decade as a reporter and foreign correspondent for ABC News, KOIN-TV, and WNCN, and served as Director of Communications for the City of Portland, Oregon. Her film “Lynda (RYN)” screened at the 2021 Vancouver Asian Film Festival. She serves on the Global Board of Directors for the International Fund for Animal Welfare and is an ambassador for #Elimin8Hate. She lives in the Greater Vancouver area with her husband, Gregor Robertson.
show-anne-marie-slaughter.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Anne-Marie Slaughter, globally recognised scholar, policy innovator, former Director of Policy Planning at the US State Department, the first woman to hold that position, former CEO of New America, and author of nine books including the landmark Unfinished Business: Women, Men, Work, Family. Her 2012 Atlantic article “Why Women Still Can’t Have It All” became the most-read piece in the magazine’s history and sparked a global conversation that has not stopped. Anne-Marie mapped her career in high school. She knew exactly what she wanted and exactly how to get there. Then she walked out of the law firm she had spent her whole early life planning to join because she felt interchangeable with every other associate. A six-year period of drifting began that produced everything she had not planned: a professorship she had never wanted, a marriage she pursued for three years, and eventually a dream job at the State Department that also broke her when it collided with her family. This conversation covers the Belgian-American childhood that gave her an instinct for living between worlds, the drifting years she rarely speaks about publicly, the tsunami that arrived when she told the truth in the Atlantic, the care economy capitalism does not measure, and what it will take to rebuild a world order that begins with people. She was twenty-six. She had done everything right. Oxford for a master’s. Law school. The New York firm she had identified from the outside as the precise institution she needed to pass through on her way to the State Department. She had drawn up the plan in high school, which is either precocious or unnerving depending on the day, and then she had executed it with unusual discipline. She arrived at the summer internship and she looked around and she thought: I am interchangeable with every other associate in this building. Fungible. That was the word she used, years later, sitting across from me on this show. Her college roommate had told her she was the most organised, most driven person she had ever met, that her entire career was mapped out. And standing inside the map, she felt nothing. She walked out. Not at the end of the summer, not after careful deliberation, but as a woman whose body had registered something her plan had not accounted for. A marriage was cracking up. She quit smoking. She didn’t know what to do. What followed, she describes as really drifting. Six years of it, between 26 and 32. A PhD she enrolled in because she couldn’t think what else to do. A professorship she would have told you she would never want. Anne-Marie Slaughter had mapped every road in. She had no map out. And the drifting, it turned out, was where everything she has actually built began. The world she was made between There is a particular quality of attention that comes from growing up between two things. Cultures, languages, ways of eating, registers of feeling. You learn early that neither world is the whole world. You learn to read rooms. You learn that what looks like normal from inside one life looks foreign from the other direction. Anne-Marie grew up in Charlottesville, Virginia, in the 1960s, the daughter of a Virginian lawyer and a Belgian mother who had been put alone in a British boarding school during the Second World War, a small girl who spoke no English, displaced from everything familiar. Her parents met when her father travelled to Brussels on a Rotary fellowship after the Navy. He walked into a party, looked across the room, and saw a 22-year-old Belgian woman. They were engaged three months later. In Charlottesville, the Slaughter family ate differently. Spoke differently. Her mother had a funny accent. They were half European, which was not common in Virginia in the 1960s, not in a city that was still, as Anne-Marie puts it, a long way from the kind of sophisticated, food-literate place it has since become. Every couple of years, the family would travel to Brussels for six weeks. When Anne-Marie was seven, she flew alone. They put her on the plane in Washington. Someone took her off in Brussels. And suddenly she was in a world where everyone spoke French, where dinner was served in the middle of the day with china and crystal and silver, where carrots tasted like something she had no name for. She still talks about the carrots. There is a part of me that comes alive here in a way that just doesn’t happen at home. That is what she knew, at seven. And she knew that her friends back in Virginia had no idea this other world existed. Her mother, who is 91 now and has been painting for sixty years, taught her children not a map but an orientation: a way of seeing. On her 90th birthday, every grandchild and child said essentially the same thing to her. You have taught me to see beauty in unexpected places. A reflection in a puddle. A patina on a light pole. The configuration of grates in a sidewalk. Her father’s contribution was quieter and, in its way, more radical for its era. He had watched the marriages around him come apart in the 1960s and 1970s, watched the women who had put their husbands through law school and medical school left with no way to support themselves. He decided his daughter was not going to be in that position. He never told her this while she was growing up. She only found out much later, when she asked him. He laughed. He said: I wanted you to have a career. You kind of overdid it. She knew one woman lawyer. She did not know a single woman doctor, a single woman professor, a single woman engineer. Her father’s encouragement was not abstract. It was, within his world, a form of quiet resistance. The years that looked like nothing The plan had been elegant. Go to great schools. Study foreign policy. Oxford. Law school. New York firm. Partner who would go to State; go with that partner. In and out career. Everything mapped. It went well until it didn’t. The summer at the firm was enough. She felt fungible. She couldn’t do it. And the thing about having a map that detailed, a plan that precise, is that when it stops working, there is nothing underneath it. She hadn’t planned an alternative. She had only ever planned the one thing. I had to drift and I got a fellowship. I re-enrolled in a PhD programme because I didn’t know what else to do, but I didn’t want to teach. I didn’t have an idea. And that process for someone who had been so directed was painful. She was, she says, doing a little of this and a little of that. She had to support herself. When people asked what she was doing, she had a twenty-minute answer. What she came out of it knowing was this: things fall apart and you can support yourself. And the falling apart holds the door open for things you would never otherwise have considered. She had never considered being a professor. Over three or four years of spending time around professors, particularly one law professor who became a mentor, she began to live his life vicariously. She realised she loved law. She had just never loved practising it. She loved teaching it. She was, it turned out, a person who thrived in the world of ideas. When she eventually told the people at the New York firm she wasn’t coming to join them, they said that had always been fairly evident to them. It had not been evident to her. A law teaching job came. Then the man she had been pursuing for some time, who had always been resistant, finally saw what she had always seen. She tells this story without apology. She had known him while she was still married to someone else. After her first marriage was cracking up, she went to Paris and encountered him again, and it was like a bolt of lightning. She knew. He was used to having women fall in love with him. It took him a while to understand she was different. She had to break up with him once when she felt she was being jerked around. At some point she told him plainly: I am not going to keep pursuing you. This is your loss if you can’t see it. He changed. They married. Thirty-three years later, they are still married. And then, in 2009, thirty years after she graduated from college, she arrived at the State Department as Director of Policy Planning: the first woman ever to hold that position. The plan, which had been dead for years, had somehow arrived at its destination by a completely different route. The tsunami By the time Anne-Marie Slaughter reached the State Department, she was a figure in a particular world: foreign policy professionals and international lawyers. A relatively small, specific community. She was known inside it. She was not known outside it. She was commuting from Princeton to Washington each week, leaving at five in the morning on Monday, arriving home late on a Friday. Two sons. Her elder son was, as she has written about, having a very difficult time. And she was running up against the thing she had not only believed but preached to younger women for years: that if you are ambitious enough, if you manage your time well enough, you can make it all work. She had money. She had a supportive husband. She had every structural advantage. And it was not working. She wrote the article. Nine months of drafts. The Atlantic decided to make it a cover story. The publicity team could not get her booked on radio the week before publication. Every producer thought it was same old, same old. This argument had been made in 1982, in 1992, in 2002, and here it was again. The article published. Four million people read it. Letters arrived from Burundi. From above the Arctic Circle. From the Middle East. Her mother called and asked what she had done. Former law students called in tears. Women told her they felt validated. Women told her she had betrayed the cause. Women her own age, who had fought for decades to get where they were, felt she had handed ammunition to every man who had ever said women would just go home to their families. She had not said that. But you write words, and they get understood differently. It was like a tsunami hit. She had been a rising foreign policy figure. Suddenly she was this: whatever the public decided she was. Feminist or anti-feminist. Fighting Sheryl Sandberg, which was not true. Saying women should go home, which was not what she had said. What she had said was that the revolution was half-finished. Women were now doing the jobs men had traditionally done. They were also still doing every job women had traditionally done. Career paths and cultural norms had not changed to account for this. Something was required from the systems, not just from the women inside them. She looks back at the article now as a fork in the road. She does not think she would have gone to New America without it. What the Atlantic article was actually about The book that grew from the article, Unfinished Business: Women, Men, Work, Family, published in 2015, went somewhere the article had not quite reached. In the years between writing the article and writing the book, Anne-Marie had thought a great deal about men. Many men had written to her after the article. They said: I want to leave at four o’clock for my son’s baseball game, and I can’t. And if I try, I will be told I am not professional, not committed, not dedicated. I will be told I am less of a man. She came away from those letters with a conviction that she has held since: the deeper issue is the devaluing of care. The economy measures competitive, individualist activity. It does not measure the part of human life that is care: the people who tend to one another, who raise children, who sit with elderly parents, who cook, who maintain the texture of belonging in a household. It does not measure family in any form, biological or chosen. We have to value care, which is women’s traditional work, just as much as we value men’s traditional work. This is the argument she makes now. Whole people feel the full arc of human needs: connection, care, belonging, alongside achievement and competition. The economy, as currently constructed, accounts for only part of that arc. The part it ignores is the part that is, in her reading, foundational. She and I spoke about this before we recorded this episode and she said what she says now without hesitation: she does not think men can have it all either. The system does not work for anyone. It is not that women have been failed by a men’s system. It is that the system was built to measure and reward only one dimension of human beings, and that dimension is not the whole. The world she is building now New America is not a think tank. Anne-Marie is careful about this. It is a think and action tank: an organisation of extraordinary thinkers and doers who believe that ideas matter only when they become solutions, and that solutions are only real when they are tested. The questions New America works on are large: how to fund schools without tying the quality of a child’s education to the wealth of their neighbourhood; what a genuine multi-party political system might look like in the United States; how technology can serve the public good; how to build a world order that begins with people and planet rather than with states bashing each other to see who is largest. This last question is, in some ways, the one that was always underneath the career she mapped in high school. She wanted to do foreign policy. She wanted to work at the top of the State Department. She did. And what she saw there, and has been thinking about since, is that the international system built between 1648 and 1945 is no longer adequate. Nation states matter. She is not an advocate for dissolving them. But the system they created does not account for the world’s people or the planet they share. It was built to stop the kind of religious warfare that had bloodied Europe for thirty years. It served that purpose. It has not evolved to serve the purposes that are now required. She is clear-eyed about what will probably be needed to change it. She does not think democratic nations will come together to build a new world order because it is the right thing to do. She thinks something catastrophic will probably need to happen first. She has seen how these inflection points work: the League of Nations came from the First World War; the United Nations from the Second; much of international law from the Cold War. She does not look forward to the crisis that is coming. She believes the ideas need to be ready when it does. She will raise her hand. She has already said so. What her life is asking us to see There is a particular kind of courage that comes from having had a plan and losing it. Not the courage of boldness, which is something else entirely. The courage of continuing to navigate after the map is gone. Anne-Marie Slaughter spent six years between 26 and 32 in exactly that condition, and she carries the knowledge of those years differently from the way she carries her credentials. The credentials are real and she has earned them. But the drifting years are what she mentions when she wants to say something true. She said to me, quietly: things fall apart and you can support yourself. I have been sitting with that sentence. The simplicity of it. The amount of experience compressed inside it. She is not speaking theoretically. She is speaking as a woman who had built her life around one plan and had to find out, in real time, whether there was anything underneath it. There was. For anyone reading this who has ever been navigating without a map, who is in a period that looks like nothing from the outside but feels enormous from within: that period is not failure. Anne-Marie would not be what she is without hers. The drifting years were not a detour from the life she was meant to build. They were where the life she was actually capable of building became possible. She also gave us something else. A woman who spent years arguing that the systems are failing people, who wrote the most-read piece in Atlantic history and got called every name in the opposite direction of every name she was also called, who stood in the middle of an enormous public conversation and held her position: she does not make that look easy. She makes it look like what it is. Hard, and worth it, and grounded in something that does not shift. She says she believes in goodness. She calls it conviction, not prediction. She knows human beings are capable of the full range of what humans do. She chooses to work from the belief that the good prevails, because it has prevailed in the past, and because working from that belief is how the work gets done. Her mother taught her to see beauty in a reflection in a puddle. Her father made a quiet decision when she was small that she would never be left without the means to support herself. She carried both of those gifts into the law firm where she felt fungible, into the drifting years, into the State Department, into the tsunami of the Atlantic article, into New America, into this conversation.
