She is 67. Her parents are 91 and 94. She is still close to both of them. She says she won the parent lottery. Perhaps. But what she has done with that inheritance, the decades of work and the willingness to tell a truth that nobody wanted to hear, belongs entirely to her. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Anne-Marie This is a long conversation and an unhurried one. Anne-Marie speaks carefully and warmly, and there are several moments where she pauses and changes direction midway through a sentence because she is actually thinking, not performing the memory of having once thought. You feel that throughout. There is a section near the end where the conversation opens out into the largest questions: what will it take to rebuild a world order, whether human beings have the capacity to come together in time, what role love plays in political thinking. It is one of the most honest conversations about hope I have recorded, because it is completely free of sentimentality. She says she is not certain. She says she is convinced. She means something precise by the difference. There is no hurry. The library is always here. Never judge your insides by someone else’s outsides. In an age of social media where only the best side is shown, there’s plenty of pain and anger underneath. We have got a half-finished revolution, or not even half, maybe a third. And women are now, many of them doing jobs that men have traditionally done and they are still doing the jobs that women have traditionally done. And our culture and our career paths have not changed enough. Things fall apart and you can support yourself. And that process held the door open for things that I’d never considered. Anne-Marie Slaughter is a globally recognised scholar, policy innovator, and author of nine books. She served as the first woman Director of Policy Planning at the US State Department, was Dean of Princeton’s School of Public and International Affairs, and served as CEO of New America, the think and action tank she ran from 2013 to 2024. Her 2012 Atlantic article “Why Women Still Can’t Have It All” became the most-read piece in the magazine’s history. Her book Unfinished Business: Women, Men, Work, Family was published in 2015. She lives and works at the intersection of ideas and change.
show-joanna-barsh.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Joanna Barsh, Director Emerita of McKinsey and Company, creator of the Centered Leadership model, and author of three books including the bestselling How Remarkable Women Lead. Joanna spent more than 30 years at McKinsey advising Fortune 100 companies and developing a leadership framework now used by hundreds of thousands of leaders across the world. She is also a woman who, at 72, entered therapy for the first time, not from crisis, but from a refusal to fossilise. In this conversation Joanna talks about the darkness that arrived only after she stopped working, held at bay for decades by extraordinary achievement and now finally asking to be seen. She talks about the somatic workshop in 2011 where she encountered that darkness in a room full of people. About the mother whose approval she still waited for, long after her mother was gone. And about the question that changed everything: not what am I missing, but what have I simply chosen not to unlock? This conversation covers the hum of a life well integrated, four practices for the inner journey, and why people who stop growing fossilise. Whether you lead an organisation, are in the middle of your own becoming, or have been telling yourself the journey is behind you, this conversation will stay with you. She is sitting in her apartment in New York City. The year is 2007. A man has spread crayons across her table. He is from Australia. His name is Peter. He runs something called Passion Mapping. He says: talk to me until I see energy. And then draw what you feel. Joanna Barsh starts talking and, somewhere in the middle of it, the energy comes. She feels it. He sees it. He says: draw that. She draws herself on a stage, shining, with rays of light coming out of her in all directions. And then she takes another piece of paper and places it on top. “It’s not right,” she tells him. “It’s not nice. I shouldn’t be on stage. I shouldn’t shine like this. That’s wrong. It’s embarrassing.” She covers the drawing. She covers herself. And the man waits. This is the story of Joanna Barsh. A story about a woman who spent three decades building one of the most rigorously human frameworks for leadership development in the world, who interviewed more than five hundred senior executives about what was alive in them and what they were afraid to let out, who facilitated the healing of other people’s light, who saw clearly that most of us are standing on our own bushel. And who kept covering her own drawing for thirty years. The woman who walked in wanting to be a father Long before there was Centered Leadership, long before McKinsey or the workshops or the books or the 600 speeches, there was a small girl in the 1950s watching the front door. Her father left through it in the morning and came back in the evening with money and authority and a life in the world. Her mother stayed inside, miserable. The girl decided, at age six, that she would grow up to be a father. She said it simply, in our conversation, and I sat with it for a long time afterwards. She meant she would be in charge of herself. She would earn. She would not be contained. Financial independence was a word she used later, but the impulse was older: a child deciding that the life available to women was not the life she intended to live. The other thing she wanted, from the very beginning, was to be a painter. Her mother was a painter. A beautiful woman, Joanna described her, full of life and full of talent. The mother arrived in Joanna’s life the way certain people do: in flashes of brilliance, light and music and dancing and art, and then gone again. Back to herself. Unavailable. And the small girl waited in the shadows. She learned, during the waiting, to go quiet. To be still. To hold her breath and endure the absence until the light returned. She did not know, at six or at sixteen or even at fifty, that the waiting had shaped something in her as permanent as bone. She only knew she liked to draw. She liked to paint big, round, heavy women leaping through the air. And she had a creative force in her that was looking for a way out. The way out, when it came, was serendipitous in the way that destiny sometimes disguises itself as accident. She was told she was unqualified and would never get into Harvard Business School. So she applied and got in. She was told she was not a good candidate for McKinsey. So she applied and was the only one accepted. Her marketing professor described the firm to her class and Joanna thought: I should try that. A pattern was forming: tell me I cannot, and I will charge through a brick wall. “I’ve never felt not good enough,” she told me, and I believed her. What she felt, underneath the drive, was something more complicated. She felt she was missing something. She could not name it yet. She only knew she wanted to be a leader and was certain, in a way that coexisted entirely with her defiance, that she was not one. She joined McKinsey. She would stay for more than thirty years. The beginning of something she did not have a name for In 2004, Joanna was a senior partner at one of the world’s most influential consulting firms. She had done well by most measures. She was travelling, speaking, working on the most difficult problems she could find. She was, by her own description, an extraordinary doer. And she had a tremendous need she could not account for. She had looked around at the women at the top of their fields, all over the world, and found herself wanting to sit with them. Wanting to understand what they carried. Not their strategies or their credentials, but the thing underneath. What had enabled them. What had cost them. What they were quietly carrying that nobody had thought to ask about. She started interviewing women. She had no strategy. She did not know she was beginning something that would change the field. She just had the need. McKinsey tolerated it for a while, then the head of the firm said she could do twenty interviews. She interpreted that as twenty more. Then a young colleague said they had to write a book with this material, it was too good not to share, and there was a moratorium on books so they wrote a pamphlet, fifty-eight pages, and it was so good she took it to a client who happened to be a literary agent and he said: write me a book proposal. And then she went back to the man who had said no books, and told him she had a book deal. He said: that is so like you, Joanna. She told me that for one second, she heard her father’s voice. And I understood then that she had been chasing something much older than a publishing deal. What emerged from those interviews was Centered Leadership: a framework built on five capabilities, each one excavated from real conversations with real women at the heights of real careers. Meaning, framing, connecting, engaging, energising. Each one a different door into the self. Each one a question about what was actually alive in you, as opposed to what you were performing. The centring image she kept using was the woman who had everything externally and was still suffering privately. The senior executive who had never told anyone what she was carrying. The leader who had been so fully shaped by the system around her that she could no longer locate the person she had been before the shaping began. Joanna knew this person intimately. She had interviewed more than five hundred of them. She fell in love with every single one of them. She loved their flaws with the specific tenderness of someone who has been paying close attention. The thing she was slower to see was how precisely she was describing herself. The somatic exercise in 2011 She volunteered. That is the part that stays with me. Of all the people in the room, Joanna stepped into the fishbowl. She agreed to let a facilitator move through her, in public, in front of her colleagues. An electrical engineer turned somatic guide. A Mobius workshop. The year is 2011, and Centered Leadership is already in the world. The facilitator listened to her describe what she wanted: to bring Centered Leadership to everyone. He created a movement. She was supposed to mirror it. He was crushed to the floor. He battled something she could not see. Then he swam, or flew, and the movement opened outward. She began. She was crushed to the floor. And she could not get up. Every time she tried, something pushed her back down. A force she described, years later in therapy, as dark and enveloping and genuinely frightening. The dementors from Harry Potter were her image for it: something that grabs the soul. She kept trying to rise and the thing kept pushing her down until the facilitator said: Joanna, get up. And she heard him. She battled it. She flew. She said so herself: not swimming, flying. Everyone in the front row was weeping. She had no idea, at the time, that she had just walked into something traumatic. She thought she was doing an exercise. She wrote it down, filed it, returned to the work. The dark force had receded. She was good at what she was doing. When you are good at what you are doing, the darkness can wait. It waited thirty years. What she found when she stopped She retired from McKinsey at sixty. She wrote three books. She did the research on Black talent, then on Latina leaders, 160 interviews with some of the most fierce and determined and overlooked people she had ever met. She taught. She spoke. She travelled. She was busy in the specific way that people who have a dark force waiting for them are busy: productively, meaningfully, without rest. And then the work slowed down enough that the thing came back. At 72, she walked into therapy for the first time. Her therapist told her she had done all these things and didn’t need anybody. Joanna said she still wanted her book published. She still needed that. The therapist said: let’s talk about why. The question she had been asking herself, she told me, was: why aren’t I fixed? She had gone through the workshops. She had done the centred leadership programme over and over, as a facilitator and as a participant both. She had wept in rooms with women who were breaking open for the first time. She had loved every human being she had ever sat across from. She had given the gift, a thousand times over, of helping someone see what was already inside them. And she was still, at the deepest level, waiting for someone to come back and say: you did a good job. Her mother was a painter who left and came back and left again. Her father left when she was six and did not come back in the same way. The waiting she had learned in childhood had become the architecture of her emotional life: go still. Be patient. Do extraordinary work. Wait for the recognition that says you are allowed to exist fully now. She said it plainly: “I am still a person who needs external validation.” I find this one of the bravest things I have heard a 72-year-old woman say. Not because it is an unusual feeling; it is perhaps the most universal feeling in the world. But because Joanna Barsh said it after a career in which she helped thousands of people understand and accept exactly this about themselves, and after decades of applying a framework that specifically addresses the internal drivers of leadership, and after knowing, intellectually, that this fear of not being enough is a childhood wound that no amount of achievement can close. She knew. And she was still inside it. And she chose to say so. “People who don’t change fossilize,” she told me. She said it as a warning to herself. The thing she was always teaching Here is what Centered Leadership actually is. It is a body of work that requires the body, not just the mind. Joanna was clear on this: the left brain is not really needed for this work. What is needed is the willingness to dig into your own life experience, the high points and the low points, the relationships and the ruptures, the moments where you came alive and the moments where you went quiet, and to look at those things clearly enough to understand what is actually driving you. The framework has five doors. Meaning: what are your genuine strengths, not the ones you were told to have, the ones that actually light something in you. Framing: what are you afraid of, and how does that fear distort the way you see a difficult situation. Connecting: why do you not fully trust, and what would it take to build trust with the people around you. Engaging: what is your voice, and what is stopping you from using it. Energising: where does your energy come from, and what is costing it. Each door leads somewhere different. The woman who emerges from a serious engagement with these five questions is someone different from the woman who walked in. Or rather, she is more herself. That is what Joanna found, over 500 interviews and years of facilitation: the people who most needed this work were not lacking something. They had chosen, out of fear, not to open certain doors. “I have chosen not to open doors because I am afraid,” she said. “I have not unlocked certain pieces of myself because I am afraid. And I’m going to go ahead with the help of the people around me and unlock those doors and love the flaws that will come out.” The flaws. This is where Joanna’s thinking goes somewhere that most leadership frameworks do not follow. She does not ask people to fix themselves. She asks them to open. The act of trying to be perfect, she told me, means you keep locking more and more stuff away. A pebble that is trying to be a rock cannot move. A woman who is trying to be what the organisation needs her to be cannot grow. Only the person who accepts and inhabits her own shape, with all its apparent irregularities, can actually contribute what no one else has. At McKinsey, early in her career, she was told in a review that she was too young, too bouncy, too short. She wore black. She wore higher heels. She stopped doing the bouncy, silly things she loved to do. A recruiter told her she was a pebble and that she needed to become a rock if she wanted to get far. She tried. Rocks don’t move. She couldn’t stay still. “I have to be the pebble,” she said eventually. And she decided to be the best pebble she knew how to be. What she is doing now The EVE Programme runs in France, and in Mexico, and in Africa, and in Asia. Around 700 people a year pass through it in France alone, hosted by Danone and L’Oreal, drawing from companies across the European continent. Joanna teaches there. She teaches at Tecnológico de Monterrey in Mexico, a private university with campuses across the country, working with executive women and with the teachers who carry the work forward. The EVE Programme includes men now: Joanna long ago established, through research, that men have exactly the same capacity for this inner work as women. Gender is incidental. The question is simply whether you are willing to look. She is looking for a co-author for a book about Latina women in leadership, built from 160 interviews with leaders across Latin America, Spanish-speaking US, and Spain: what she found, over and over, was women who were fierce and loyal and energetic and warm and systematically blocked at every turn. She has the research. She needs someone with the standing inside the community to carry it. She is not giving up on the book. She is drawing a children’s book. By hand, with the same love for art that she had when she was drawing leaping women as a teenager. On one page, a set of rabbits are reading a romantic poem aloud, and the rattlesnakes nearby are weeping because the story is unjust and beautiful, and the trees are also weeping, and everyone has stopped being whatever they were to feel something together. She does not care whether it sells. She is making it because she needs to express what she is thinking and feeling. Because connecting, finally, is what she most wants to do. “Connect and express,” she said. “That’s all I want to do now.” She is also in therapy. At 72, for the first time in her life, she is in therapy. The light they cannot see There is a woman in every cohort Joanna has ever worked with who will not go to the retreat. Who will find a reason. Who will be in the building but not in the room. Who needs the work desperately and is afraid that doing the work in public means people will see her, and being seen is the thing she has spent her whole career managing. Joanna knows this woman. She is this woman. I think about this often: how many of us are facilitating, for others, the very journey we have not yet begun for ourselves. How many of the people who most eloquently describe the inner life are doing so from a safe theoretical distance. How many of us can describe the exact texture of another person’s fear and still find a reason to not go to the retreat. Joanna did not go to the retreat. The other seven women colleagues bonded and laughed and came back changed. She stayed in her apartment, certain they had not noticed her absence. She is still working on what it means to accept that people want her in the room. “I can’t wait,” she said at one point in our conversation, and for a moment I was not sure she was talking about her mother any more. “I’m fucking old. Why are we waiting? What the hell are we waiting for, Joanna?” She was talking to herself. She has spent most of her life talking to herself in the background of her own extraordinary output. Now she is letting the conversation be heard. This is what I most wanted to offer you from my time with Joanna: the idea that you do not have to be finished with your own journey to do great work. You do not have to have resolved the thing in yourself before you can help others find it. You can be the woman who built Centered Leadership while still, quietly, covering your own drawing. You can interview 500 people about what is alive in them and still be learning to tolerate your own aliveness. What you cannot do, Joanna would say, is stop. The moment you stop growing is the moment you begin to fossilize. And Joanna Barsh has never stopped. Not at 30. Not at 60. Not at 72, on a therapist’s couch, learning at last that the recognition she was waiting for was always going to have to come from inside the room she was already in. What her life is asking us to see There is a kind of person who carries the work of healing in one hand and the work of their own becoming in the other, and who spends decades convinced that the second hand is somehow shameful. As though you forfeit your right to guide others through the interior if yours is still in progress. As though authority requires completion. Joanna Barsh has never been complete. She has been in motion, in creative, determined, laughing, weeping motion, her whole life. And the motion has mattered. The five hundred interviews mattered. The framework mattered. The workshops where women say, for the first time aloud, I am not guilty because I love to work: those mattered. None of it required her to have solved herself first. She described the journey she is now on, the therapy, the sitting with darkness, the learning that a break in a relationship does not mean the relationship is over, with the same generosity she has brought to every person who has ever walked through one of her workshops. There was no performance in it. She was simply honest about being a person in progress, which is the most useful thing any of us can offer anyone. At 72, she drew a picture she did not cover. She would like to write more children’s books. She would like to finish the research on Latina talent. She would like to keep coming back to the work for as long as the work keeps teaching her something. She has a granddaughter who is nine months old and does not yet speak any language Joanna recognises, and Joanna talks to her nonstop anyway, because connection does not require shared vocabulary, only presence. She got on the train decades ago and has been riding it ever since. She is not, I think, ready to get off. But she is learning, finally, to travel with her window open. To let people see her through it. To resist the habit of covering what she draws. For anyone who has spent time helping others see what they carry while quietly hiding their own: this is the kind of permission Joanna’s life is offering. You are allowed to shine. The drawing does not need to be covered. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on the conversation This conversation runs for nearly an hour and a half, and there is not a single moment in it that wastes your time. Joanna is funny and raw and precise and unexpectedly willing to go to the exact place you would not expect a former McKinsey senior partner to go. She curses. She talks about her mother. She sits inside questions without rushing them toward answers. The conversation between her and Katherine is two people recognising themselves in each other: the same hunger for expression, the same early confusion of love and absence, the same long journey from achievement toward something quieter and realer. Watch it when you have the evening for it. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I battled this thing and I knew it didn’t go away because it was still watching me. And then I walked and did my paces. I can’t… I’m not swimming, I’m flying. I have chosen not to open doors because I am afraid. I have not unlocked certain pieces of myself because I am afraid. And I’m going to go ahead with the help of the people around me and unlock those doors and love the flaws that will come out. People who don’t change fossilize. And so I had to discover this at 72. Joanna, you’re still vulnerable to the lack of external validation. Okay, let’s work on that. Joanna Barsh is the creator of Centered Leadership, a framework developed over a decade of research at McKinsey and Company, where she was a senior partner for more than thirty years. She is the author of three books including How Remarkable Women Lead and Centered Leadership: Leading with Purpose, Clarity, and Impact [TEAM NOTE: please verify these titles against Joanna’s actual bibliography before publishing]. She teaches at the EVE Leadership Programme, which runs across France, Mexico, Africa, and Asia, and at Tecnológico de Monterrey in Mexico. She is currently conducting research into Latina women in leadership, from interviews across Latin America, Spanish-speaking US, and Spain, seeking a Latina co-author for the resulting book. She lives in New York City, is a new grandmother, and is learning, at 72, what it means to finally stop covering the drawing.
show-colin-campbell.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Colin Campbell, writer, theater director, Academy Award-nominated filmmaker, and author of Finding the Words: Working Through Profound Loss with Hope and Purpose. In June 2019, Colin and his wife Gail were in the car when a drunk and high driver struck their family at speed on a California highway. Their two teenage children, Ruby, 17, and Hart, 14, were killed. Colin and Gail survived. What Colin did with that fact is the subject of this conversation. He and Gail have since adopted two teenagers through the foster system, fulfilling a vision Ruby herself shared with them a year before she was killed. He wrote a book built on one central insight: most people who disappear after a loss do not disappear from indifference. They disappear because they do not know what to say. And learning to ask for what you need is one of the most generous things a grieving person can do for the people who love them. This conversation covers grief, forgiveness, the long road toward opening your heart again, Ruby and Hart as the specific and extraordinary people they were, and what it means to choose love as a deliberate daily practice when it is the most difficult option available. There are large photographs of Ruby and Hart on the walls of the living room. Three by two feet each. Their faces filling the frames, smiling. Colin put them there in the weeks after the crash because something about seeing them helped. It was the only thing that helped. One morning, early in the grieving, he came downstairs and looked away. He didn’t plan to. His eyes simply slid past the photographs the way eyes sometimes do when what they’re about to see carries too much weight. And then he stopped on the bottom stair. He stood there and he thought about what he’d just done. He had looked away from his own children because he was afraid of the pain of looking at them. Colin Campbell told me this story sitting still, in the particular way people become still when they’re telling you the thing that most changed them. He said: the only reason to look away is fear. And how can he let fear of pain get in the way of loving Ruby and Hart. He won’t do that. He won’t do it. That moment, small as it sounds, is the whole architecture of the man. Every choice he has made since, every book and every performance and every adoption and every advocacy hearing, runs through that question asked and answered on a staircase. Face the thing you most want to turn away from. The photographs. The grief groups. The woman in the prison. The new children who might break your heart all over again. Face it all. The pain is the form the love takes. Who he was before Before the crash, Colin Campbell was a filmmaker. A theater artist. A teacher. A husband. He and his wife Gail Lerner met at Columbia University, both MFA students in the theater directing programme, class of 1996. They married shortly after graduation and built a life in Los Angeles shaped by art. Together they co-created Seraglio, a short film that won the Grand Prix at the Deauville American Film Festival, aired on HBO, and earned an Academy Award nomination. His stage work, Golden Prospects, was nominated for five LA Weekly Theater Awards and received critics’ pick notices in both Time Out New York and The Los Angeles Times. He taught at Chapman, Loyola Marymount, and Cal Poly Pomona, and ran workshops through The Unusual Suspects, a programme for incarcerated youth. He was, by every account including his own, someone who had found the particular satisfaction of a life oriented toward meaning. He was also, by his own description, a man who had grown up with no cultural tools for grief. He was raised an atheist WASP, his phrase, in a family where loss was not discussed. Where the protocol around pain was something closer to silence and getting on with things. He had no framework. He had never needed one. His children were Ruby and Hart. Ruby was 17. Hart was 14. Ruby was an artist, deeply gifted, a proud lesbian who her father describes as a warrior for social justice. Hart was the clown at the centre of every room he walked into, magnetic, so funny and so beloved that when Colin and Gail would arrive to collect him from a sleepover, his friends would literally pile on top of him to hide him from them. Hart’s not here. He left already. They both had crowds around them. They were both, as Colin says simply, larger than life. The four of them went to Joshua Tree regularly. They would pull up by the side of the road and scramble out into the rocks until they were half-lost, laughing, trying to find their way back to the car. They had just made an offer on a small two-bedroom house in the desert, their own place, with amazing views and the possibility of a pool, Ruby’s idea. They had been accepted. Colin had started making the calls. He went back to the desert one Wednesday evening in June 2019, all four of them, to meet with someone about whether a pool was possible and where it might go. Ruby had insisted on coming; she was the one who’d thought of the pool. She had to be there to say where it should go. A drunk and drugged driver travelling at 90 miles an hour T-boned the car as they turned into a petrol station. Ruby and Hart were in the back seat. They were killed. Colin and Gail were knocked unconscious. When they came to, the children were not moving. The driver never touched the brakes. What the first days were I asked Colin what the days looked like after that, and he paused for a moment in the way that people do when they are trying to give an honest answer to a question that has no honest answer. He said the denial was complete. His brain was worrying away at it, trying to fix the situation. He was searching through Ruby’s computer files for anything he hadn’t seen yet: stories, drawings, scraps of writing. Searching for her. He said he would go through two or three hours without weeping and begin to feel physically ill, almost nauseous, as if the grief needed to move through his body at regular intervals and holding it back was its own kind of sickness. He was scared to weep fully, afraid that if he started he would never stop, afraid his mind would shatter with the enormity of it. It took him two days to understand that was not true. He and Gail were both certain the other was grieving better. She thought he was weeping more. He thought she was. They were both wrong, both judging themselves against a standard that did not exist. He found that moment, strangely, clarifying. He had no framework of his own, and so he trusted himself to Jewish ritual. Gail is Jewish; Ruby and Hart were raised Jewish. He was not, but the structure was there and he needed structure. Shiva arrived, which for those unfamiliar is the Jewish tradition of sitting with the bereaved for the seven nights after a funeral. Friends came to the house. At first it seemed impossible, counterintuitive, that strangers and acquaintances should be in the house two days after the children had been killed. Then something shifted. He found he needed to talk about Ruby and Hart. He needed to tell people what was happening inside him because the inside of him was so strange and so overwhelming that he could not process it without speech. That realisation, in those first raw days, became the whole foundation of what he would eventually build. “There are no words” is the phrase our culture most often offers to the grieving. Colin’s work, across every form it has taken, is a sustained argument that this is wrong. Not unhelpful. Wrong. Grievers have all the words. They are overflowing with them. What they need is someone willing to receive the words, and the permission to speak them. The morning on the stairs Six months in, the photographs were still on the wall. They have never come down. He told me about the morning on the stairs with the particular clarity of someone who has thought about that moment many times, who understands it as the decision that preceded all other decisions. He had looked away. He had caught himself looking away. And he asked himself: how can I let fear of pain get in the way of me loving Ruby and Hart? He won’t do that. He won’t do it. What he means by this is not a single act of courage. He means the ongoing, repeating choice to face rather than turn away. The same question comes up in different forms, constantly, in grief: will he go back to the restaurant they loved? Will he look at the videos? Will he walk the same hike? Will he go into their rooms? Each time, the answer requires the same small act of will. Each time, he chooses to face it. He told me that a woman in his grief group, about four or five months after the crash, said she missed the early days when she wept every day. At the time he thought she was mad. He told her so, gently. And then, six years on, he got there. He knows what she meant now. The daily weeping was the form his love took in those months, the way it expressed itself, and its absence is its own kind of loss. Grief changes shape but it does not leave. He holds both the relief of that and the particular sadness of it. For anyone reading this who has wondered whether the intensity of early grief means something is wrong with you: it does not. And for anyone who has wondered whether the lessening of it means you have stopped loving the person you lost: it does not mean that either. Colin has sat with enough bereaved people to say this with certainty. The woman in the prison For five years, Colin did not think about the woman who killed his children. He made a deliberate decision not to. She had ended their lives but she was a stranger, and strangers do not deserve the space inside you that belongs to the people you love. He was not going to give her that. He compartmentalised her into a box labelled nameless monster and closed the lid. He drove the car the night of the crash. He made a left turn in front of a distant vehicle that appeared safe to pass. The woman was going 90 miles an hour, forty above the speed limit, and never once touched the brakes. He could not have known. And yet he makes left turns now, every time, and thinks about that turn. The guilt lives in his body. The woman’s name is Rebecca Packer. She was charged with two counts of second-degree murder. She pled to a lesser charge and was sentenced to fourteen years and nine months. She was, Colin says, a repeat offender; the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration estimates that by the time a person is first pulled over for drunk driving, they have driven drunk an average of eighty times without being caught. About five years after the crash, Colin’s dentist recommended a book: The Many Lives of Mama Love, about a woman imprisoned for fraud, struggling with addiction, who found her way to sobriety and eventually ghost-wrote Bishop Desmond Tutu’s The Book of Forgiving. He read Tutu’s book. And in it he found a passage that stopped him. Tutu writes about the way grieving people sometimes deny the humaneness of the person who harmed them, turning them into a monster, a nameless thing, to make the pain of it more bearable. Colin read this and understood immediately what he had been doing. He had been compartmentalising Rebecca Packer the same way he had vowed not to compartmentalise the pain of losing Ruby and Hart. And the reason was the same reason. Fear. He is preparing to meet with her. There is a victim-offender dialogue programme, part of restorative justice practice, run by trained facilitators. She will be brought from prison. They will sit together and have a conversation. He does not know exactly what he will find there, or what it will give him. He says only that it feels connected to his unfinished work with guilt, that there is something about the encounter that is, mysteriously, helpful to him already, just in the preparing for it. What Ruby said Ruby said it a year before she was killed, at sixteen years old, in the particular offhand way teenagers sometimes say the things that turn out to matter most. We should foster-adopt some kids. She said it to Gail and Colin one afternoon. They were surprised; it is not the most obvious thought for a sixteen-year-old from a comfortable Los Angeles family to have. Ruby explained: We have so much love in our family. And there are so many kids out there who need a family. Colin said gently that they already had a family, that they were full up, that the thought was beautiful but they had their hands full. Ruby dropped it. When Ruby and Hart were killed, Colin and Gail had that conversation again. What they both felt, in the wreckage of those first months, was that they had this enormous amount of love and nowhere for it to go. Ruby and Hart were gone. The love was still there. Gail and I had just this gush of love that had nowhere to go, he said. And then he remembered what Ruby had said. Three months after the crash, Colin and Gail signed up for a foster-adoption training class. They showed up, red-faced, to an intake interview. The facilitator asked how long it had been since their loss. They looked at each other. Nine months too early, they were gently told. Come back in a year. They waited. One year on, they began meeting children. A thirteen-year-old girl connected with them, chose them, came to live in their home. They felt, both of them, that their hearts were working again, that something had opened. Then it was revealed that she had decided she did not want to be adopted. She had started to care for them and the vulnerability had frightened her; in her history, opening your heart had led to betrayal, and she would not risk it. She left. She chose to age out of the system instead. Colin said: by then, we had lost three children. They waited another two months. They began again. This time they were shown a brief blurb and a photograph of two siblings: a boy and a girl. They were given no opportunity to meet them first. In California, as Colin explains it, a prospective adoptive family must decide before meeting the children, sight unseen, because these children cannot stand more rejection. The adults are the ones who can absorb the risk. He and Gail said yes without meeting them. Andrew and Gladys were adopted on June 17th. They have been in the family for three years now. They are teenagers, both carrying the particular, complicated damage of having been failed by every adult before Colin and Gail. They act out. They struggle. Colin and Gail take their daily walk with the dog and talk through what is working and what isn’t, and remind each other to be kind to themselves. Colin says: we are parenting. That’s what we’re in. There is a lot in that statement if you sit with it. He and Gail have buried two children and then chosen, twice, to open their hearts to children who might leave or might hurt them or might find the love too frightening to stay inside. They know what loss feels like. They are doing it anyway. Ruby thought of it first. The work Finding the Words: Working Through Profound Loss with Hope and Purpose was published by Penguin Random House in 2023. It has been praised by Sheryl Sandberg, Congressman Jamie Raskin, and Rabbi Sharon Brous. It is a practical book, which is what makes it unusual in the grief genre. Colin’s contribution to the literature of loss is not a theory of stages or a spiritual framework. It is a set of tools for keeping your community close while you grieve. He and Gail developed what they call a “grief spiel”: an explicit description, given to the people around them, of what they needed. Talk to us about Ruby and Hart. Say their names. Ask how we’re doing. Offer specific help rather than a general “let me know if you need anything.” He had noticed early on that Shiva created a container for people to show up, but that once Shiva ended, those same people became frightened of mentioning Ruby and Hart in case it reminded Colin and Gail of their loss. As if, he says drily, they had forgotten. The book teaches the bereaved to ask for what they need, and teaches everyone else what asking for it looks like. He also wrote and performed Grief: A One Man ShitShow, a solo theatrical piece that premiered at the 2022 Hollywood Fringe Festival where it won a Best of Broadwater Award, and subsequently ran for a month at Theatre Row in New York City. The title is deliberate. He wanted something that conveyed the messy, ugly, unglamorous reality of grief as most people actually live it: the comparisons of whose loss is worse, the rage at the universe, the dark comedy of continuing to eat and sleep and shower while your world has ended. NPR and The New York Times reviewed it. Colin performed vulnerability publicly as a gift to the people sitting in those seats who had never found a room where grief was allowed to be exactly what it is. He joined the National Board of Directors for Mothers Against Drunk Driving in 2025. The work there is specific: the HALT Act, a bipartisan piece of legislation already passed by Congress, mandates the installation of anti-drunk-driving technology in all new vehicles. The technology would prevent a car from being driven by an impaired driver. The Act is law. It is waiting to be implemented. Colin is fighting for implementation alongside other families who have lost people to impaired drivers, the 10,000 families a year in America who know exactly what he knows. He writes for The Atlantic and The Los Angeles Times. He speaks at conferences. He keynoted The Compassionate Friends National Conference, which is the largest bereaved parent organisation in America. He still teaches. He still makes films. What grief is for There is a question that hangs over lives like Colin’s: how do you hold the horror of what happened alongside the life that has been built from it? He is clear that he does not want to be better for having lost his children. He finds the idea, as he says plainly, repulsive. Ruby and Hart were not the price of his evolution. They were his children. And yet the man sitting across from me had spent six years walking toward the things that frightened him, loving two new children, fighting a legislative battle in the names of 10,000 families a year, performing grief in theaters so that strangers might feel less alone in theirs. He had followed Viktor Frankl’s central insight from Man’s Search for Meaning: that what allows people to survive unimaginable suffering is the search for meaning and purpose, and that the most reliable place to find it is in service to others. Frankl observed this in concentration camps. Colin confirmed it in the years after a crash on a desert road. He told me that the most important things he could say to anyone navigating loss are two: don’t be afraid of the pain, and choose love. Don’t be afraid of the pain. He knows the fear of it. He knows the terror that if you let yourself fully weep you will never stop, that you will go mad with it, that the grief will swallow you whole. It does not swallow you whole. The pain is the correct response to losing someone you love. It is the measure of how much you loved them. Choose love. He said it the way people say things when they mean them without decoration. He means: when the question of whether to open your heart again arrives, and it does arrive, choose to open it. Choose to go back to the restaurant. Choose to look at the photographs. Choose, sight unseen, to say yes to two teenagers who need a family. It is always worth it. He has not found an exception. Katherine offered a third, at the end of their conversation: choose service. Colin accepted it without hesitation. He finds, he said, real value in being of service to other people. It actually helps me. The help is not incidental. It is the medicine. What his life is asking us to see There is a particular kind of courage that our culture rarely honours because it is not dramatic. It does not arrive with fanfare. Colin Campbell’s courage is the kind that happens at the bottom of a staircase, in the moment before his eyes slide past a photograph. It is the courage of the repeated, ordinary, daily choice to face what is hardest to face. He has faced it every morning for six years. He will face it every morning for the rest of his life. Ruby and Hart are not a story he survived. They are present in his life as ongoing companions: in the house in Joshua Tree they almost bought together, in the love that Ruby named and Gail and Colin are now attempting to give to Andrew and Gladys, in the annual beach memorial where 120 people spell Ruby and Hart’s names in rocks on the sand, shout their names into the open air, and wade into the Pacific together. I know something of what it is to go looking through old photographs you have been avoiding, and to sit with them for hours, and to emerge from that sitting changed. I did not go through what Colin has been through. His specific grief is his own and I would never claim otherwise. But there is something he offers that is for all of us, something in the architecture of his choices that speaks past the particular horror of his circumstance and addresses something broader about what it means to be a person. The thing we most want to protect ourselves from is the thing most likely to be worth going toward. The pain that feels as if it will break us is often the pain that, if we stay inside it without flinching, becomes the ground we stand on. This is not a silver lining. It is not consolation. It is just what Colin’s life has shown to be true, slowly, over years, in the company of other people willing to say their loss aloud. He did not arrive anywhere. He is still in the middle of it. Andrew is still doing his homework under protest. The facilitators are still preparing the meeting with Rebecca Packer. Gail and Colin still take their walk each day and talk through what is hard. The grief for Ruby and Hart is still there, changed in shape but not in weight. He will always be the father of four. What he has found, in the middle of all of it, is that the middle is where the living happens. The turning toward rather than away. The finding of the words. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Colin The conversation between Colin and me runs close to two hours. It is quiet, mostly. Colin is not a man who performs his story; he lives inside it while he tells it, and the difference is visible. There is a moment toward the end where he shares a story about Hart and his hairdresser, a story about a fourteen-year-old boy who was simply and completely at ease with someone his father found more complicated, and it is one of the most beautiful things I have heard on this show. Watch it. Or listen. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I was scared that I would lose my mind. That if I started to weep, I would never stop. If two hours went by and I hadn’t wept, I was starting to feel ill. It was almost nauseous. I had to just feel their loss and weep. I missed the weeping. I missed just weeping for Ruby and Hart every day. Now it’s so complicated, because I don’t every day, and that’s hard in a different way. Don’t be afraid of pain. And choose love. If the question comes up, choose love. Colin Campbell is an author, filmmaker, theater artist, and grief educator based in Los Angeles and Joshua Tree, California. His memoir Finding the Words: Working Through Profound Loss with Hope and Purpose (Penguin Random House, 2023) has become a resource for grieving people worldwide. He is the writer and performer of Grief: A One Man ShitShow, which ran at Theatre Row in New York City and earned rave reviews from NPR and The New York Times. As an Academy Award-nominated filmmaker, he co-created Seraglio with his wife Gail Lerner. He serves on the National Board of Directors for Mothers Against Drunk Driving. His writing has appeared in The Atlantic and The Los Angeles Times.
show-dr-john-izzo.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Dr. John Izzo, public philosopher, bestselling author of eight books, and one of North America’s most prominent voices on purposeful living and intentional leadership. He has advised over 500 companies, spoken to more than one million people across four continents, and spent four decades asking the question that anchors everything: what does it mean to live and lead with genuine intention? John’s father died at 36, having not seen his son since the boy was one year old. For decades John judged him quietly. Then he arrived at a different understanding: his father was not a bad man. He simply was not intentional. That realisation became the foundation of John’s life’s work. Near the end of this conversation, he did something he had not planned: he left the call, went to his wall for a photograph of his father, and said what he had been carrying for 67 years. This conversation moves through John’s Staten Island childhood, the mother who shaped everything he became, the fractal insight that what we manifest outwardly is always a manifestation of the inner life, and the conviction, held with humility, that the work of becoming more intentional is never finished. He reached the end of the conversation, paused for a beat, and said he hadn’t planned to do this. Then he held up his phone to show us a photograph. A man in a Navy uniform, young, his face carrying something a little unresolved. And John Izzo, who is sixty-eight years old, who has spent four decades studying what makes a human life well-lived and is one of the most respected voices on the subject in the world, looked at that photograph and said: Thank you, Dad, for bringing me into this world. And I want you to know I forgive you. He had only been ready to put that photograph on his office wall one year earlier. His father died at thirty-six, of a sudden heart attack, when John was eight years old. His parents had separated when John was six months old. In the entirety of those eight years, his father, who lived two hours away, had come to see him once: apparently when John was about a year old, so young he has no memory of it. Not because he was cruel. Because, as John came to understand far later in life, he simply was not intentional. He did not think deeply enough about the choices he was making. The grace of that understanding took sixty years to arrive. There is a pretty good chance they took it as far as they could, he said. And you may never like or appreciate that they could only take it that far. But forgive them if you can, because it is good for you. I have been sitting with that sentence since the moment he said it. What shaped him John Izzo grew up in Staten Island in the late 1950s, in a white working-class neighbourhood of police officers and firemen and boys, many boys, and almost no nature. His mother raised him alongside his grandmother, and his grandfather prayed by the side of his bed each night; his mother prayed too, and told him that life was about service. The Jesus on the wall in their home was a loving, forgiving one. A take-up-your-cross-and-serve-the-world Jesus. Not a punishing one. John says he had no religion to recover from, and I believed him completely. His mother was, by every account he gave, a woman of unusual moral clarity. One afternoon, young John stole a piece of candy from Mr. Miller’s grocery store. Mr. Miller was bald, severe, feared by every child in the neighbourhood. When his mother spotted the candy, she dragged John three blocks by his ear to the front of that store and made him return it and apologise. He has never forgotten standing at that counter. She also, without hesitation, said yes when John asked if he could go to dinner at his friend Howie’s house. Howie’s family was Black. No other child in the neighbourhood had been invited inside. His mother’s response was: Why would you ask that question? Of course you can go. And don’t ever ask that question again. He told me these stories not as anecdotes about himself but as an invitation. Think about your own ground, he said. The humus from which you grew. What are the things that shaped you that you may want to integrate differently? And what are the things you ought to be deeply grateful for? There was one more thing he told me about his childhood, and it is the detail I keep returning to. In the neighbourhood where he grew up, there was an old retirement home for former Navy sailors. It sat behind a fence, surrounded by a kind of nature that didn’t otherwise exist in that part of New York City. He and his friends used to sneak in. And he would find, inside those grounds, a small stream. He sat beside it often, a curious boy, alive to something he could not name. He was small enough that it could find him. The accidental tourist John has described his entry into the corporate world as accidental, and the description is precise. He had trained as a Presbyterian minister, spending years sitting beside people in their final days, conducting more funerals than most people attend in a lifetime. He watched, in those years, how differently people arrived at the end. Some came to it with a quiet completeness, few regrets, a sense of having lived into themselves. Others came haunted by the life they had not quite managed to live. The question that generated was simple and became the animating inquiry of everything that followed: why do some people live well and die happy, while others don’t? When a hostile takeover ended his role as Vice President at a healthcare consulting firm in the early 1990s, he and his colleague Eric Klein, a Buddhist yogi, sat down to write about what they had each been circling from opposite directions. The result was Awakening Corporate Soul, published in 1994. It was, in those days, a genuinely lonely position to take. When a Speakers Bureau recommended him to a major bank as keynote speaker, the senior VP loved the book so much he gave away ten copies. Then he rang to say they would not be booking John. It would not be good for my career, he explained, to suggest a speaker who had the word soul in the title of his book. John told that story with the ease of a man who has long since had the last laugh, but also with something warmer: genuine affection for how far the conversation has come, and honest humility about how far it has not. He went on to write nine books across three decades, each one tracking a shift he could see before most others named it. The changing values of working generations. The rise of purpose-driven consumers. The architecture of personal responsibility. But two books sit at the centre of the body of work, and both emerged from a single, sustained act of listening. Eighteen thousand years of life experience For The Five Secrets You Must Discover Before You Die, published in 2008, John asked people to nominate the wisest older person they knew. From over two thousand nominations, he selected and interviewed two hundred and fifty of those elders, aged sixty to one hundred and six, across backgrounds that ranged from Holocaust survivors and indigenous chiefs to town barbers and chief executives. He was looking for the signal through the noise. Across eighteen thousand years of combined life experience, five things kept appearing. Be true to yourself. Leave no regrets. Become love. Live the moment. Give more than you take. He shared two of them with us on the show, and the way he spoke of them was not like someone reciting conclusions. He spoke like someone who had sat with those people and had his understanding of the world quietly rearranged. On giving more than you take, he told us about a native chief from the BC coast, a man nominated by others as someone who had found genuine happiness and had something to teach. When this man was fifteen, the salmon were running so abundantly that within an hour and a half, the boat was full. The teenage boys wanted to go straight back out. The father said no. He pointed to the neighbours who were struggling with their nets, and the ones who were struggling with their boat. Why don’t we go and help them so they can have enough? At fifteen, the son didn’t want to. At the end of that day, what made him most happy was not the catch but the helping. And it is in giving that we receive most deeply, John said. I forgot that story until you asked, but it was beautiful. On being true to yourself, he extended the idea further than I expected. The original Greek meaning of sin, he told us, is to miss the mark. To miss what you intended your life to be. His observation was that the most authentic self of humanity as a species is to extend and improve life itself, that when we act from that truest self, good things follow. He asked, quietly, whether humanity was acting in accordance with its truest self right now. He did not wait for an answer. We both knew it. What he could not sustain Here is the thing John did not plan to say in the keynote, did not put in the press release, probably hesitated to admit even to himself for a while: after twenty-five years of studying happiness, interviewing elders, speaking to audiences around the world about how to live well, he found he could not sustain it consistently in his own life. He took ten months away. He has written about walking the Camino de Santiago across northern Spain and living in the Andes of Peru. He was not seeking more information. He was seeking what was underneath information. What he found were not more secrets. They were thieves. Five patterns that steal happiness from the inside, named in The Five Thieves of Happiness. The compulsion to manage outcomes. The ego’s insistence that our small story is the central story. The belief that what we don’t have is what we need. The equation of acquiring with thriving. The avoidance of discomfort as a life strategy. He named these not as a researcher reporting findings but as a man who had gone looking for something in himself and found it. The Five Thieves of Happiness is a different kind of book from its predecessor. Quieter. More personal. Written by someone who, after decades of helping others think more carefully about their lives, turned the same question on himself and was startled by what he found. What the sabbatical represents, in the arc of his work, is an act of honest stopping. A recognition that the gap between what he knew and how he lived had become impossible to ignore. The Camino was not a cure. It was a willingness to stop pretending the gap wasn’t there. That willingness, as John would say, is itself a form of integrity. The boy by the stream Last June, John was in Ireland for a gathering with a poet and a group of people. The poet said something that caught him: What if his work was done and the rest was just gravy? On a walk that afternoon, John wrote a poem. He read it to us near the end of our conversation, quietly, with no preamble, as if he was reading something private and had decided, in the moment, to let us in. What if your work is truly done? What if you let go of all the grand ambition that has carried you and tortured you all this way? Surely, surely more has come to you than you could have reasonably expected, yet always seemingly so much less than you had unreasonably longed for. What if you just lived more generously, became again that warm, inviting, curious boy who once sat by a tiny stream alive to the sacred beauty of tiny things? What if you became small enough that the world could find you again, whether you needed it to or not? The boy by the stream in Staten Island, sneaking into the sailors’ home because it was the only place he could find real nature. That boy, at sixty-eight, writing a poem about what it might mean to become him again. John is recording songs now, working on a novel, doing daily videos, continuing to speak. He told me honestly that he is waiting for the current of what comes next to be strong enough to carry him out. Something is forming. He doesn’t know its shape yet. He is being patient with the not-knowing, which he acknowledged is its own kind of practice, and not an easy one. I said to him, watching him, that I wasn’t sure he was waiting so much as already following a current. He paused. Maybe, he said. What the question has cost and given John has spoken with great care throughout his career about the men he has worked with through the Men’s Initiative at UBC, later named Blueprint. He co-founded it with his friend and colleague David Kuhl, motivated by two things that were, for him, inseparable: the evidence that men and boys were struggling in measurable ways, falling behind across education, relationships, health, and mental wellbeing, and the honest acknowledgement that so much of what has gone wrong in the world has been perpetuated, disproportionately, by men. He shared a story he has carried for years, told to him by an African American man who grew up in the Bronx. This man’s brother was killed as a teenager. The family drove out to Long Island to bury him. On the long drive back, the women wanted to stop for a rest. It was just the young boy and his father left alone in the car. The father, who had not cried at all during the burial, began to wail. What the boy remembered were two things: his father kept apologising for crying. And he kept praising his son for being so strong. John was making a point about how much men hold inside. But the story went somewhere deeper than a point. It landed as a kind of grief, for all the fathers who could not cry in front of their children until they were alone on the drive home, and all the sons who were praised for not flinching. The work John describes, helping men find permission to speak, to name what they are carrying, to sit in a room with other men and say this is where I am not aligned with who I want to be, was not therapy. He was clear about that. It was human work. Work that happened to be most urgently needed in the rooms where men gathered. He told me that most of his closest friends are now men, which surprised him and would probably surprise anyone who met him in his thirties, when his closest friends were almost all women. He found his way into the company of men, and found comfort there. He speaks about male loneliness with unusual directness: the number of men who die within two to five years of losing a spouse, who had only one person in the world with whom they were fully real. He names that not as a comment on helplessness but on isolation. On the cost of a life where you have never told the full truth to a single other person. What he is asking us to see John describes himself as a public philosopher, and the description is careful. He said something early in our conversation that I wrote down immediately: that everything, at every fractal level, is a manifestation of the inner life. What individuals produce is an expression of their inner life. What organisations produce is an expression of theirs. What humanity is producing right now, the wars, the fracturing of trust, the deteriorating relationship with the earth, is the collective manifestation of our collective inner life. He said this plainly, without drama, the way someone says a thing they have been thinking about for a very long time and have finally found words for. The wars and the social fracture and the relationship with the planet are not separate problems to be solved with better policy or better technology, though both may help. They are symptoms. And the question he has been asking since he was a young minister sitting beside people who were dying, the question about what it means to live well and why so few of us do it, turns out to be the same question, taken to scale. What would it mean for a society to be its most authentic self? What would it mean for a species? He is still asking. He has never stopped. Taken a little further At the end of our conversation, John held up his father’s photograph in a Navy uniform. He spoke quietly, directly, looking at it, and then at us. He said his father was not a bad man. He was not evil. He just wasn’t intentional. He did not think deeply enough about the choices he was making. And now, at sixty-eight, John has spent his entire adult life helping others do exactly what his father could not: consider their choices before they become the shape of a life. He said, without performance, that he thought he had taken it a little further than his father. And he hoped that every person he had ever met would take it a little further than him. Not perfect, he said. But a little further. And if you do that, then you’ve done something good in the world. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on the conversation This episode runs for nearly an hour and a half. It is unhurried and wide-ranging, moving from John’s ministry years to his mother returning stolen candy, from indigenous wisdom and the fractal nature of happiness to democracy and the men he watched learn to grieve. John is a remarkable presence: warm, genuinely funny, philosophically serious without ever being remote. There is a moment near the very end when he holds up his father’s photograph that I suspect many people will need to watch twice. There is no hurry. The library is always here. And again, at every fractal level for individuals, including myself, because we all take people on the journey we most need to go on. What if you became small enough that the world could find you again, whether you needed it to or not? There is a pretty good chance they took it as far as they could. Forgive them if you can, because it is good for you. And all I hope is that I will help the next generation take it just a little further. John B. Izzo, PhD, is an author, speaker, and public philosopher whose work spans forty years and six continents. He is the author of nine books, including The Five Secrets You Must Discover Before You Die and The Five Thieves of Happiness, both international bestsellers. He has spoken to more than one million people and advised over five hundred organisations, including IBM, Apple, Microsoft, the Mayo Clinic, and Qantas. He is adjunct professor and co-founder of the Men’s Initiative at UBC, a Distinguished Fellow at the Stimson Center, and co-host of the podcast The Way Forward. He lives in Vancouver, British Columbia.
show-sophie-gregoire.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Sophie Grégoire, mental health advocate, bestselling author, speaker, and yoga teacher whose book Closer Together became an instant number one bestseller on the Toronto Star and Globe and Mail lists. For over two decades Sophie has been a passionate advocate for youth self-esteem, gender equality, and emotional literacy, and she brings that same quality of honest, open inquiry into this conversation. Sophie grew up in the Laurentians, raised by a father who told her to jump off cliffs and a mother who noticed every detail. She built a public life of enormous scope, and quietly, alongside it, did the inner work: learning to stop performing, to sit with what is difficult, to reclaim the parts of herself she had suppressed to fit spaces that seemed to require her to be less. Her closing gift to Katherine in this conversation is also its most complete teaching: your heart cannot break. It can only break open. This conversation covers Sophie’s childhood and the qualities she suppressed for years, what Gabor Maté said to her on a stage in Vancouver that made her weep immediately, the science behind why hypersensitivity is so often mistaken for aggression, and why the most radical act of leadership available to us right now is the willingness to know and love ourselves honestly. The morning of our conversation, Sophie’s uncle sent her a photograph. She is three years old in it. She is standing outside the cabin in the Laurentians where she spent the first years of her life, in the kind of light that only exists in the woods in early morning. She looked at it and wept. Not from grief exactly. From recognition. The little girl in the picture looked back at her, and Sophie saw it all at once: the innocence, the presence, a tad of sadness she hadn’t known was visible in a child that young. She told me about it at the start of our recording, still close to it, still a little undone. And then she said something I have been turning over since. I’m holding her now. That is Sophie Grégoire, in four words. A woman who has spent decades learning to feel rather than flee, and who has quietly, steadily turned that practice into one of the most honest bodies of work on mental health and human connection that Canada has produced. She is fifty years old. She is funny, fierce, occasionally profane, and so genuinely open to the person in front of her that you feel seen simply by being near her. She wrote a bestselling book. She was Canada’s de facto First Lady for eight years. She has stood on stages in front of tens of thousands of people. And none of that is the interesting thing about her. The interesting thing is that she can look at a photograph of herself at three and feel tenderness rather than distance. That she earned that tenderness. That she knows exactly what it cost. The cabin and the cape Sophie grew up in a small cabin in the Laurentians, in a village called Sainte-Adèle in Quebec, the kind of place where a child has a frozen lake to cross and a mountain to skidoo over and a father who will tell her to jump off a cliff and mean it as an act of love. Her father was action-oriented, confident, physically brave. He gave her the message that her body was capable, that the world could be met rather than avoided. Her mother was tender, observant, attuned to details, soft in the way that teaches a child their interior life matters. Sophie received both. She absorbed the fierce and the gentle in equal measure, and it gave her, as she put it, a solid home base inside herself, a place she could move from. It also gave her something harder to name. There was addiction on both sides of her family. Alcoholism, depression, people living with wounds they had no language for because that generation, as Sophie says, wasn’t looking at their trauma. It wasn’t accessible the way it is now. Little Sophie, an only child surrounded by adults, learned early to read the room. To sense what was unspoken. To wear what she called “the cape of wanting to save.” She absorbed the emotional weight of the people around her with the hyper-attunement of a child who has never been taught it isn’t hers to carry. No child should wear that cape, she told me. And she said it with gentleness, not blame. It is simply what happened. It is how she became someone who could smell dishonesty from across a room, who defaulted to seeing beauty first, who carried a deep sensitivity beneath the rambunctiousness, the fort-building, the hanging out with the boys who always did the crazier things. The sensitivity was the point. It always had been. The night she flew over herself By her late teens, Sophie was using food the way some people use alcohol or work or the noise of being constantly available. As a drug of numbness, she says. As a way of finding temporary relief from a pain she hadn’t yet learned to sit with. Bulimia, for years, in secret. On the surface: a good student, athletic, popular, living in an affluent Montreal suburb with, as she puts it, all of it. On the inside: shame, and the particular exhaustion of a person performing a version of themselves that doesn’t quite fit. One night she trembled in her single bed in a small room. She had purged too hard, too long. She could hear her mother through the bathroom wall, just the ordinary sounds of someone moving through their evening. Sophie lay there and felt something she had not felt before: she flew over herself. She looked down at the girl in the bed and said, no more. You don’t have to do this to yourself. I was aware that I was aware. Holy. She called for her mother. Her mother came. Sophie told her she was sick, that she had an eating disorder, that she needed help. And her mother said: I knew something was off. I’m going to be here for you. What followed was chaos in the body, she told me. Sadness and anger at once. Feeling alone and then accompanied. Feeling understood and then misunderstood. The emotions didn’t resolve themselves into something clean and manageable. They came all at the same time, which is how emotions actually come when you stop suppressing them. Sophie sat in the middle of it. And something in that sitting changed her. She had discovered that someone inside herself was watching over her. From that night on, she decided she was going to understand what was happening to her. The eating disorder didn’t vanish overnight. Recovery is not an event. But a direction had been chosen. She was going to know herself rather than flee herself. That choice, made in a small room in the dark, is the hinge on which her entire life turns. What you suppress, and what it costs A few years later, in her mid-twenties, a girlfriend was setting up a foundation for people with eating disorders in Montreal. There was almost nothing then, she told me. People weren’t talking about it. The girlfriend asked Sophie if she would tell her story at a press conference. Sophie was a newcomer in the television and radio scene. She was terrified she would lose every contract she had. She thought of how people would see her: the girl who vomits, the girl with no control, the girl who couldn’t handle herself. So much stigma. So much she had internalised. She did it anyway. “I don’t want to live with this lie to myself,” she said. And the response, when her story came out in magazines and on television, was what she describes as a big exhale from the public. Finally. If she could say it, maybe others could too. Maybe they didn’t have to carry it alone. That press conference was the beginning of twenty years of advocacy for mental health, for emotional literacy, for the right of ordinary people to access the knowledge that had been kept in therapy rooms and academic journals and the expensive offices of private practitioners. But even as she was giving others permission, she was still learning to give it to herself. There were parts of Sophie she had suppressed, she told me, for those same twenty years. Her creativity, the way she reads poetry and feels something light up inside her. Her sensuality, her eroticism. Her ambition, expressed through what she now calls feminine leadership. She thought she had to be masculine to lead. She thought the world required a certain shape from her, and she gave it that shape, and it cost her the parts she had to squeeze out to fit. She named them to me directly, without hesitation, which is itself a form of the work. Not “I struggled with self-expression” or “I found it difficult to be authentic in certain domains.” She named the things: creativity, sensuality, ambition through feminine leadership. The specificity is the honesty. And the honesty is the beginning of recovery. Closer together, and what Gabor Maté named Sophie’s book Closer Together: Knowing Ourselves, Loving Each Other became a number one bestseller. It is part memoir, part guide, woven through with interviews she conducted with some of the most respected voices in human behaviour: Gabor Maté, Terrence Real, Liz Plank, Harville Hendrix and Helen LaKelly Hunt, among others. Hillary Rodham Clinton called it “candid, enlightening, and an intrepid exploration into achieving a life filled with purpose, meaning, and a sense of wonder.” Sophie wrote it because she had been lucky. She had access, through her platform and her connections, to conversations and knowledge that most people never get near. She sat with experts who had spent their careers understanding why we do what we do, why we hurt the way we hurt, why the patterns of our childhoods play themselves out in our marriages and our workplaces and our bodies decades later. And she kept thinking: this cannot be only for people like me. This has to be available to everyone. The workshops she runs now cost forty dollars. Not forty thousand. Forty. That number is deliberate. Sophie knows what it is like to need something and not be able to afford it. She knows what it is like to have a pain with no container. She is building containers at a price that doesn’t require privilege. At the Vancouver launch of Closer Together, Sophie stood on stage with Gabor Maté. There was a first question planned. He looked at her and didn’t ask it. He said: “This is not a book.” Sophie waited, uncertain. He said: “This is your love letter to the world, isn’t it?” She was in tears within the first five seconds. She told me this story with the quiet wonder of someone who has been seen so precisely that words fail. The person who had helped her understand trauma looked at the work she had made and named it more accurately than she had named it herself. That is what Sincerely calls witnessing. Not analysis. Not praise. Simply: I see what this actually is. The book is a love letter. And that Gabor Maté named it that means something that transcends the review or the endorsement. He was telling her what she had already known but hadn’t quite let herself say out loud. The gene for aggression is not aggression There is a thread in this conversation that runs from Sophie’s tiny bedroom all the way to the state of democracies, and it is the thread I most want to pull at here. Sophie learned something from genetic research that she keeps returning to: the gene associated with what we commonly read as aggression is, in fact, not aggression. It is hypersensitivity. The person in the boardroom who lashes out. The leader who doubles down when challenged. The colleague who goes silent and then explodes. All of them are, at the root, a nervous system that was never given the tools to regulate the emotions it is carrying. They are not villains. They are overwhelmed. Sophie links this directly to the fractured world we are living in. She references Todd Rose’s research on collective illusion: eighty per cent of what we consume on social media is created by ten per cent of users, and that ten per cent is not representative of who we actually are as a collective. What is happening now, particularly in the United States and across western democracies, is that the loudest, most repeated voices are mistaken for the majority. The validation of fear has become a political tool. You find the person who is already dysregulated, already struggling, already feeling left behind, and you tell them it is someone else’s fault.
