You tell them who to direct the pain at. And it works, because it names the pain without healing it. “We are dysregulated children in adult bodies,” Sophie said. She said it without contempt. Without despair. She is describing a diagnosis, not a condemnation. And the diagnosis matters because it points toward the cure. Emotional literacy is not a soft skill. It is the skill that makes every other skill possible. A person who can sit with their own pain, name it, stay with it long enough to understand what it is asking, is a person who does not need a scapegoat. A person who has been given the tools to regulate is a person who can build something with their anger rather than burning things down. This is what Sophie Grégoire has devoted twenty years to saying in rooms large and small, in books and workshops and conversations and advocacy campaigns: you are not broken. Your pain is not your fault. And you can learn to sit with it. All of you can. What it means to hold your own child Late in our conversation, Sophie described something small that has stayed with me. When her nervous system is overwhelmed, when fear or grief or shame comes flooding in, she holds herself. Both arms wrapped around her own body, butterfly taps on her upper arms, a soft voice speaking to whatever part of her is frightened: you are not alone. You are not being abandoned. This too shall pass. You are loved. She calls it a somatic technique, which it is. But she also calls it what it actually is, which is an act of tenderness toward the child who still lives inside her. The child who felt alone in the small room. The child who wore the cape. The child who got her first photo sent from the Laurentians that morning and immediately wept. Sophie is fifty now. She has navigated a very public marriage and a very public separation. She has raised three children while advocating for the inner lives of millions. She has been photographed and scrutinised and praised and criticised and reduced to a surname that was never her only name. She is reclaiming the one she was born with. And she is still unfolding. She said this without apology. She said it with something close to joy. Rainer Maria Rilke wrote: I want to unfold. Let there be no space in me that holds itself closed, for where I am closed, I am false. Sophie knows these lines. She closed our conversation with them. She said: I don’t want to be false, baby. I want to unfold and open, and I wish the same for everybody else. The “baby” is characteristic. She says it the way she says everything: like she means it, like it costs her nothing to be warm, like warmth is not a performance but simply what comes out when she stops trying to control the shape of herself. What her life is asking us to see Sophie Grégoire has spent her entire adult life arguing, in every form available to her, for one idea: that to know yourself is not a luxury. That self-knowledge is the foundation of every other form of love, every other form of leadership, every other form of repair. That the pain you are carrying has something to teach you, if you are willing to stay with it long enough to hear. This is not a comfortable argument to make in public. Sophie made it twenty years ago when eating disorders were still largely unspoken, at the cost of television contracts she could not afford to lose. She made it through the years of public life when her role was officially ornamental and her interior world was nobody’s business. She made it through a marriage and a separation that were conducted in full view of a nation. She is still making it. What I witnessed in our conversation was someone who has arrived, in the most honest sense of the word. She is not performing equanimity. She is not reciting lessons she has learned. She is someone who has done the actual work of sitting with her own pain, and who has come out the other side with a tenderness for every person she meets, including the cashier at the grocery store, including the person across the political divide, including the little girl in the photograph her uncle sent her that morning. “My soul dances with your soul,” she said to me at one point, without any apparent irony. I believed her. Because she had already spent an hour being completely, undefendedly present. Nothing about her was performing. She was just there. That quality, that capacity for full presence, is itself a form of the work she teaches. You cannot be fully present when you are running from your own experience. You cannot really see another person when you are busy managing how they see you. Sophie has stopped managing. She is just here. Fiercely, gently, totally here. The heart cannot break, she told me as we finished. It can only break open. She has lived that. It shows. Every word she spoke carried the weight of someone who learned it not from a book but from the long, quiet, hard work of staying with herself until the staying felt like home. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on this conversation This episode runs for approximately one hour. It is warm and unhurried, the kind of conversation where both people are fully present and completely undefended. Sophie and Katherine have known each other for several years, and that ease comes through in every exchange. Two women who have walked through something real, talking honestly about what they found on the other side. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I was aware that I was aware. Holy. Being able to sit with your pain and your truth is the greatest freaking gift you will ever gift yourself. Ever. Your heart can’t break. It can only break open. Sophie Grégoire is a mental health advocate, author, global speaker, and certified yoga instructor based in Canada. Her book Closer Together: Knowing Ourselves, Loving Each Other is a number one bestseller, combining memoir with expert knowledge on human behaviour, emotional literacy, and the roots of connection and disconnection. It is currently being adapted into a documentary series. Sophie has devoted more than twenty years to making self-knowledge accessible to everyone, not only those with the resources to seek it privately. She is the First National Volunteer for the Canadian Mental Health Association and Youth Leadership Global Ambassador for Plan International Canada. She has received multiple United Nations recognition awards for her humanitarian work.
show-delphine-le-serre.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Dr. Delphine Le Serre, founder and president of EdHu2050, a global think tank dedicated to reimagining education in the age of artificial intelligence. Delphine is a physicist, behavioural scientist, former university professor, and entrepreneur ranked by Forbes among the Top 20 Women Transforming EdTech in Europe. She is also the creator of the MOON pedagogy framework, now being implemented in schools across North America and beyond. Delphine’s path to this work was not linear. She left France at 40 having sold her company, enrolled her four-year-old son Moon in a Montreal school, and then did something she had never done in her adult life: she stopped. She walked without a destination, sat in a church not for religion but for quiet, and slowly learned to listen to her own heart. What emerged from 18 months of stillness was a framework she had first needed to live herself before she could offer it to anyone else. The MOON pedagogy organises human development across four essential relationships: with self, with others, with nature, and with intelligent machines. It is, at its core, a pathway to wholeness. In this conversation Delphine and Katherine explore the science of it, the soul of it, and what it means to build an education system that begins by asking a child: do you know who you are, and do you love what you find? A 40-year-old woman walks into a church in Montreal. She does not believe in the religion. She is not there for the religion. She has just left France. She has sold her company. She has enrolled her four-year-old son in a Montreal school. She has decided, for the first time in her adult life, not to be useful. She walks her son to school in the morning, takes the metro back, walks through the parks, watches the birds, drinks her coffee on a bench, and then, slowly, finds her way inside the church because it is quiet. She sits for thirty minutes. Forty minutes. Sometimes an hour. She tries to listen to her own heart. She does not know, yet, that she is meditating. She only knows that it feels good. This is so good, she says to herself, sitting in the cold of an unfamiliar church in an unfamiliar city. No constraints. No phone calls. No emails. Just me with myself, and I’m listening to me, and it is good. This is the moment Dr Delphine Le Serre walks into the rest of her life. She does not know, yet, that the framework being born inside that silence will be adopted by schools across North America and welcomed at the tables of ministries of education redesigning curriculum for an AI-shaped century. She does not know that the woman she is becoming, slowly, in a building she does not believe in, is the woman who will write the book that explains what a child actually needs in the world artificial intelligence is making. None of that is in the room yet. In the room there is a heartbeat she has never properly heard, and a quiet that is finally large enough to contain her. This is a portrait of who she is, what those months gave her, and what her life is quietly trying to teach the rest of us about education, about leadership, and about what it costs to wake up. The full conversation is at the top of the page if you want to spend an evening with her. The piece that follows is for those of you who want to understand her first. The warrior on paper There is a French word for what Delphine was, in the years before that church. Malheureux. It does not translate cleanly. Unhappy gets close and misses entirely. Malheureux is the precise word for a life that looks like a success from the outside and feels incomplete from the inside. Happy in the wrong way. Whole in the wrong shape. Built but not lived. She had built a great deal. She is a physicist by training. An engineer in microelectronics and nanotechnology at Grenoble. A PhD in behavioural science earned at night while she ran teams of seventy people in industry. Fifteen years as a university professor and academic researcher at HEC Montréal, INSEEC and across European business schools. The founder of two companies, the first launched while she was still teaching, both later sold. In 2018 Forbes named her among the Top 20 Women Transforming EdTech in Europe. She has the kind of CV that explains itself. She has, by her own description, never cried in a professional context. She calls the woman she was for the first forty years Delphine the warrior. And on paper, she says, her life was a complete success. Really. Underneath the paper, she was malheureux. The formation that produced this woman is worth slowing on, because the most important pieces of it are the pieces no recruiter would ever notice. Delphine grew up in Brittany, near the ocean. Her mother worked in the public library. There was a younger sister and an older brother and a middle child who learned early to be calm, to listen, to read. She was eight when she taught herself the rotation of the Earth, reading Copernicus and Kepler and Galileo at her mother’s library and building her own presentation on the heliocentric model. There was no audience for it. She built it because she wanted to understand. At the same time, she was reading Greek mythology. The wars between the Titans and Zeus. The goddess Athena. The Oracle in a city called Delphi, from which her own name was drawn, and whose meaning she would not understand for decades. And then there was her uncle. Not a blood uncle. A philosophy teacher who taught her tennis on the side. From the age of nine onward, he picked her up from her parents’ house and drove her to the tennis court. In the car, he asked her things. By the time she was ten, the questions had become these. Do you think reality exists? What do you think the truth is? Do you think there is only one truth? Most ten-year-olds are not asked these questions. Most ten-year-olds would not know what to do with them if they were. Delphine remembers them as gifts. A mother who answered every question. An uncle who asked impossible ones. A library that contained more than she could finish. A Greek goddess whose name she had inherited. The combination produced the kind of mind that would later sit at the intersection of quantum physics and human consciousness without finding the combination strange at all. Then the formation became forty years of doing. Physics. Engineering. The PhD. The professorships. The companies built and sold. The digital transformation work inside European higher education. The Forbes recognition. A warrior at the apex of her field.And the warrior was malheureux. Three acts of courage Before Montreal, there were three thresholds, and each one required her to disappoint someone she loved to stay true to herself. The first was a relationship. A wonderful man. The kindest man on earth, in her own words. She was engaged to him. The life being assembled around the engagement looked, again, like a complete success on paper. Inside her, something was quietly saying no. The voice was not loud. It was not dramatic. It simply did not stop. She listened. She ended the engagement. It was, she says, the first time in her life she had disappointed people by choosing herself. She had been raised, like most of us, to satisfy others. Disappointing them was the unthinkable thing. She did the unthinkable, and survived it. The second was her career. She left engineering. She was successful. She came from a family in which no one had been to university; she was the first one with a well-paid job. Are you having a nervous breakdown? people asked her, because nothing about her decision was rational in the language anyone around her spoke. She enrolled in the PhD anyway. She gave her first university lecture, walked off the stage, and said to herself the sentence that has stayed with her for thirty years. I could do that for free. That was how she knew. She would have done it for nothing. The work was a calling, and the calling had announced itself in the form of a simple, almost embarrassing sentence about money she did not need. The third was love. She fell in love with a woman. She came out. Her family did not understand. She talks about this, in the conversation, with the gentleness of someone who has lived inside the difficulty long enough to be tender about it. Coming out, she says, is the act of courage in which the very people who are supposed to love you unconditionally may be the ones who reject you. There is no safe house to return to, the way a child of colour can return to a home that understands them, the way a Jewish child can return to a family that shares the heritage. The gay child often comes out alone. She came out anyway. She thought, at that point, that her transformation was done. She was wrong. The church that arrived She sold her company in 2018. She moved her family to Canada in 2019, six months before the world locked down. She landed in Toronto, decided the energy was not what she needed, and three days into Montreal said this is the place. She enrolled her son. And then she did the thing she had spent four decades being unable to do. She did nothing. No projects. No company. No clients. No deck. No keynote. No salary depending on her performance. She did not even take a car. She walked. She walked to the school in the morning. She took the metro back. She walked through the parks. She drank coffee on benches and listened to people laughing and sometimes crying. She walked under rain and snow. She did this for weeks, then months. And then she started stopping at the church. It does not matter that the building is a church. Delphine says it clearly. She was raised Christian, she is past the dogma, the theology is no longer her language. What the church offers her, in this season of her life, is the thing the rest of her life has been failing to offer: quiet. A place where her phone does not ring. A place where nobody needs anything from her. She sits inside it for thirty, forty, sometimes sixty minutes, and she tries to listen to her own heartbeat. I didn’t know at the beginning that I was starting to meditate. The sentence is worth sitting with, because it is the sentence on which her entire next decade turns. A woman who has been running so fast for forty years that she has never properly heard her own heart. A woman with no spiritual vocabulary for what is happening. A woman who walks into a quiet building because she needs quiet, and discovers, slowly, that what she finds inside is the part of herself she has been too busy to meet. Later in the conversation Katherine names it for her. The place acted as a Sincerely blanket, holding you as you went through the storm. Delphine nods. Yes, she says. Yes. Definitely. The storm was real. She does not romanticise the 18 months. She calls them heavy. She calls them dark. She had what she calls a dream team: a therapist who specialised in emotions and family configurations, an osteopath because she believed in epigenetics and what the body carries from the people who came before us, and an energy practitioner because the quantum physicist in her had never stopped believing that there are dimensions of reality our instruments have not yet learned to measure. It took 18 months. It was a nightmare in places. It was the most important thing she had ever done. Most women who go through a passage like this come out with a more peaceful life, perhaps a different relationship, perhaps a meditation practice. Delphine came out with a pedagogy. The physicist in her had been there the whole time, watching, taking notes, mapping the territory. By the time the silence began to break, she had a structure for what she had learned. The structure became MOON. What she built It is worth slowing down on what MOON is, because what Delphine has built deserves to be understood and not skimmed. MOON is a pedagogical framework that organises a child’s development across four relationships. Me with myself. The inner pillar. Knowing who you are. Identifying your emotions, accepting them, learning to deal with them. Naming the talents you came in with, because honouring them is how you find your way to the work that feels like teaching for free. Loving the person you find inside. Me with others. The relational pillar. The capacity to see another human being for who they are. To hold difference without violence. To stay in connection through disagreement. Me with nature. The reconnection with the natural world. The understanding that human beings have, until very recently in our history, known how to communicate with vegetation, with animals, with the larger field of life. Jane Goodall, Delphine notes, said before she died that she had twice asked the rain to stop and the rain had stopped. Me with intelligent machines. The newest pillar, and the one that gives the whole framework its urgency. The cognitive and ethical relationship with the AI systems that will be the largest fact of the lives our children are walking into. AI literacy. Critical thinking. Discernment. The capacity to use these tools without being used by them. Four pillars. One curriculum. A complete map of what it means to be a whole human being in the century that is arriving. Katherine names something inside the conversation that I want to put a marker on, because it is the sentence the framework itself is built around. The first pillar carries most of the weight. Maybe seventy percent of it. You cannot raise a child to know and love others if you have not raised them to know and love themselves. You cannot teach a child to connect with nature if they cannot connect with the nature inside their own body. You cannot teach a child to use intelligent machines well if you have not taught them what an intelligent human being actually is. The other three pillars rest on the first one. The first one is the one Delphine had to learn last. She founded EdHu2050 in 2022 to carry the framework into the world. It is a Montreal-based foundation and equity fund building, eventually, one hundred schools designed around this question: who is the human being on the other side of this curriculum, and what kind of life is the curriculum preparing them for. The first school is in Ottawa. Fifteen to twenty more are joining the network across the next two years. Her book, The Future of Human Intelligence, is out in French and arrives in English in March. There is a MOON virtual assistant in development for families, students, and entrepreneurs. There is a certification for schools that want to formally adopt the framework. And, in a detail Delphine almost throws away in conversation, the schools came to her. She did not seek them. The work calls its people. The work does not have to chase them. What the parents already know There is one finding in this conversation that organises everything else. Two parents came to Katherine in the months before this episode was recorded. Loving parents. Successful in corporate Canada. They sat in her office and told her, almost in shame, that they thought they were making a mistake. They had raised their children to be heart-centred, gentle, attuned, kind. The children were being bullied at school. The parents were wondering, out loud, whether they should have made them tougher. More aggressive. More armoured. Better equipped to compete for jobs in the world they were going to enter. Katherine asked them. Do you really think that’s the answer? They cried. Both of them. We’re afraid, they said. We know that what is in our child’s best interest, long term, is that they love themselves and find peace within and develop a love for nature and for others. We know. But we are afraid. This is the conversation parents are quietly having with themselves all over the world right now. They know what their children actually need. They are afraid the world will punish their children for needing it. What Delphine has built, in the calmest and most rigorous voice imaginable, is the answer to that fear. She names the four crises that frame the lives our children are walking into. Social fracture. Economic fragility. Planetary breakdown. Information collapse, with AI as the gasoline on that fourth fire. Each one impossible to solve from the same operating system that produced it. What children need is the capacity to build a different system than the one they are inheriting. To know who they are and love what they find. To hold space for others who are different from them. To feel into the natural world as if they belong to it, because they do. To develop a discerning, ethical, alive relationship with the intelligent machines that are now part of the family. Competing harder inside a broken system will not get a child to a life worth living. Building a better system might. Delphine has built a curriculum for the world that is coming, the one her physicist’s eye saw arriving years before most of us were ready to look at it. You don’t need to know exactly what the jobs of the future look like. All you need to do is be guided by your heart and what you know to be true. That is Katherine speaking to Delphine, near the end of the conversation. It is also, in a way, Katherine speaking to every parent and every teacher who has been holding the question and not finding an answer that did not make them complicit in something they did not want to perpetuate. There is an answer. It is being built. It is already in a school in Ottawa, and in fifteen to twenty more across the year ahead, and in a foundation in Montreal run by a woman who learned what whole human beings need by becoming one herself. What her life is asking us to see The agreement of The Sincerely Show is a simple one. The guest is witnessed. They sit, they are seen, they tell the truth about the path they have walked, and the meaning is made together with the listener. But because Delphine has lived the way she has lived, the witness becomes a teaching anyway. Her life teaches, even when she does not. What her life teaches is this. You can spend forty years building a life that looks complete on paper and discover, in your forties, that you are malheureux. Happy in the wrong way. Successful in the wrong shape. Built but not lived. That word is the beginning of the conversation with yourself that you have been too busy to have. It is also, if you let it be, an invitation into the years that come next. The voice inside you is real. It will ask you to disappoint people you love to be honest with yourself. It will ask you more than once. Each time you listen, the next time gets clearer. The third or fourth time, you may find yourself in a foreign city with no plan, walking to a church you do not believe in, sitting down inside it for an hour, and discovering that the quiet has been waiting for you the whole time. The work you are uniquely here to do is being prepared inside everything that has happened to you, including the parts that felt like prisons. I am very grateful for all the prisons, all these opportunities that have been prisons, that life has placed on my path, Delphine says. Because I understand now that they were here to prepare me for what I was supposed to do. You will not see the shape of it at twenty-five. You will see it at forty, or fifty, or sixty, looking back across the puzzle pieces and finally noticing the picture. The picture was there the whole time. You needed to live long enough to see it. And the most important thing you can give a child is the capacity to know who they are, to love what they find, to recognise the inner life of others, to feel into the natural world they belong to, and to live with discernment alongside the intelligent machines that will be the air they breathe. The world we are leaving behind cannot teach them this. The world that is coming will demand it. The skills for that century are being designed right now by a woman in Montreal who spent forty years not knowing what her own heart sounded like, and who became the person who could design them on the day she finally sat down and listened. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on the conversation The full conversation with Delphine is at the top of this page. Almost ninety minutes, unhurried, the way we do the show. We move through her childhood in Brittany, the philosophy lessons in her uncle’s car, the years inside engineering, the move to Montreal, the church, the dream team, the founding of EdHu2050, the architecture of MOON, the first school in Ottawa, and the conversation we keep having with parents who are afraid the world will punish their children for being kind. You will hear her say things, in her own voice and her own quietness, that no portrait can fully carry. The way she pauses before she answers. The way she returns to the body without making a point of it. The way she speaks about quantum physics and the Oracle of Delphi in the same breath, without finding the combination strange, because for her it is not. Take the conversation slowly. When you have time. With a cup of something warm. There is no hurry. The library is always here. I didn’t know at the beginning that I was starting to meditate. We can live an entire life without knowing our talents. And most of the time it’s sad. And we know it. On paper, my life was a complete success. Really. Dr Delphine Le Serre is the founder and president of EdHu2050, a Montreal-based foundation and equity fund dedicated to financing the creation of one hundred schools of tomorrow built around a different way of thinking about human potential. She is the creator of the MOON pedagogy, now being adopted by schools across North America and beyond. A physicist and engineer by training, with a PhD in behavioural science, she spent fifteen years as a professor and researcher at HEC Montréal, INSEEC, and other leading institutions in Europe. She holds a Professional Certificate in AI, IoT, Blockchain, and Cloud from MIT Professional Education, and was ranked by Forbes among the Top 20 Women Transforming EdTech in Europe in 2018. Her first book, The Future of Human Intelligence, was published in French and arrives in English in March.
show-amy-elizabeth-fox.html: Katherine Dudtschak sits down with Amy Elizabeth Fox, co-founder and CEO of Mobius Executive Leadership, a global transformational leadership firm she has led for 20 years. Amy has spent her career at the precise intersection of corporate rigour and deep human healing: working with Fortune 500 companies and professional services firms while drawing on psychology, somatics, trauma-informed practice, and spiritual wisdom to help senior leaders become more whole. She is also the co-author of the 2026 book Leading in Chaos, written with Nicholas Janni. Before any of that, Amy survived non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma in her twenties, lived through childhood trauma, spent two years in silence near a lake after leaving the Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine in New York, and had a heart cracked open by a kirtan circle she almost walked out of. This conversation moves through all of it: the formation, the collapse, the rebuilding, and the 20 years of bringing love into organisations that weren’t sure they wanted it. Amy also shares what she has observed across thousands of senior executive screenings: that collective trauma is not the exception in leadership. It is almost universal. And that the most important work any organisation can do begins not with strategy, but with the people carrying the weight of the past into every room they lead. Inside the most powerful boardrooms in the world, a woman walks in. She arrives quietly. The credentials never lead. By the time she has crossed the room and found her chair, she has already taken the temperature of every person in it, and what she does next has nothing to do with strategy decks or quarterly targets. She helps the people in the room drop their armour. This is the work of Amy Elizabeth Fox. For twenty years she has practised it in Fortune 500 boardrooms and the world’s most demanding professional services firms, with global CEOs and the people two and three levels below them who will run those companies next, at Oxford, across continents. Around it she has built a global firm of more than three hundred practitioners, united by a single, almost audacious intention. They are trying to bring love to business. When Amy says it that simply, you do not hear it as a slogan. You hear it as twenty years of practice. And you sense, immediately, that the woman saying it is the reason it has worked. What follows is a portrait. Who she is. What she has built. What her life is quietly teaching the rest of us about leadership in this moment. The full conversation sits at the top of the page if you would like to spend an evening with her. The piece below is for those who want to understand her first. A figure unlike anyone else in her field Amy is the co-founder and CEO of Mobius Executive Leadership, the firm she and her sister Erica Ariel Fox started in 2005. Mobius sits at an intersection most consultancies cannot reach. On one side, the rigour. Harvard-trained methodology, evidence-based interventions, the kind of senior expert network that reads like a graduate-level reading list: Otto Scharmer, Adam Kahane, Peter Senge, Amy Edmondson, Bob Kegan, Linda Hill, Tom DeLong. On the other side, the depth. Trauma-informed practice. Somatics. Mythology. Shadow work. Expressive arts. Meditation. The patient work of integration. Mobius programs feature poets and cellists on the same stages as Fortune 500 executives. The faculty come from psychology, theatre, philosophy, and the great spiritual traditions. The clients are some of the most demanding organisations on earth, and they have stayed for a decade or more, because the work changes people. What makes Amy unusual is that she could only have built what she built. Plenty of people have built unusual firms. The architecture of Mobius is a direct expression of the woman who designed it. Walk into a room she is holding and you understand instantly. She has actually lived everything she helps other people see. She is, in the language we use here at Sincerely, an Athena. Fierce and strategic and wise. Creative and discerning. Humbling, nurturing, kind. Whole in her essence. She became this through a particular kind of formation, the kind most leaders never go through because almost no one would choose it. The illness that became the gift When Amy was twenty-two, she was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. She spent a year in chemotherapy and radiation. In the decades since, she has refused to call it the worst thing that ever happened to her. She calls it the greatest gift she has ever been given. Everything I’ve become, or done, or chosen, was really informed by the wisdom I took from my illness. The reframing is not denial. Amy is too honest for that. The illness was soul-shaping. The CAT scan machine. The nights of not knowing whether she would live to twenty-three. In dissolving the ego of a young woman in her twenties, the illness returned her to a question that has shaped every choice she has made since. What are you here for, now that you know how short it is. The question was already in her when she walked into the Cathedral Church of Saint John the Divine, in New York. It is what made her say yes to a posting most people her age would have considered eccentric. In the late eighties and through the nineties, the Cathedral was a crossroads. Ram Dass was teaching there. Carl Sagan was a regular presence. Paul Gorman ran the National Religious Partnership for the Environment from an office in the building. Vice President Al Gore came through to talk about climate. Amy, as Director of Public Affairs, spent ten years inside that ecosystem, translating between scientific evidence and parish congregations, helping faith communities find language for the planetary breakdown they could feel but could not yet name. Most people in her generation who went into climate work in the late eighties were moved by urgency. Amy was moved by survival. The cancer had already taught her how brief this is. The Cathedral years were the first long answer to the question her illness had handed her. The cathedral that arrives Toward the end of her decade at the Cathedral, Amy was invited to a week with Ram Dass. On the final night, the group was chanting Hindu Sanskrit names of God. Amy is tone deaf and self-conscious about it. She almost did not go. She sat in the back row, ready to leave. Then the singing started. Some part of my heart just broke open. It was the quality of devotion and the quality of unconditional love. And that frequency, I’ve been following ever since. Take her seriously on her own terms. She is telling a story about a frequency. Something that arrived in a back room on a night she almost skipped, and now orders the rest of her life. Forty years on, she is still listening for it. She has built a global firm around it. The boardrooms she walks into now are, in a sense, larger versions of that back row, full of people who do not yet know what they came for. She gave me language for this, and I have not been able to put it down. In the journey to consciousness and to service and to self-love, there’s a cathedral that arrives. The image is precise. A cathedral. Something that arrives, rather than something you build. Something you walk into rather than something you achieve. Something that finds you in the most unlikely places and is unmistakable when it does. This is Amy’s most profound spiritual proposition, and it deserves time. Most of us are taught to think of becoming as a construction project. We acquire practices, frameworks, identities, achievements. We build and build, until we believe we have constructed the person we were meant to be. Amy lives in a different model entirely. The cathedral is something the soul recognises when the soul is ready to recognise it. You can be sitting in the back row of a chanting circle. You can be reading a book that has been on your nightstand for four years. You can be standing in a hospital corridor in your twenties listening to a diagnosis. You can be in a Mobius retreat, or a long conversation, or a quiet kitchen at three in the morning. The setting is incidental. What matters is the recognition. For Amy, the cathedral was a Sanskrit chant. For her clients, it might be something inside a Mobius programme. For someone reading this, it might be the sentence in this paragraph that has just made you pause. The cathedral arrives more than once. We come back to that. Two years carrying her own water When the decade at the Cathedral ended, Amy did not know what would come next. What she did next was the quietly radical decision of her life. She went into the woods. She lived near a lake. She lived in silence. She carried her own water. For two years she metabolised the unprocessed grief, the unprocessed terror, the unprocessed joy of the decade behind her. The frequency she had heard in the back row needed somewhere to land inside her body, and the woods was the only place quiet enough to let it. Most leadership stories edit this part out. The two years where nothing was happening. The years where you cannot point to a title or an achievement. The years where you are not building anything visible. They are usually mentioned, if at all, as a “gap” or a “sabbatical” or a “period of self-discovery.” Amy speaks about hers without that softening. She describes a season of carrying her own water and learning what she was made of when nobody was watching. There is a teaching here, and it is one of the hardest teachings to hear in a culture that measures everything by output. Some of the most important work of a life happens during the years that look, from the outside, like nothing at all. The years of integration. The years when what came before is being digested and what comes next is gestating. Amy’s two years near the lake are the hidden chapter of the Mobius story. Without them, Mobius could not have been built. When she came out, she went and got a master’s degree in counselling. She worked in an alcohol rehabilitation centre. She trained at Harvard with Doug Stone, Sheila Heen, and Bruce Patton, the team who later wrote Difficult Conversations. She taught negotiation. She helped people have the conversations they had spent years avoiding. And then, in 2005, she and Erica decided to build something of their own. They called it Mobius. The single continuous surface with no separation between inside and outside. The work and the woman became one piece. What she has actually built What Amy has built deserves more than a skim. Mobius is a constellation. More than three hundred practitioners working across continents, in service of senior executives and the organisations they lead. The methodology draws on adult development theory, neuroscience, trauma-informed practice, psychology, mythology, somatics, expressive arts, and what Amy, with characteristic gentleness, calls “the deep wisdom of spiritual traditions.” The clients are Fortune 500 companies. The faculty include therapists, scholars, mystics, and artists. The work has been delivered to thousands of executives across more than a decade of partnership with the global leadership advisory firm Egon Zehnder. Amy is also lead faculty on Thomas Hüebl’s Timeless Wisdom Training and co-leads a first-of-its-kind year-long certification in Trauma Informed Consulting and Coaching with him. She teaches at Oxford’s Saïd Business School through the African Leadership Institute’s Desmond Tutu Fellows Program. None of these institutions are soft. They pay for it because it moves people. What Mobius proves, in the simplest possible terms, is that the world’s most demanding organisations do not need their leaders to be tougher. They need them to be more whole. They need them to drop the armour. They need them to lower the level of fear in the systems they hold. They need the kind of inner work most leadership development has spent forty years pretending was a private matter. This is the radical thesis underneath the soft language. Amy has been quietly running an experiment on the most senior people in the world. The experiment has been working for twenty years. She lets the work speak for itself. Underneath the modesty there is a proposition. The proposition is that the inherited model of leadership rests on a pretence. The pretence is that we can develop people from the outside in, by accumulating frameworks and competencies and behaviours, without ever acknowledging the inside. The pretence has run its course. Amy is part of what comes next. A universal pandemic There is one finding from Amy’s twenty years that organises everything else. Before every Mobius leadership programme, the participants are screened for trauma. Thousands of senior executives have now sat in that screening. The pattern is consistent. I have hardly ever met anyone from anywhere in the world where there isn’t some kind of trauma. So this is a universal pandemic. Generations of violence, addiction, mental health issues, poverty, racism, colonialism. She said it as data. This is the empirical finding of two decades of working with the most senior leaders in global business. Almost universally, they are carrying something. Generational wounds, family wounds, cultural wounds, personal wounds. Most of them have never told anyone. Many of them have not allowed themselves to know it. And they carry that unhealed history into every boardroom, every difficult conversation, every culture they build, every team they lead. Amy is naming the model of leadership that pretends the inside does not exist. That model can hold for as long as the world is stable. It cannot hold now. The complexity is too high. The pace is too fast. The interconnection of the four existential crises, social fracture, economic divide, planetary degradation, and the proliferation of disinformation and misinformation accelerated by ai, is asking leaders to bring a kind of presence the old model never trained them for. Her proposition is gentler than this analysis sounds. She is arguing that the work of becoming whole, the slow, cyclical, embodied work of integration, is the precondition for the kind of leadership our moment requires. Skills sit on top of it. Frameworks sit on top of it. Without it, none of them hold. For anyone reading this who has been quietly carrying something, the news Amy is delivering is, in its own way, the kindest news in leadership development today. You are not broken. You are not behind. You are not alone. You are in the company of almost every senior leader in the world. And the work of integrating what you carry is, quietly, the work of our whole species. On cycles, and never being done There is a particular trap in the transformation industry, and Amy refuses it. The trap is the promise of arrival. The promise that there is a version of you, somewhere ahead, that is finally healed, finally whole, finally finished. Most spiritual marketing, most leadership development, most personal growth language is built around this implicit promise. Do the work, and you will arrive. Amy lives in a different model. It isn’t like there was a dark phase and now there’s a light phase. I wish I could say it that way but that’s not been my experience. It’s cyclical. And in a way that’s very beautiful, because it just means we’re never done. This is one of the most important sentences anyone has spoken on the subject of becoming. The authority in it comes from forty years of practice. In early 2023, Amy spent four months in bed. Michael Singer’s books had been on her nightstand for four years before that, unable to be read. In the season of collapse, they finally made sense. The teacher had been there the entire time. She had not been ready. This is the cycle. The light phases give way to dark phases. The dark phases give way to light. The teacher arrives when you can finally hear them. The cathedral arrives more than once. Each return adds another layer. The shape of the work is spiral. It deepens through cycles. For anyone in a long, dark season, the gift Amy offers is the release from the burden of waiting for it to end. The dark season is itself the path. The path is cyclical and it is beautiful, and we are never done. This is, I think, the most important shift Sincerely is trying to make in how we talk about becoming. Amy says it more clearly than I could. What it looks like to step down at the apex In November of 2025, Amy told me that the thirty-first of December would mark the end of her twenty years as CEO and co-founder of Mobius. She is stepping down. Not from the work. Not from the movement. Someone else will run the firm. Amy is moving toward something quieter. She described it as “a restorative renaissance.” Local. Intimate. Person by person. The kind of healing of collective trauma that does not happen on a stage and does not scale through technology. There is a story about leadership that says the apex is the goal. You climb. You arrive. You hold the position as long as possible. You optimise for visibility and influence and scale. Amy is, with this decision, refuting that story. She is at the apex. The firm she built will continue to grow under different leadership, and her name will continue to carry weight in the field. She is stepping out because she has heard the next frequency, and she has spent forty years following the frequencies as they arrive. She is internally referenced. She trusts the inner compass over the external scoreboard. In a culture that mistakes momentum for meaning, this kind of choice is itself a teaching. The achievement model has limits. The internally referenced life is the real life. You can have built one of the world’s most extraordinary firms, and the right next move can still be to step out of it. There is also something specific Amy has named about the moment we are in. She has been a lifelong social activist. She no longer believes outer agitation alone will carry us where we need to go. Activism as activism has hit the wall. What she calls the restorative renaissance is the work that comes next. It does not happen on stages. It happens in living rooms and small circles and intimate retreats and one-to-one conversations over a long time. It is the slow healing of collective trauma at a local level. It is the patient repair of the relational fabric. Amy is going where the work is asking her to go. Whatever she steps into now will, in her quiet way, move something. Her instincts have not led her wrong in forty years. What her life is asking us to see The agreement of The Sincerely Show is a simple one. The guest is witnessed. They sit, they are seen, they tell the truth about the path they have walked, and the meaning is made together with the listener. Because Amy has lived the way she has lived, the witnessing becomes a teaching of its own. Her life is the lesson. What her life teaches is this. You can live through what you cannot imagine living through, and what emerges will be more whole than what entered. The cathedral arrives, often when you least expect it, and once you have heard the frequency, you can follow it for the rest of your life. The work of integrating what you carry is the work of our whole species, and you are in the company of almost everyone leading anything. The path is cyclical. We are never done. And the real story is quieter and slower and more beautiful than the achievement story. It asks more of you than you knew you had. And love can be brought into business. Into the most demanding business. Into Fortune 500 boardrooms full of strategy decks and quarterly targets. Amy has practised this for twenty years, and the proof is in the firm she built, in the people who have come through it, and in the next chapter she is now walking into. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A few hours with Amy The full conversation with Amy sits at the top of this page. Two hours, unhurried. We move through her childhood, her cancer, the Cathedral years, the kirtan night, the two years in the woods, the founding of Mobius, what she has learned about trauma in leadership, what comes next, and the cycle she lives inside. You will hear her say things, in her own voice and her own quietness, that no portrait can fully carry. The pauses. The slight catches of breath. The way she universalises her own pain the moment she names it. The frequency she has been following for forty years, audible in the way she speaks. Take the conversation slowly. When you have time. With a cup of something warm. There is no hurry. The library is always here. Some part of my heart just broke open. It was the quality of devotion and the quality of unconditional love. And that frequency, I’ve been following ever since. I have hardly ever met anyone from anywhere in the world where there isn’t some kind of trauma. This is a universal pandemic. In the journey to consciousness and to service and to self-love, there’s a cathedral that arrives. Amy Elizabeth Fox is the co-founder and CEO of Mobius Executive Leadership, a global transformational leadership firm she has led for twenty years. Before Mobius, she worked at the Cathedral Church of Saint John the Divine alongside Ram Dass, Carl Sagan, and Vice President Al Gore, engaging American faith communities in the environmental movement. She is a senior student and faculty member with mystical teacher Thomas Hüebl, and teaches at Oxford’s Saïd Business School through the African Leadership Institute. In 2026 she co-authored Leading in Chaos with Nicholas Janni. She holds a Master’s in counselling from Lesley College and a BA in Psychology from Wesleyan University.
show-katherine-dudtschak.html: For the first time on The Sincerely Show, Katherine Dudtschak is the one in the chair. This welcome episode is an origin story: of a woman, a book, a platform, and a movement that began with one decision to stop performing and start living. Katherine grew up on a mink farm in rural Canada, the daughter of two parents who survived the Second World War and carried its weight into the life they built. She was neurodivergent in a school system that did not know what to do with her. She was deeply feminine in a world that required her to be otherwise. For nearly five decades, she built a career of extraordinary scope, rising to become president and CEO of HomeEquity Bank, leading 25,000 employees through cultural transformation, and earning recognition as one of Canada’s most respected senior executives. She was also, through all of it, carrying a secret. In this conversation, Katherine shares what she has rarely put into a single sitting: the collapses that cracked her open, the coming out to 80,000 people by video in 2019, the grief of retirement, the two-year journey into aloneness that became the beginning of herself, and the vision for Sincerely as a blanket, a cathedral, a place where human beings can come and hear each other’s stories without judgement. She was somewhere between twelve and eighteen months old. It was the first of many such escapes, the climbing out and the exploring would carry on all through her childhood. Her mother had gone out to the farm to tend to the animals. Her father was away at work. The house was quiet, and she was alone in her crib, and that was not going to hold her for long. She climbed out. That was always how she was, even then, even before she had words for it: curious enough to go looking, determined enough not to stay put. She tore through the house. She looked in every drawer, opened every cupboard, picked up every object that didn’t make sense to her and tried to understand it. In her father’s drawer she found an old wind-up alarm clock and thought: this is boring. In her mother’s drawers, she found something else entirely. Silk slips. Beautiful camisoles. A jewellery box with clip earrings that fit over the ears of a toddler who had never once, in her short life, been told she shouldn’t want them. She put them on. She went to the bathroom and found the lipstick. She put that on too. And she felt free. She felt, in her word, alive. That child is Katherine Dudtschak. She is sixty years old now, and she is sitting in a room full of people who came to witness the birth of something: a book, a show, a platform, a movement. She has built all of it. She carries the farm and the lavender and the bees and the long dining table set for gathering. She carries the thirty-seven years inside one of the world’s largest financial institutions, the four children, the career that looked, from the outside, like exactly what a determined person could build. And she will tell you, quietly and without any performance of drama, that the little girl with the clip earrings and the borrowed lipstick never left. She just had to wait a very long time to be let back in. The formation Katherine was born on March 9th, 1966, to parents who arrived in Canada carrying the weight of a world that had nearly destroyed them. Her mother grew up in what is now Poland, born in 1935 in a region then called Prussia. She became a child refugee around age eight, spending time in a refugee camp where she was responsible for protecting her little sister. Her father was born in a small lumber village called Kummer in what was then Sudetenland, now the Czech Republic. At fifteen, when the war ended and Russia moved in, he and the other young boys were captured and spent the next three years across multiple Russian prison camps, living on bread and water, waking beside bodies, surviving things that have no name. Both his parents died during the war. When it ended, he crossed from East Germany to West Germany in darkness, skin and bones, with a bolt of cloth in his backpack that he traded for food and transport to go find his brother, who was only ten months his senior. They came to Canada and built a life on a mink farm. They brought everything with them: the love and the terror, the warmth and the yelling and the deep, cellular anxiety about whether there would be money, whether there would be Christmas presents, whether the world would hold. Katherine grew up in that atmosphere and learned to navigate it with the fluency that neurodivergent children develop when their survival depends on reading the room. She was hypersensitive and hyperaware, the kid who wanted to milk every teacher for knowledge and forgot there were twenty other children, the kid who ended up banished to the corner of a Grade Two classroom because being sent to the hall wasn’t working. She was dyslexic before anyone had a word for it. She was told, repeatedly, that she wasn’t applying herself. She decided, sometime in her early teens, that she was going to prove every last one of those people wrong. She also knew, from the time she was very small, that there were things inside her that didn’t fit the world she was growing up in. The feminine tendencies, as she puts it. The way she was drawn to beauty: to her mother’s silk things, to elegance, to a great outfit glimpsed on the street that made something in her ache. This never went away. It was never an experiment. It was just there, and she learned, the way children learn everything, that some things are better buried. She went on to build a beautiful family, a demanding career, a life that looked, from the outside, complete. It worked,” she says. “Yet it wasn’t complete. It wasn’t complete. The life she built, and what it cost Thirty-seven years inside one of Canada’s largest financial institutions. CEO. Award-winner. The kind of leader her colleagues called, privately, one of the strongest communicators they had ever encountered. Heart-centred, empathic, the executive who could spin twenty plates at once and did not consider this a metaphor. She was also, for all of those years, performing. Not performing badly. Not performing without love or skill or genuine care. But performing in the sense that the full Katherine, the one who had been in her mother’s jewellery box as a child, remained invisible. She had built guard rails. Anxieties. Belief systems. She had become, in her words, a guy’s guy: laughing at the right things, fitting into the world that was asking her to fit. She had developed a set of skills so refined that she could suppress whatever threatened to surface and simply get back to being busy. You can run,” she says, “but you can’t hide. Around age forty-five, the running got harder. She led a corporate restructuring that required her to let go of forty percent of a workforce in countries where those people might never find work again. The board applauded her. The CEO told her he had no idea she had it in her. She cried in private. She had gone into that career imagining that reaching the top would bring wisdom, enlightenment, some sense of having arrived at the thing she had been chasing. Instead it gave her a clear-eyed view of what the system actually was. It wasn’t working. It was hurting people. And there was a growing ache in her, quiet at first, then louder and louder, that had nothing to do with strategy decks or quarterly targets. She chose, for the first time, the job that she knew she could do intuitively. The one that would let her lead from her heart. It was around this same time that the four children were growing up, leaving home, and the suppressed feminine side of her began to be, as she puts it, “really, really loud.” The lunch that undid fifty years In 2017, she had lunch with a colleague. She had recently read about Caitlyn Jenner and had genuinely not understood it. This detail matters: the walls she had built were that high. She asked her colleague to explain. He explained that gender is who you go to sleep as. Your inner self. That sexual orientation is who you go to sleep with. They are not the same thing. You could have pushed me over with a feather. Within hours her anxiety went through the roof. Within days, she was searching the internet differently than she had ever searched it before, looking for stories of people like her: people with a strong feminine side who had built a more masculine life to survive the world that was asking it of them, and who had found their way to the other side. Within a week, she told her spouse. I think I’m wired female on the inside. They cried together for weekend after weekend, night after night. What followed was a year she describes as a next-to-impossible journey. Fear of rejection. Fear of abandonment. Friends from childhood who were deeply religious. A corporate world she was not sure was ready. And, underneath all of it, the absolute certainty of what she now knew about herself: a scab she had been scratching for fifty years and had finally, at fifty, named. She wanted life to be over. It was a dear friend, Lee Anne, who read her signals and sent her intergenerational trauma research on the children of parents who die by suicide. Katherine was stopped cold. Her plan, she saw, was flawed. She wrote a letter of intention: to embrace her whole self, to go on a journey toward it, whatever that cost. She came out to her children. She came out to the CEO. She saw herself for the first time, in a mirror, in New York, in March of 2019. And then, on June 17th, 2019, she came out to 80,000 people by video. She told them the truth. She showed them her heart. She asked them, without saying so directly, for a second chance to prove that she could be as good a leader as she had been before, so she could keep her job and finish putting her children through school. Within ten months, hundreds of emails. People writing about bravery and courage, words she says she hated. Not because she was modest. Because she knew how much it had cost. There’s nothing elegant about it at all. It’s literally death-defying. The collapse that began everything The story could end there. Coming out as a public figure, at scale, with grace: that is one kind of remarkable ending. But Katherine was not done collapsing. And she seems to know, now, that the collapses were never setbacks. They were the path. In 2022, she was given a new opportunity within the company she had spent thirty-seven years serving. She sat with it and felt the weight of it settle in the wrong way. She broke down. She said no. She retired. For two months, she cried daily in the park near her house. She grieved her work family, with their specific faces and their specific stories, stories people had trusted her with for twenty years: the woman from the Caribbean whose family had been stoned because she was gay, the man from India who had carried guilt his whole life for ostracising a friend who was later forced into an arranged marriage and died by suicide. She grieved her children growing up. She grieved her divorce, which she had not yet allowed herself to grieve. And she sat with an aloneness she traced all the way back to a crib on a farm: that oscillating pattern of deep love and sudden absence that her mother’s comings and goings had established in her before she had language. Her coach, Theano, taught her to feel into her body and release pain that had been trapped there. She learned to meditate. She learned to sit with hurt and let it move through without trying to control it. In that darkness, you find yourself. She turned sixty last year. Her gender journey is nine years old. In that nine-year period, she says, she experienced two or three very heavy collapses, and then another, about nine months ago, inside a CEO role with record performance, when the weight of the quarterly board meetings and the same PowerPoint deck and the steady grind of completing things began to feel, again, like the wrong shape for a life. She did not fight it this time. There’s a heaviness here. And I’m not going to fight this. I’m going to surrender to it. She surrendered toward Sincerely. What she has built Sincerely, Inc. is a platform, a podcast, a library of stories, a farm, and something harder to name than any of those things. Katherine describes it as a blanket. A place where people can come and not be judged, where they can sit inside a warmth and hear other people’s stories told with the kind of honesty that makes you feel less alone. She traces the impulse all the way back to her reading, in the two years between learning who she was and coming out to the world: fifty to seventy books in that period, searching for people like her, searching for proof that it was possible to get to the other side and keep the family and the job and the life. Story was what she needed. Story is what she is now offering. The show itself is built around her singular gift. She has been described, by the person who introduced her on the night of Episode Zero, as someone who does not ask questions to extract information. She asks questions to set someone free. The distinction is not a small one. It is the whole difference between an interview and a witnessing. The research arm of Sincerely, called Sincerely Human, is being built to validate the models Katherine has developed through her own journey and the framework she calls the Sincerely way. The Three Pillars: Sacred Structure, Sacred Flow, and Sacred Union. The Integration Journey: Shaped, Crossing, Becoming. The idea that from the beginning of time, humanity has transmitted knowledge, lesson, meaning, and hope through story, and that in a world drowning in information and disinformation, this ancient technology may be exactly what is needed. The book, Sincerely, Katherine, published by Page Two, is the first story the platform has told. It contains a letter of intention she wrote to herself in 2017, when Lee Anne’s intergenerational trauma research stopped her cold, and it ends with the modus vivendi that has become her mantra: Slam your heart into the people and the places and the things that ignite something deep within your soul, and I promise, I promise: the right things will stay. Maison Millefleurs is the physical anchor. The farmhouse and its fields, somewhere in Canada, are where Katherine has planted the lavender and the bees and the long table for gathering, and where, in time, retreats and salons will be held. She drove onto that land not knowing what she was looking for. She knew when she arrived. And then there is the show itself: the library of extraordinary lives that is just beginning. Katherine has been, as she says, curious about the human condition since before she could name what curiosity was. She has spent her professional life in rooms where people came to her with the stories they carried in silence. She now has a place to put all of that attention and all of that care. I could interview people every day for the rest of my life on their stories. She will. The thing about collapse There is a pattern Katherine returns to throughout the night of Episode Zero, and it is worth sitting with. She calls it collapse, crawling back, awakening, emergence. It goes in cycles. Most people, she says, experience it at least once; many of the people who have come into her orbit have experienced it multiple times. A period of darkness in which aspects of identity built to fit into the world begin to fall away. An aloneness. A meeting with yourself at the bottom. And then, always, a return: more whole than before, more accepting of the natural gifts and the natural essence, more able to build a life around the things that are actually true. She does not romanticise this. She would not wish it on anyone. She is also clear that it cannot be rushed, that there is no light switch, that her own journey has been anywhere from nine to fifteen years long. What she offers is not a shortcut. It is company on the road. There’s hope,” she says, and she says it twice, and the second time it lands like something she has earned the right to mean. The world we are living in is, she knows, a difficult one. She has named its four crises with the precision of someone who spent thirty-seven years inside the institutions that helped create them: social fracture, economic divide, planetary degradation, and the proliferation of disinformation and information accelerated by AI. She does not look away from any of this. She carries it, actively, as a weight and as a responsibility. She is also, somehow, at peace. The aloneness and the grief of 2022 did not produce bitterness. They produced a woman who says, without any performance of it, that she lives now with a level of love and joy and freedom and creativity that she could not have imagined. That peace is not the absence of awareness. It is the consequence of having gone all the way through. What her life is asking us to see There is a version of this story that emphasises the courage. The coming out at scale. The choosing of oneself over the performance. The walking away. Katherine is wary of that version. She hates the words brave and courageous, not because they are inaccurate but because they suggest that the particular thing she went through is exceptional, and she does not experience it that way. She experiences it as the human condition, lived with more visibility than most. What strikes me about sitting with this conversation is something quieter than courage. It is the through-line. The child who climbed out of the crib again and again through her early childhood and put on her mother’s earrings and felt free: that was not a phase. It was not confusion. It was not something that needed to be overcome or grown out of. It was the self, accurately reported. Everything that followed, the farm and the dyslexia and the guard rails and the thirty-seven years and the collapses: all of it was, from some angle, the path back to that child. Not a path away from her. A path around and under and through the whole accumulated weight of a world that asks us to perform, back to the thing that was there before the performance started. Katherine’s framework names this as coherence: living from your essential self, through your physical and inherited self, out into the world as an offering. She has a rigorous way of thinking about it. But underneath the framework is something very simple. The self that is most true in you is also the self that is most useful to the world. You were not built to suppress it. You were built to find your way back to it. There is also something she said about story that I have not stopped thinking about. From the beginning of time, she said, humanity transmitted knowledge, lesson, meaning, inspiration, and hope through story. Long before Western civilisation, long before the institutions and the quarterly targets and the information overload: story. The indigenous cultures in Australia, with continuous threads stretching back 20,000 to 40,000 years, found a way to live in harmony with self, each other, and the land through story, through quiet, through observation. The sitting in circle, the passing of flame, the remembering through the telling. Katherine is not offering a solution. She is offering a space. A blanket, held open, for stories told with enough honesty to help someone feel less alone. That is, she would say, enough. If it touches one person. If it helps one person find their way back to the child in the crib who knew exactly who they were. There is a wholeness within each person waiting to arise,” she says, “when the time is right for you. She has built Sincerely so that the time, for a few more people, might arrive a little sooner. This is the kind of leadership our moment requires. It is the kind of leadership Sincerely was built to honour. A note on the conversation The full conversation sits at the top of this page. It runs for just over an hour and was recorded live in front of a room of people gathered to witness the birth of something. Katherine was, for the first time, in the guest’s chair. She was interviewed by the woman who had built The Sincerely Show alongside her. It is unhurried, warm, and completely honest. There is no hurry. The library is always here. You can run, but you can’t hide. If there is something deep within you that is from your soul, you can run but you can’t hide. And if you don’t give it oxygen, it steals oxygen from you. Slam your heart into the people and the places and the things that ignite something deep within your soul. And I promise, I promise: the right things will stay. You will never lose what is for you. There is a wholeness within each person waiting to arise when the time is right for you. You’re on your journey. I hope these stories help. Katherine Dudtschak is the founder and host of Sincerely Inc. and The Sincerely Show, and the author of Sincerely, Katherine: Life, Gender, Inclusivity, and Leadership for the Future (Page Two, 2026). She spent thirty-seven years as a senior executive and CEO inside one of Canada’s largest financial institutions. She came out as a transgender woman to 80,000 employees in 2019. She is a recipient of the Catalyst Honours Award. She now lives on Maison Millefleurs, the lavender farm that is the physical home of Sincerely, and devotes her life to creating a platform where human stories can be told with the honesty that helps people find their way back to themselves.
letter-the-black-sheep.html: A few days ago, I was talking with a friend, someone I care about and deeply admire. We were talking about family, about the things we carry through our lives, and about her journey of breaking a cycle of intergenerational trauma. At one point, she referred to herself as the black sheep of the family. Those words stopped me. I have never seen her as a black sheep. I see an extraordinary mother, an incredibly curious, creative and talented human being, and someone who is beautiful inside and out. Someone who has found the courage to journey deeply within herself, to embrace more of who she truly is, and to live from that place. Her essence. Her uniqueness. Her beauty. I asked her, “Does claiming your authentic self mean that you’re the black sheep of the family?” Her answer was “yes”. I have been contemplating that conversation ever since. I had never thought of myself as the black sheep of my family either. And yet, when I began the journey to understand and eventually affirm my gender, I was confronting something I had known from a very young age. I was different. I knew what I was doing as an adult was rare and could be deeply disruptive to people I loved. I carried fears of judgement, rejection and abandonment. I deeply contemplated suicide. I had no idea how to take on the journey or how my family, friends, colleagues or community would respond. Perhaps some of them did see me as the black sheep. I really don’t know. What I do know is that I wasn’t trying to be different. I was trying to understand something deep within me that had been there since childhood. Something I had never fully understood or known how to express. And that journey became so much more than affirming my gender. It became a journey towards understanding, accepting and loving more of who I am. My essence. As I’ve reflected on my friend’s words, I’ve become curious about the expression itself. Historically, naturally white wool was more commercially desirable because it could be dyed into so many colours. Think of all the beauty created through fashion, textiles, design and art. And yet, there is something interesting about how we assign value. White wool could be transformed, transmuted, even muted into what someone else wanted it to be. A performance shaped by another’s expectations. Black wool, with its own natural colour, was considered less desirable for some of those purposes. And it too can be woven into beautiful textiles, designs and creations while retaining its natural colour. Its natural essence. The more I thought about it, the more I realised that both black and white wool are beautiful expressions of nature, of life, each with its own qualities and perfection. It was we humans who judged one as more valuable based on what we wanted it to become. And that got me reflecting again about ourselves. How much of our lives do we spend learning to become what others want or expect us to be? From childhood, we learn the ways of our families, our communities, our workplaces and the broader human family. We learn what is acceptable, what earns approval, what helps us belong. Sometimes we become so good at fitting in that we lose sight of parts of ourselves that were always there. Our uniqueness and beauty. Perhaps the so-called black sheep is someone who has begun to release those expectations and live more fully from their nature, their natural essence. Their uniqueness becomes visible, and sometimes that makes others uncomfortable. Witnessing someone living more authentically can stir something deep within us, something we don’t yet understand or haven’t found the courage to express ourselves. We may react defensively and judgementally to what feels unfamiliar, or to something within ourselves that is quietly asking to be explored, while fear encourages us to resist. The person standing before us becomes a mirror, reflecting parts of our own essence that are longing to be seen. And there is a beautiful gift in that. My friend spoke about healing intergenerational trauma, about breaking a cycle. I’ve been thinking about the word healing too. It can suggest that something was broken and needed to be fixed. What if our original essence was never broken? What if it was perfect, whole and complete? What if, through our experiences of judgement, rejection, shame and trying to fit in, we accumulated layers of protection around something that was always beautiful and whole? It’s like scar tissue, formed through experiences that hurt us and through the ways we learned to protect ourselves in a family, group or world that values fitting in to what it values. Perhaps healing is less about fixing ourselves and more about gently releasing what no longer serves us. Learning to understand why those layers formed, finding compassion for ourselves and the people who came before us, and allowing more of our original essence to become visible once again. I think about my own parents and ancestors, whose lives were shaped by war, displacement, loss and survival. I have come to understand how fear, silence and ways of protecting ourselves can travel through generations. And how love, courage and resilience travel too. What if breaking a cycle is an expression of love for our family and our ancestors? A releasing of something we no longer need to carry, while honouring the lives and experiences that came before us. And what if, in doing so, we create more room for the generations that follow to simply be themselves? This brings me back to something I explored in my earlier letter, Entelechy: A Doorway. Aristotle spoke of Entelechy, an ancient Greek word that has come to mean something deeply personal to me. The quiet longing within us to know and express what has always been there. Joseph Campbell said, “The privilege of a lifetime is being who you are.” I love that word, being. Being. Perhaps the privilege of this lifetime is to discover and love the beautiful being who has been there all along, rather than spend our lives trying to become someone more acceptable to others. And as we learn to love more of ourselves, perhaps something else begins to happen. I think about the love I have received from my children, my friends and so many others throughout my journey. Their love helped me find more love within myself. And as I have learned to love myself more deeply, I have found a greater capacity to offer that love to others. When someone finds the courage to release what has obscured their natural essence, their light becomes more visible. And perhaps that light becomes a mirror for someone else, awakening a longing to live more freely, more truthfully, more lovingly. They may begin their own journey, in their own way, towards their own beautiful essence. I find this knowing extraordinarily beautiful. Each of us carries our own unique gifts, our visible and invisible dimensions of human uniqueness, our own light. As we find the courage to live from that deeper place, perhaps we contribute to something much larger than our individual lives. A collective journey towards greater compassion, greater wholeness and greater love. I keep coming back to my friend and the conversation that started all of this. She saw herself as the black sheep of her family. I saw her beauty, her courage, her truth. I saw someone who had journeyed deeply within herself, who was breaking a cycle and allowing more of her natural essence to shine into this world and beyond. The black sheep was never less beautiful or less whole than the rest of the flock. We simply hadn’t learned to see its profound beauty. Its light. The black sheep is sometimes someone who has found the courage to stop hiding their natural colour, to reclaim the love and wholeness that have always been within them, and to let their light shine. What a beautiful gift to give to ourselves. Thank you, Black Sheep.
