letter-running-away-from-home.html: Remember wanting to run away from home? To escape something? There is a pattern I’ve come to recognise in the human journey. For many of us, it seems we spend the first half of our lives running away from home, from the child we once were, and the second half running home. I’ve been curious about the human condition for as long as I can remember. About who we are, the lives we inherit, the lives we create, and how we find our place in this world. Over the past decade, I’ve been on what feels like a journey of transformation. Yet I wonder. Has it really been a journey of transformation, or have I been finding my way home? Some of my earliest and happiest memories are of being a deeply curious, creative, sensitive and playful child. And a little mischievous, too! My mother called me Snoopy because I was into absolutely everything. When I was three, I took apart our radio, looking for the little man whose voice was coming out of it. I was terribly disappointed when I couldn’t find him! I loved anything mechanical. Tractors, cars, trucks, motorcycles. I loved driving the tractor and cutting the grass on our farm, enjoying the solitude and making something look beautiful. I built forts and clubhouses with my sister, explored the little forest near our home, and created imaginary worlds of my own. One of those worlds was in an old root cellar beside the barn. Part of the wall had fallen in, leaving sand that became the landscape for my very own farm. I also built farms in the upper level of the barn. I made roads and long fence lines with corn cobs that the rats had stripped of their kernels, and drove my toy tractor around the little farms I had created. Oh, how I loved imagining and creating things! I was also drawn to beautiful things. I loved exploring my mother’s jewellery, trying on her earrings and clothes, and making little outfits for my sister’s Barbie doll. I loved singing, drawing, painting and pottery. I loved skipping with the girls at school. There were feminine and masculine qualities within me that I didn’t yet have the language to understand. They were all simply part of who I was. Of course, childhood wasn’t all adventure and play. My parents carried the experiences of war, hardship and survival into our family. They worked incredibly hard to build a life in Canada, and our humble mink farm brought its own financial pressures and challenges. There was love, but there was also anxiety, fear and the emotional weight of experiences I wouldn’t begin to understand until much later in life. School was difficult for me, too. I learned differently, and I struggled to understand why the very things that came naturally to me weren’t always valued in the world around me. Somewhere along the way, I began to learn what was acceptable. I remember thinking, “Adults don’t do that. Good people don’t do that.” Little by little, parts of that curious, expressive, feminine, playful child began to disappear from view. I became determined. Determined to prove that I was smart enough, capable enough, good enough. I wanted to build a better life than my parents had known and create opportunity and security for myself and the people I loved. And in so many ways, I did. I’m deeply grateful for my life. Four extraordinary children, dear friendships and a career that took me to places I could never have imagined as a child on that farm. So much love, joy, learning and meaningful contribution. I wouldn’t trade those experiences or the people who shared them with me. Yet I can also see how good I became at adapting, and how much of myself I learned to hide or dismiss. Some of those hidden parts carried guilt, shame and fear. Over the past decade, so much of my journey has been about letting go of that guilt and shame and pressure to perform, and learning to love the qualities of the child I once was. The child inside of me. Affirming my gender was a profound part of that journey, but it has been about so much more. My sensitivity, my curiosity, my sense of adventure, my femininity, my appreciation of beauty, my creativity, my playfulness. Even my mischievousness! I’ve come to appreciate that the child I once was didn’t need to become someone better. She needed to be understood, welcomed and loved. And I needed to learn to love her myself. I’ve long believed that we arrive in this world perfect, whole and complete, with an essence that is already beautiful and full of love. It comes from somewhere deep within us, and perhaps from somewhere beyond us. We have lots to learn and experience in this lifetime, but perhaps we don’t need to become someone else to be worthy of this life we’ve been given. As I listen to the stories of others, particularly through The Sincerely Show, I recognise how many people have experienced their own version of this journey. Some have travelled a long way from the child they once were, while others seem to have remained much closer to the things they loved and the ways they naturally expressed themselves. It makes me wonder what kind of world we might create if more of us felt safe and loved enough to remain close to those beautiful parts of ourselves throughout our lives. Perhaps we wouldn’t have to travel so far, or experience such painful crashes and crumbling, to find our way home. I smile when I think about where my own journey has brought me. Here I am in midlife, living on a small farm again. I ride my tractor, walk the fields and tend the gardens, surrounded by nature and beauty. I’m creating things, exploring, learning, playing and enjoying the freedom to express all of who I am. The farm I’m living on today is so close to the very farm I imagined and built as a little child, with sand, corn cobs and my toy tractor. Only now, it’s real. I carry decades of living, loving, learning, accomplishments and heartbreak. I wouldn’t wish those years away. I cherish the life I’ve lived and the people who have shared it with me. But how beautiful to be doing so many of the things I loved as a child again, with the freedom to be me. All of me. I think about that little child walking through the fields, full of questions and wonder, with no idea of the life that lay ahead. And here I am, all these years later, walking the fields again. Still curious, still sensitive, still playful, still learning. Only now, home. Home in myself. It feels like we spend the first half of our lives running away from home, and the second half running home. How beautiful is that?
letter-human-uniqueness.html: This past Monday, I had the honour and privilege of joining the Human Resources Professionals Association (HRPA) for its annual Summit, The Human Advantage, Canada’s largest gathering of human resources professionals. I was invited by Desjardins to join Lance Lambert for a conversation about unlocking human potential, and what it means to live and lead in a world that is experiencing immense stress and changing so profoundly. What a beautiful opportunity to share some of the lessons and reflections from my journey through life and leadership and the work of Sincerely, and to explore together what might become possible for humanity and our world. Afterwards, I spent time meeting people and signing copies of my book, Sincerely, Katherine. I was deeply moved by the warmth, kindness and openness of those who came forward. Some entrusted me with deeply personal parts of their lives. Those exchanges are sacred to me, and I carry them with tremendous gratitude. I’ve been thinking about those conversations all week. What does it mean to be human? And what makes each and every one of us so beautifully unique, especially now, in a world increasingly shaped by AI, stress and conflict? For much of my life, I’ve struggled with the word diversity. Not with the importance of honouring our differences, but with the word itself. To me, it has often suggested division, or even the act of dividing. I’ve also struggled with the labels we place on ourselves and one another. They can help us describe aspects of who we are, yet no label, identity, role or characteristic can possibly contain a whole human being. It’s something I have been making sense of in my own life. I’m a woman who affirmed her gender. I’m also a mother, a daughter, a sister, a friend, a writer, a former bank CEO, a deeply curious, playful and loving soul, and so much more. None of these descriptions, individually or together, fully captures the whole human being I am. The same is true of every one of us. Somewhere along my journey, an expression came to me that felt more loving, more expansive and more reflective of how I’ve come to understand humanity. Visible and invisible dimensions of human uniqueness. I love the word human. It begins with what we share: our desire to feel safe, to love and be loved, to experience belonging, to find meaning and to contribute to something beyond ourselves. Our shared humanity does not require sameness. I love the word uniqueness. It speaks to something special, something beautiful, something worthy of being discovered, understood, loved and allowed to belong. The visible and invisible dimensions speak to the extraordinary fullness and depth of every human being. So much of who we are cannot be seen from the outside: our histories, fears and dreams; the ways we think and perceive the world; our talents and gifts; our hopes and aspirations; the stories and experiences that have shaped us; and the parts of ourselves we may only reveal when we feel safe enough to do so. Human uniqueness, for me, is not another way of categorising people. It’s the opposite. It is a reminder that no category can ever contain a human being. I’ve come to see the whole human through what I call the Three-Self Architecture: our physical and inherited self, our lived-experience self and our essential self. Our physical and inherited self carries the characteristics and attributes we arrive in this world with. Our lived-experience self is shaped through our relationships, culture, education, work, joys, hardships, achievements and the countless experiences that shape our lives. And then there is our essential self, that beautiful spark within us from birth, with our curiosity, imagination, creativity, playfulness, sensitivity, intuition and capacity to love. I often think about the little child within each of us, fiercely curious, exploring, playing, creating and loving. Then life met us. Our families, schools, religions, communities and workplaces began teaching us how to behave, how to succeed and how to belong. Some of those lessons were beautiful gifts. Others taught us that certain parts of ourselves were not welcome, so we learned to protect ourselves and to perform to fit in. Some of the parts we tucked away began to carry guilt or shame because expressing them had once brought judgement, rejection or a loss of safety and belonging. Hiding and adapting may have been exactly what we needed to do at that moment in our lives. Yet what once protected us can eventually separate us from our deepest and truest self, our own essence. Some parts of ourselves may remain protected for very good reasons. Feeling safe should never come with an expectation that we disclose, confront or express something before we are ready. Whether in a family, a friendship or a workplace, we can create conditions of love, care and belonging without asking another person to reveal what they wish to hold privately. Their story remains theirs. When I affirmed my gender publicly in 2019, a video was shared with approximately 80,000 colleagues. I was terrified. I expected judgement and rejection. I worried about my career. More than anything, I worried about hurting the people I loved. The year before, that fear had taken me to one of the darkest periods of my life, to wanting life to be over. What happened next changed me profoundly. I experienced an extraordinary outpouring of love, kindness and compassion, and then people began trusting me with deeply personal parts of their own lives. I had spent decades working with people and considered myself a compassionate and empathetic leader, yet I had no idea how much hurt, fear, longing, beauty and human experience was sitting quietly all around me. I was humbled to my core. I became less judgemental, more curious and more compassionate. I listened differently, and I began to understand something I had missed through much of my career: there was so much more in people than I had learned to see. I also began to understand how many of us carry fear, guilt or shame around the parts of ourselves we have learned to hide. I’ve come to think of our human journey as one towards greater coherence. Not becoming some better or more acceptable version of ourselves, but learning to see, reconcile and love more of the whole human being who is already here. Grieving what needs to be grieved, healing what asks to be healed, gently releasing what no longer serves us, and allowing more of our natural essence and whole self to find expression through our lives. Unlocking human potential begins there, not by putting more into people, but by creating conditions where people have greater freedom to be themselves and bring forward their gifts, in their own way and in their own time. I find this question particularly important now. We are living through a consequential moment in human history. Social fracture, economic inequality and the degradation of our planet are profound challenges, all unfolding within an overwhelming environment of information and disinformation. Artificial intelligence is accelerating all of it. I don’t see AI as inherently good or bad. I see it as an extraordinary accelerator of the orientation from which we choose to use it. Used from fear, scarcity, competition and extraction, it can accelerate those things, making us even more efficient at extracting value from people, communities and our planet. Used from a different orientation, it can help create greater space for human creativity, imagination, relationship, discernment and contribution, and help us solve problems that have challenged humanity for generations. The technology will continue to become more capable, which leaves us with a deeply human question: what are we behaving from, and what are we putting all of this extraordinary capability in service of? For generations, we’ve built many of our organisations around efficiency, productivity, standardisation and control. We’ve often asked human beings to perform and adapt themselves to the systems we created. This moment gives us an opportunity to turn that question around. How might we build and steward organisations where the whole human can flourish? I’ve had the privilege of exploring that question with extraordinary people throughout my career. At RBC, 25,000 of us were navigating a profound digital transformation together, and people were understandably worried about what technology might mean for their jobs and their families. Our shared aspiration became larger than digitising transactions. We wanted to help move work away from the purely transactional and create greater opportunity for people to bring more of their uniquely human gifts into the lives of the Canadians we served: empathy, curiosity, context, judgement, understanding and meaningful advice. We certainly didn’t get everything right, and I’ve made more than my share of mistakes throughout my career. Yet that experience reinforced something I continue to believe deeply. There are extraordinary gifts inside people that become even more important as technology becomes more capable. This changes what it means to lead. Leadership carries a responsibility to see those gifts, nurture them and bring them together in service of something meaningful. Management is an accountability we can be given, while leadership is something recognised through the experiences others have of us. A manager manages. A leader may be recognised for their wisdom, for the vision and inspiration they offer, for the morality they embody when choices are difficult, for their courage and discernment, and for their ability to recognise beautiful gifts within others, sometimes before those people can see the gifts within themselves. Most importantly, leadership is about bringing those gifts together in a movement towards something greater than ourselves. Leadership, for me, is increasingly about stewardship. It carries responsibility for something greater, for nurturing life itself and creating the conditions in which the whole human can flourish, while holding responsibility for the wider community and living world of which we are part. Another responsibility of leadership is to create the field, the conditions of safety, trust and belonging, while remembering that each person retains sovereignty over what they share, what they hold privately and when. Belonging should never require disclosure. Disclosure is sacred. This is part of the world I hope we can continue to build: one that is more socially and economically inclusive, where we learn to live more harmoniously with ourselves, each other and our planet, and where the systems we build support that harmony rather than exploit and fracture it. None of this removes the difficult responsibilities of leadership. I learned that painfully while working alongside thousands of colleagues across nineteen Caribbean countries to preserve the future of a bank and save as many jobs as possible. Together, we accomplished something important, and the restructuring required decisions that affected people, families and communities in ways that broke my heart. Compassion does not relieve us of the responsibility to make difficult decisions. It asks more of us. It asks us to create space to feel, reflect, listen, observe and understand their consequences; to honour the dignity of the people, communities and living systems affected; and to remain human when the pressures around us generate fear and pressure within us, making it tempting not to. Financial performance matters. Accountability matters. Innovation matters. None of these should become ends unto themselves. What are they in service of? Leadership for today and tomorrow asks us to hold a vision for something better for all, while remaining deeply present to the people, communities and living world around us. It asks us to listen, remain curious, see the whole human being rather than the label, and create the safety and belonging that allow more of another person’s uniqueness to find expression, if and when they choose. Then it asks us to bring all of those gifts together towards something none of us could create alone. I think back to the people I met after the HRPA conversation. Each a whole human being, carrying a lifetime of experiences, a depth I could never fully know, and gifts that are uniquely their own. What a privilege it is when another human being allows us to see a little more of who they are. Unlocking human potential begins there: learning to see and love more of the whole human being, within ourselves and within one another, and bringing our visible and invisible dimensions of human uniqueness together in service of something greater than ourselves. A world where the whole human can flourish. A world where humanity and all life can flourish together.
letter-sacred.html: What does sacred mean? What is sacred? It’s a question I’ve been contemplating deeply this past week or so. It began with a moment between two people. A sudden, unexpected moment of deep sharing, vulnerability and trust. Something was shared that touched me profoundly, and almost immediately I felt the desire to share what I had experienced and what it had awakened in me. There was meaning in it. There was a lesson in it. Perhaps even something that might help another person. Then the words came to me, “this moment was sacred.” The moment did not belong only to me. It had been created between two people through unspoken trust, vulnerability, care and a willingness to be seen. No one had said, “Please don’t share this.” There had been no agreement of confidentiality, no rules established, no boundary spoken aloud. Yet I felt something deeper had been shared. The moment itself carried the boundary. That feeling has stayed with me. It has caused me to think much more deeply about the word sacred. About what we recognise as sacred, what we hold sacred, and perhaps most importantly, how we honour what is sacred. I have been thinking about the stories we carry from the people in our lives. The beautiful things they tell us, the fears they reveal, the longings they name, the wounds they expose, the hopes they are still learning how to hold. When another person allows us into those places, there is something extraordinary in the trust of that moment. Someone’s story is their story. Their experience. They get to decide whether they want to share it, when they want to share it, how they want to share it, and why. Of course, sometimes we ask permission. Yet even permission has caused me to reflect more deeply. Is the other person simply agreeing because I asked, because they care about me, because they want to support me? Or do they genuinely want their experience shared? Does the desire to offer it to others come from their own deeper place because they believe there may be meaning, support, hope or some other gift in sharing it? That distinction feels important to me. A moment of vulnerability between two or more people creates an opportunity to honour the vulnerability itself and the trust that made it possible. Being part of the moment does not necessarily give any one of us the right to make all of it public. Sometimes the lesson is ours to carry while the story remains with the person who entrusted it to us. Sometimes simply knowing that I felt the sacredness of the moment is enough. I can hold it gently, honour it and cherish it. This matters particularly to me because sharing stories is such a part of my life. I write these letters. I have written books about my own journey. I host The Sincerely Show, where people choose to share beautiful acts of service and contribution, and often the difficult, painful and awakening journeys that brought them there. What makes those conversations meaningful is that the stories are offered. The guest decides what they want to share and why. Together we try to create a space that feels safe, loving, curious, kind and free of judgement. There is something sacred about being trusted with another human being’s truth, and about allowing them to remain the steward of that truth. All of this has caused me to look at myself honestly too. What causes me to want to share something? Sometimes it is love. Sometimes it is genuine excitement about an insight or a lesson that feels important. Sometimes it is the hope that another person might feel less alone or see their own life differently because of something I have experienced. And sometimes ego speaks. A desire to be seen, to be appreciated, perhaps even a little insecurity seeking affirmation. The awareness of all of those possibilities has made me more interested in the space between desire and action. That brief space where something deeper can speak. Where I can ask myself whether what I am about to do honours the person I am trying to become, the relationship I have with another person, and the trust and care that exists between us. What has surprised me is how that one reflection has opened something much larger over the course of this week. I began noticing sacredness everywhere. Yesterday afternoon, a friend stopped by the farm with her family and friends while they were visiting Prince Edward County. We first came into one another’s lives through the Catalyst Awards, and over time that connection became a friendship I deeply cherish. There was no agenda to the visit. She simply chose to come by, spend a little time together and say hello. I was touched that she had chosen to stop by. Earlier, four women I went to public school and high school with had driven five hours to Prince Edward County to visit me and attend an event where I was speaking. I felt deeply humbled by their visit. A couple of them I had not seen in almost forty years, and one I have known for more than fifty-five. What struck me was how quickly the years disappeared. It was as though no time had passed. We walked the farm together, sharing memories from childhood and adolescence, laughing about joyful moments and talking about some of the very difficult ones too. We had tears for people who have died. So much had happened in each of our lives since those early years, yet the familiarity was still there, as though no time had passed. They chose to drive five hours simply to be together again. I have been thinking about what a gift that is. Later that day, I experienced sacredness in a completely different way. A group of friends and I participated in the Pumpkinfest parade here in Prince Edward County. Our float was inspired by The Ballad of Peter Pumpkinhead, a song that has already found its way into another Sincerely Letter. I got to be Farmer Katie, driving the tractor while my friends rode behind me dancing and wearing their papier-mâché pumpkin heads. It had been at least forty-five years since I had been in a parade. For more than an hour, we drove through the village of Wellington, which seems to explode with life every year for Pumpkinfest. Pumpkins weighing close to two thousand pounds are entered in the competition. Families line the streets. Music is playing. Children are waving. People are laughing and cheering. We played Peter Pumpkinhead and danced our way along the route. It was pure joy. The planning had been joyful too. These are friends who have adopted me since I moved to Prince Edward County. We imagined the float together, created it together, laughed together, and then had the wonderfully ridiculous experience of driving and dancing through the village wearing giant pumpkin heads. It reminded me that sacredness can be playful too. It can be laughter and music and a tractor moving slowly through a little village while friends wave at strangers and, for a little while, everyone seems simply delighted to be alive together. Then three of my four children came home for our belated Thanksgiving. I love Thanksgiving and Christmas because they bring people we love together. What began as our family dinner grew to include three families. Biological family and chosen family gathered around the same table, sharing food, gratitude, stories, laughter and love. Food has always been one of the ways I show love. Preparing a Thanksgiving meal, gathering people around the table and watching different parts of my life come together carries such meaning for me. I felt so grateful to have my biological family and chosen family gathered around the same table. Over the course of this week, I began to see sacredness in so many different places. In an intimate conversation between two people. In a friendship that has travelled across fifty-five years. In people who enter our lives much later and somehow become family. In a Thanksgiving dinner. In the joy of a village parade. In the simple act of someone deciding to stop by because they care. It can be present in grief, in joy, in vulnerability, in belonging and in love. Here at the farm, I feel it in the living world around me too. In the old oak trees, Joey and Maggie. In the flowers and the bees. In the birds moving through the land. In the changing light across the inland sea. In the gardens giving their final gifts before winter. In the quiet awareness that this land existed long before I arrived and will continue long after I am gone. I do not own any of it in the deepest sense. I get to witness it and care for it for a while. Perhaps stewardship is part of sacredness too. Recognising that something has worth beyond what it can give us, and allowing that recognition to change the way we care for it. I think the same may be true of one another. The more I have contemplated all of this, the more I wonder whether sacredness has less to do with making something extraordinary and more to do with recognising what is already extraordinary. Life. Another human being. Trust, spoken and unspoken. Friendship and love. A tree, a flower, a bee, a bird. A table surrounded by people we care about. Honouring those we love who have died. A moment of complete vulnerability. A rare morning of complete joy. We live in a time when sharing has become easier than ever. So much can be captured, posted, reproduced and amplified, and emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence are causing me to think even more deeply about what it means to be human. I keep returning to love, care, compassion, empathy, curiosity, intuition, respect and this deeper moral knowing. That quiet place within us that recognises another person, their life and their story as sacred before our own desires begin to take precedence. The part of us that feels the significance of another person’s vulnerability and knows that some things can be shared while others deserve to be protected and honoured quietly within the connection itself. I’m beginning to think sacredness is not simply something we experience. Perhaps it changes something in us. It can make us more present to what matters, more grateful for what we have been given, and more careful with what has been entrusted to us. It can remind us to make time for the people we love, to show up, to gather, to play, to care for the land and to honour another person’s story as their own. Sometimes sharing something beautiful can be an extraordinary gift. Sometimes the most loving and beautiful thing we can do is hold it quietly within our hearts. The moment that began this contemplation is still private. An intimate moment I hold with love, honour and respect. I have shared what it awakened in me, but not what another person entrusted to me. Perhaps that is part of the answer I have been looking for. Some moments are sacred because we share them. Others remain sacred because we choose not to. I think both can be profound expressions of love. Perhaps that is what I have been discovering this week. Sacredness is reverence. Reverence for life itself.
letter-is-this-me.html: On a recent Friday evening at Decanter, my friend Karen Palmer was sitting at her typewriter, writing poems for the people gathered there. It was one of the final weeks of this special place as we know it. MJ and Angie have fostered and nurtured such a loving community here in Prince Edward County, and these Friday gatherings have become a cherished part of our lives. Karen calls her typewriter Olive. She’s an Olivetti, and Decanter was the first place Olive made her debut. And here they were again, Karen and Olive, in one of the final weeks of Decanter as we know it. There is something magical about watching them together. You give Karen a word, and she sits down at Olive and begins, spontaneous and in flow, channelling her poetic gifts from somewhere deep within, from an emptiness beyond what we can imagine or see. A short while later, she brings you your poem. Then she reads it to you, and the tears flow. The word I gave her was sincerely. Is this me? Such a small question, with so much within it. I love that our sense of self can whisper on some days and roar on others, and that the practice is to listen. With so much around us trying to shape who we are, I wonder how often we pause long enough to hear ourselves. And how often we recognise something of our soul in what we feel drawn to create and share. Karen has given so much of herself to promoting Prince Edward County and shining a light on the people who make it what it is: the artisans, the winemakers, the painters, the antique shop owners, the people behind our bed-and-breakfasts, our shops and businesses. Bringing them to the world, and bringing the world to them. She is also the author of Spellbound: Inside West Africa’s Witch Camps. And here she is, at her typewriter, sharing another of her gifts. MJ and Angie have brought their gifts into our lives through Decanter, through the warmth and hospitality they offer and the friendships they have nurtured. MJ shares her gifts through yoga too, and I am so touched that she has offered to bring her practice to Maison Millefleurs. We will miss Decanter as we know it, and we are looking forward to the new ways they will share their gifts with the County and beyond. We are such multilayered, multifaceted human beings. How beautiful it is when we slow down enough to observe, to witness, to be curious about all the facets of another person. And of ourselves. We may know someone through their work, through one part of their life, and there is still so much more to discover. I think again of Karen and Olive, in this gathering that MJ and Angie have brought into being. A poem about listening to the soul, offered in a place where so many people have shared something of their own. Thank you, Karen, for the gift of this sincerely poem and for your friendship. And thank you, MJ and Angie, for all the love you have brought into our lives.
letter-an-exchange-of-love.html: This week, I had the honour of joining my friend Susan’s book club at her cottage north of Toronto. What a beautiful group of women. Susan had invited me to also join them for a sleepover too, at a place my family and I once called home.Her cottage is our old cottage, where my former partner and I raised our four children and shared more than twenty years of family life. The lake, the road, the neighbours and the cottage were all part of a place of safety, of love, of belonging. Returning brought back so many memories. The games and the dance parties, the movie nights, the meals, the gatherings with friends, the time on the lake and the countless adventures we shared. There were no tears, only warmth. Such a beautiful chapter in my life and in the lives of my family. Susan and I have become good friends, and it means so much to see the love she and her family have for this cottage and this lake. To witness how a place that brought our family together is now doing the same for theirs. They also hold such care and respect for our history here, for the years when we were the stewards of this beautiful place. There is something deeply moving about being welcomed back into a home where you have shared so much love, and being able to experience the love that another family is bringing to it. We sat in the gazebo, exploring the many questions that had emerged as the women read Sincerely, Katherine. We talked about my life, the love and patience of my family and friends, and the fear and courage that can accompany following our hearts. That deeper calling that seems to come from our soul, from our essence, towards the fullness of who we are. What inspires us? What ignites our heart and soul? And what happens in our lives and our relationships when we begin to listen? We spoke about the anxieties and hurts that can come with facing our fears, and about the different ways people accompany us through life. Some relationships are brief, yet leave us with an experience or a lesson that stays. Others last for a season, helping us learn and grow. And some last a lifetime, moving through their own seasons, their own periods of change and renewal. After the gazebo and sunset over the lake, we returned to the cottage for a beautiful meal at the dining room table, where my family and friends once sat. More memories came flooding back, including a sing-along with my brother-in-law George, my friend Dawn and my dear friend Al, may he rest in peace. How much we had shared around that table. And here I was, gathered around it again, sharing a meal and creating new memories with friends. Later, we moved into the living room by the fire, and Patricia started the dance party. Just like old times. The kind of dance party where the group slowly thins out as the evening carries on. Some make an Irish exit, while others give everyone a hug before leaving. And then there are those who carry on into the wee hours of the morning, moving from dancing to a hypercompetitive ping-pong tournament in the garage. Over breakfast the following morning, we continued the conversations we had begun in the gazebo and replayed the antics of the night before. The deeper questions and the fun of being together, carrying on into another day. Beyond beautiful. It is such an honour to experience how Sincerely, Katherine. speaks to women and men, to people from so many walks of life, well beyond the LGBT community. This was my hope in sharing my story, and it is my hope in sharing the stories of the guests on The Sincerely Show. That in spending time with another person’s life, we might feel seen in our own. That we might feel less alone, find hope, and discover something that brings meaning or possibility to our journey. There is so much we can explore when we give one another the space, the care and the curiosity to do so. A question about someone else’s life can bring us closer to something within ourselves. Something we long for, something that inspires us, something we have been afraid to follow. And perhaps, in hearing how another person found their way, we begin to find a little more courage for our own. Fear is not the place to stop. Fear is the place to be curious. To observe what is happening within us, to listen for that deeper calling, and to explore the possibility of growing towards a fuller expression of ourselves. I hope these conversations offer some of that possibility, some sense of the love and freedom that can come as we find our own way. I look forward to seeing this group again, and to the next opportunity to gather with people who want to explore these deeper questions. There is such a gift in being curious about one another, in receiving another person’s story and allowing it to touch our own. And there was so much of that gift in this visit. The love Susan and her family have for the cottage and for one another. Their respect for our family’s history, and my joy in witnessing theirs unfold. The questions in the gazebo, the memories around the table, the dancing and the morning after. This exchange of love, of care, of curiosity, this feeling of being seen by one another, is one of the most special gifts I think we can receive. Thank you, Susan, for the gift of your friendship, and for welcoming me home to your home, the place my family and I once called ours. So much love and so much respect.
letter-we-love-and-live-on-a-life-lived-: A tribute to Cindy Clark of team Sincerely and her son, the late Corey Clark, September 26th, 1992 – December 29th, 2007. Earlier this spring, Cindy Clark reached out to me. She had heard about my book and Sincerely and wondered if there was a way she could help. She was drawn to the mission of Sincerely. Cindy and I had worked for RBC, Canada’s largest bank, for several decades, our careers crossing paths many times. Whenever I held a round table or a town hall and Cindy was there, I felt her warmth. There was a kindness in her presence, an optimism and curiosity that she brought into the room. I always felt her desire to bring something good to the lives of others. To help unlock the gifts, the talents in others. Like me, Cindy had left RBC to create another chapter in her life. We had both lived and worked in different places across this part of Canada, and here we were, our paths crossing again in Prince Edward County. When we reconnected over coffee, I felt that same loving, passionate energy. A call to serve, a desire to care and to give. As we talked, Cindy shared with me the story of her son, Corey. September 26th marks the day Corey would have turned 36 years old. Unfortunately he passed away at the age of 17. He had lived with osteosarcoma, an aggressive form of bone cancer, for four years. It was the same incredibly painful cancer that Terry Fox battled. Cindy told me about the work she and Corey had done with healers to help him endure his pain and rise above it, quite literally. She also told me that, while still a teenager, he had written his own eulogy. So young, and so thoughtful, thinking so deeply about life and what he wanted to leave with and for others. In a piece she wrote about Corey, Cindy describes his wish to inspire or help at least one person in his lifetime. At seventeen, he had begun journalling about what he was learning, hoping others might learn from it, too. She shares his own words about those four years: “There’s a whole bunch of details I could get in to but I don’t feel like writing it. Just to give you an idea about what I’ve been through, I have a lot of metal in me, I have six really long scars, and I know for sure I hate hospital food. Over the past 4 years I’ve had some of the worst days of my life and I’ve had some of the best days in my life. I’ve also learned a lot about life!” It’s special and inspiring to be able to hear his humour in those words. And his honesty about the life he was living, with its worst days and its best days. Cindy speaks of his belief in a positive attitude, in treating people with kindness and respect, and in learning someone’s story before judging them. Her memories let us see how he lived those beliefs. She remembers a woman who approached the family at a fundraiser and told them that Corey used to buy her pizza when she was hungry. An intern at the hospital shared how they had learned to cast because Corey let them put casts on all his fingers as he lay in bed after surgery. Cindy also shares the story of the boat he chose as his Children’s Wish Foundation gift, so that he could share good times with his friends. A bridge he used to take them to now honours his memory. There was such generosity in the way he wanted others to experience life with him. And then there is this memory from his best friend’s wedding, on August 22nd, 2025, eighteen years after Corey had made his request. In Cindy’s own words: “I was honoured to dance with his best friend at his wedding, a request Corey had made years earlier because he wanted me to have that experience as the mother of the groom.” I find myself sitting in tears with this dance. Corey had imagined something for his mother, and years later she stepped into it. His best friend had held that wish and made it part of his own wedding. There is such tenderness in the way love can reach forward into a life, and be there to meet us. Cindy shares that he “wanted to ensure that his legacy was not one of sickness but one of his amazing life.” Through these stories, I am getting to know something of that life, and of the extraordinary mother and family who love him. When we met for coffee, Cindy also told me about an encounter she had after Corey’s passing. She was driving north of home when an eagle or a hawk came alongside her car, flying at window height. It stayed beside her for what felt like an eternity. In the depth of her being, Cindy knew this was Corey coming to see her, letting her know he would always be with her. She has experienced many other remarkable moments like this, each reminding her of Corey’s spirit and his presence in her life. As she shares: “His spirit is all around of us all of the time and we are so truly blessed to have him in our lives and incredibly proud.” I find myself sitting with what it means to remain with one another. Cindy and Corey’s relationship continues to unfold. And now, through Cindy, I am coming to know him, too. His words are finding me. His wish to help someone is finding another expression through this letter. Perhaps this is what I am beginning to feel in the words we love and live on. Through the love Cindy shares, Corey’s life becomes part of another life. There is still something being given and received. It is an honour to have Cindy as part of team Sincerely, bringing the warmth and care I have felt in her presence for so many years. I welcome Corey’s spirit and presence as part of our team and mission, too, with the lessons and energy he shares directly and through his mother. Cindy, thank you for sharing your beautiful son with us, and for all that you bring of yourself. We love and live on. Corey, a life lived sincerely.
The hibiscus flowers are blooming in the garden, and the roses are beginning to flower again too. They are so beautiful. The depth of colour, the detail within each flower. I find myself pausing to witness them and appreciate the creativity and care that have made this beautiful garden. And when I walk through the meadows, I experience a beauty that moves me deeply, in a different way. Every few weeks, something new is flowering. There are purple asters and goldenrod now, and countless other flowers whose names I am still learning. They arrive as a surprise, a gift, each with an elegance of their own, each offering something to the meadow, and beyond. Tall purple thistles have emerged in the meadow this year. A lot of them. Their flowers are now giving way to soft white seed heads. I am seeing many more monarch butterflies here this year than last. Sometimes there are a dozen at a time around the patches of thistles, feeding on their flowers. So beautiful. Awe. Watching them together, I feel a harmony and a love between these lives that is hard to put into words. A love song. Prince Edward County is an important stopping place on their migration to Mexico. At Prince Edward Point, thousands of monarchs feed and rest in late summer and early autumn before continuing south. Thistle flowers provide nectar for that journey. Watching the butterflies in my own meadow, I feel a deeper appreciation for what this land and these flowers are offering. I watch the bees through the many seasons of flowers, moving from the lavender to the Russian sage, and on and on. As one flowering gives way to another, life continues to find its way to what is opening. Day by day, week by week, month by month, there is an ongoing melody of beauty and creativity playing out around me. It is magic to watch these lives dance, each in its own way and together, in their profound beauty. As a child on the farm, I was taught to dislike the thistles and burdock bushes. We were taught to cut the thistles down. And at the same time, my parents, with their deep Eastern European roots, also carried an appreciation for what nature gifts us. There was wild mint. My father made cream from calendula flowers. He collected stinging nettles and made nettle tea. My parents also made and drank Swedish bitters from German wild herbs as part of their health routine. Alongside what we were taught to remove, there was a knowing about what nature offered and how to receive its beauty. Now I am standing among the thistles I was taught to cut down, feeling awe. I see their colour and form, and the life moving between them. I find myself wondering how much beauty I have walked past, perhaps because I had already decided what I was looking at or where I needed to go. I still feel a profound appreciation for human creativity and talent. I love making things with my own hands, and a garden can be a beautiful expression of that creativity and love. Yet I also see how much we shape life around an image we carry of what it should look like and what it should be. We choose what belongs and what we will remove. I wonder where the pleasure of creating becomes a need to control, and how much our ego influences what we are willing to call beautiful. In the meadow, I feel a different relationship with creation. I am witnessing a beauty that has emerged through nature and the divine, with a life and a rhythm of its own. Each flower expresses what it is, and each life is part of a melody larger than itself. As I slow down, I feel part of that melody too. There is a line in A Course in Miracles that speaks to what I am experiencing: “The smallest leaf becomes a thing of wonder.” I have been thinking about unconditional love, and witnessing and reflecting on what feels like unconditional beauty. A beauty that belongs to life before I decide what to make of it. The thistle is already fully itself. Its beauty does not begin with my appreciation, or with what it offers the monarch. Something changes in me when I give myself space to receive it. Through The Sincerely Show, and through the people I meet in daily life, I experience something similar. As I slow down, listen to someone’s story and feel something of their essence and soul, I am moved by their authentic beauty. Their story opens a way for me to see them more fully. I feel such an honour in being allowed to witness another human being in this way. I wonder how much of life I have seen through ideas I inherited about what was beautiful, what was desirable, what belonged. And how much those same ideas have shaped the way I have seen other people and myself. What becomes visible when I give another person room to reveal themselves, and give myself room to see? I feel a new appreciation for what we discover when we offer ourselves that same space, that same curiosity and love. Space to hear what is true within us, beneath the expectations we have carried and the ways we have learned to measure life and ourselves. As I have come to understand and love more of my own essence, I seem more able to recognise and appreciate the beauty in others, throughout creation. This is what I am beginning to understand as unconditional beauty. The beauty that lies within each of us and throughout creation, becoming visible as we loosen our expectations and allow ourselves to see. When I walk the meadow now, I feel a profound honour in being here, in witnessing this life and feeling myself part of it. The melody continues, and I get to sing and dance with it.
letter-lessons-of-peter-pumpkinhead.html: I’m amazed by how music speaks to us. For so long, I thought I had some unique challenge in hearing the words of a song. I’ve since learned that many people experience music this way, through feeling and emotion, without fully comprehending the words… that’s my experience. I’m always amazed by people who can hear a song for the first time and then sing along. For me, the feeling and sense of meaning often arrive long before I understand what the actual words are saying. A group of us are preparing a float for the annual Pumpkinfest parade in Wellington, here in Prince Edward County. I’ve been asked to drive my orange tractor, pulling the hay wagon my friend Jo gifted to me and the farm. Our theme song is The Ballad of Peter Pumpkinhead. I’ve always loved Crash Test Dummies… their voices and folk-like lyrics. P.S. I can sing the low and high parts, lol. When the song came up, I started listening to it again and again. It kept speaking to me. Finally, I said to myself, I have to understand the meaning of this song. And then, as often happens, its words and its meaning spoke to me so deeply. The song was written by Andy Partridge and first released by XTC in 1992. In describing its beginnings, Partridge wondered what would happen to someone whose way of living encouraged people to be more humane, generous and loving, and why that person might threaten those in power. I picture Peter as this quirky, redheaded, kind and humble person. Someone who loves openly and gives what he can. His generosity and honesty draw people to him, while some of those in power feel challenged and turn against him. There is also Peter’s acceptance of love, something so simple and generous, even as others try to disgrace him. Peter Pumpkinhead put to shame Governments who would slur his name Plots and sex scandals failed outright Peter merely said Any kind of love is alright Yet the refrain keeps returning to the enemies he makes. But he made too many enemies Of the people who would keep us on our knees Hooray for Peter Pumpkin Who’ll pray for Peter Pumpkinhead? Understanding the story brought me into a deeper reflection on the world we’ve created, the world we live in, and on my own life. Peter’s humility, generosity and love are so beautiful. I find myself wondering how someone comes to live so authentically from that place. What allows us to remain open to one another, to share what we have, and to see another person’s dignity even when their life is different from our own? And why can that way of being, which holds so much possibility and truth for us, also be met with fear? I think about our desire to care for one another, and the ways fear can keep us protecting what we know or believe to be true. I wonder how often we recognise that tension within ourselves. The moments when we feel moved to reach towards someone, yet hesitate or don’t. The times when something unfamiliar asks us to look again at what we believe. How much of our free will is impaired by fear and bias and power? Peter’s story leaves me thinking about what we might discover if we could stay kind and curious a little longer, present and open a little longer. I think, too, about the people who have so generously shared their life stories with me through The Sincerely Show and beyond. People who have dedicated their lives to service and contribution. Most have experienced profoundly shaking, life-altering periods or moments. As I listen, I find myself wondering about the love that sustained them, the people who helped them, and how their experiences have shaped what they now offer the world. So many have shared with me how they would not wish their journey on another, how they feel spared, and how they have emerged more open, present, loving, kind and curious. More like Peter. Over the past several days, I’ve been bringing this research together into frameworks for my advisory, speaking and teaching work. Spending time with these stories, I continue to discover things I hadn’t understood when I first heard them. I’m grateful for the space to listen, to allow my understanding to develop, and to consider how I might share what I’m learning. Then comes the final verse. Peter Pumpkinhead was too good Had him nailed to a chunk of wood He died grinning on live TV Hanging there he looked a lot like you And an awful lot like me! I keep returning to this verse. The cruelty of what happens to Peter, and then the recognition of ourselves in him. It brings me back to the Peters in our lives, the people whose way of being reminds us of what is possible and deeply true within us. People we can honour and learn from, whose kindness, humility, courage and contribution stay with us. Perhaps honouring them includes bringing more of ourselves to one another. Sharing what we have learned, what we can offer, and the love we carry. As we prepare for the parade and the pumpkins continue to grow, I’m still listening. I’m amazed that a song chosen for our float has brought me deeper into all of this, and grateful that I have the space to be. Grateful for all of you!! Thank you, Peter Pumpkinhead!
letter-never-alone.html: I grew up on my parents’ farm outside St. Marys, Ontario, Canada. My sister Sandra died shortly after birth. My older sister, Mona, was four years ahead of me, and my younger sister, Becky, four years behind. I had one good friend who lived a short walk from our farm, but much of my childhood was spent alone. And I loved it. My mother called me Snoopy because I was endlessly curious. Apparently, even as a very young child, I managed to climb out of my crib and begin exploring every corner of the house. One day, I climbed onto a chair, then onto the kitchen table, reached high up to a shelf and took down our transistor radio. I carefully took it apart because I wanted to find the man inside. As you can imagine, I was deeply disappointed when he wasn’t there. As I grew older, my world expanded beyond the farmhouse. I explored the trees and hedgerows surrounding the farm and every corner of the big old red hip-roof barn. I wondered about what had happened there before me and imagined the lives it had held. Eventually, I ventured farther, across the fields to the forest about five hundred yards behind our farm. There was a creek where I caught tadpoles, frogs and minnows. Nearby were the ruins of an old fieldstone farmhouse, where I searched among broken pieces of glass and dishes and wondered who had once lived there. When I was ten, after travelling to Germany with my father, I would take my sleigh into that forest in winter. I had bought a pair of binoculars in Germany and somehow lost them on one of those adventures. For years afterward, I kept searching for them, convinced that perhaps I had hidden them somewhere in the rafters or between the joists of the basement in my parents’ farmhouse. I built things, too. In the upper level of the barn, I created my own farm. Dried corn cobs became fences, while my toy tractors and trucks travelled through the fields, laneways and pathways I constructed in my imagination. Over time, I built three or four clubhouses among the tree lines, using pieces of old barns and whatever materials remained from sheds my father had built. I made clothes for Barbie dolls out of Kleenex, imagining and creating with whatever happened to be around me. Looking back now, I realise how much that imaginary world resembled the life I would eventually create. Those clubhouses became, in some way, the family cottage where my children and I would spend almost thirty years. The little farm I built from corn cobs became the farm where I live today. The fields, pathways, gardens and places I created in my imagination somehow found their way into the life I would build decades later. The child wandering through those fields, tending an imaginary world and wondering what might be around the next corner is still here. I recognise her when I walk through my gardens and the lavender, watch the bees or make something with my hands. I recognise her, too, when I find myself imagining what might yet become possible. The forms have changed, but something essential has remained: curiosity, reflection, imagination, dreaming and the desire to create. Perhaps Sincerely is another expression of exactly the same thing. It makes me wonder sometimes: What is the next incarnation of this lifetime? A life seems to contain many lives. We create worlds, inhabit them, love them and sometimes leave them behind. Yet something essential travels with us from one into the next. The clubhouse disappears, but the builder remains. The cottage eventually becomes a memory, but the love that filled it remains. A corporate life ends, yet the curiosity about people, leadership, humanity and what allows us to flourish continues. The child is still here. At an early age, my earliest spiritual questions emerged during those long periods of wandering and wondering. I remember thinking about humanity. I wondered about Jesus and the Second Coming. I tried to imagine God. Was God actually a being somewhere, a man looking down upon us? Was God the creator? Or was God perhaps an energy, a force, something moving through everything? In some ways, I was doing exactly what I had done with the transistor radio. I wanted to know what was inside. I wanted to understand where the voice came from, what animated things and what was behind what I could see. I didn’t have the language or maturity then to understand what I was reaching toward. I simply knew there was something to wonder about. Today, I experience this creative force that some call God as something profoundly loving, beautiful and alive. I experience it within us and around us, moving through nature, relationship, imagination and creation itself. Perhaps the mystery was never something hidden somewhere inside life waiting to be found. Perhaps it was life itself. Perhaps the curiosity, imagination, desire to create, impulse to love and longing to understand are themselves expressions of that creative force. And perhaps that is why these childhood memories have returned to me now. As we grow older, we learn many things about separation. We learn belonging and exclusion, approval and rejection, success and failure. We learn to judge difference and sometimes to fear it. Through absence, hurt, disappointment and the ordinary imperfections of human relationships, we can also begin to associate being alone with being unloved. Our parents, doing the best they know how, leave and return. They become tired or anxious. They carry responsibilities, frustrations and hurts of their own. We experience these things as children before we have the language to understand them. Somewhere within us, a fear can begin to form that love may leave. Over time, being alone can begin to feel very different from the spaciousness we once knew. It can become loneliness. Beneath that loneliness can be an even deeper fear of separation, the fear that perhaps we are not loved, or that somehow we are not loveable. Yet when I return in memory to that little child wandering around an eight-acre farm outside St. Marys, I don’t remember being lonely. I remember being alive, curious, wondering, creating and dreaming. Perhaps the child knew something I would spend much of my adult life forgetting, and am only now remembering. There were periods of my adult life when I lost touch with that knowing. Through divorce, as my children grew and began building lives of their own, and eventually as I stepped away from a corporate world that had surrounded me with people, purpose and responsibility for almost four decades, I experienced loneliness. There were times when I feared being alone. When so many of the structures through which I had experienced relationship and belonging changed, the quiet could feel like absence. Beneath the loneliness was a fear of separation. A fear of failing or being rejected. Beneath that was something even more vulnerable: the fear that perhaps, without all of those relationships surrounding me, I might somehow be less loveable. Curiously, it was time alone that began to change this. With more space, I began spending time with myself differently. I became curious about my feelings and emotions rather than trying to move through them or beyond them. I began listening to what they were telling me, understanding where they came from and allowing myself to experience them. Time with self became a relationship too. Gradually, I began to experience something I had spent much of my life seeking and receiving through relationship with others: love within myself. It did not diminish my desire for companionship, intimacy, friendship or family. It allowed me to experience those relationships without needing them to prove that I was worthy of love. And as my relationship with myself changed, I began to see and feel connection everywhere around me. Perhaps what I am experiencing now is a return to something the child already knew. My children are grown and building lives of their own. There is more quiet in my days now, more time for curiosity, creativity, contemplation and expression. Increasingly, I find myself at peace in my own company. There is something beautiful about rediscovering the parts of ourselves that existed before the world told us who and how we were supposed to be. I see that child in myself again when I wander around the farm without needing to be anywhere. I see her when I lose track of time in the garden, imagine what might grow somewhere or make something with my hands. And I see her when a question enters my mind and I follow it simply because I want to know where it might lead. I see her in Sincerely too. The questions are larger now, but perhaps the impulse is exactly the same. What does it mean to be human? What allows us to flourish? What is love? What is consciousness? What happens when we stop trying to become who the world tells us to be and begin remembering who we already are? The little child dismantling the radio to find the man inside has simply moved on to different questions. When I walk outside today, apparently alone, I notice how quickly the idea of aloneness begins to dissolve. I spend time with Joey and Maggie, two extraordinary and magnificent old oak trees whose lives began long before mine and whose presence I experience in different but equally profound ways. I walk through the lavender and hear thousands of bees moving from flower to flower. Butterflies drift through the gardens and birds call from the trees. Beyond them, Lake Ontario, the inland sea, stretches toward the horizon, infinity and beyond. Life is everywhere. My friends and neighbours are just down the road. I see them when I walk and on Friday evenings when I find myself at Decanter sharing a glass of wine and conversation. My children may no longer live with me, but they remain deeply woven into my life. And those who have left this physical life are still with us. My parents, my ancestors, and friends like Ben and Richard who have passed remain present in another way. Their souls are with us. Their love remains. Physical presence changes, but love and relationship do not simply disappear. The more present and attentive I become, the more deeply I feel my connection to the life around me. I feel it in the land and the water, in Joey and Maggie, and in the bees, butterflies and birds. I feel it in my children, family, friends and neighbours, and in those whose souls remain with us. And I feel it in the creative and loving force I spent so much of my childhood trying to understand. Perhaps this is what time alone has given me: not an escape from relationship, but a deeper understanding of it. In the quiet, I have learned to listen to myself, to understand my emotions and to love myself more deeply. From that place, I have come to recognise how profoundly connected I have always been. The child wandering those fields understood something before she had words for it. She belonged to the land she wandered through, to the worlds she imagined, to the questions she carried, to the people she loved and to the creative force moving through her. And so do I. The creative force that moved through that little child building farms from corn cobs and making clothes for Barbie dolls is still moving through me today. The loving force I once searched for somewhere outside myself is within me and around me. The forms change. Our children grow. The worlds we build evolve. The people and places we love may no longer be part of our everyday lives, and some we love leave this physical life. Yet their souls remain with us. Love remains. Through all of it, we remain in relationship with one another, with the natural world, with those who came before us and with the loving and creative force that moves through all of life. Perhaps this is what I am remembering. We were never separate. I have never been alone.
